articles.title: Beer, wine or liquor? Massive study reveals which was linked to lower death risk
articles.excerpt:
Addiction expert Jessica Steinman discusses a recent study comparing mortality risks of various types of alcohol, and why wine’s potential health benefits should be interpreted cautiously.

Heavy drin...
articles.body_text:
Addiction expert Jessica Steinman discusses a recent study comparing mortality risks of various types of alcohol, and why wine’s potential health benefits should be interpreted cautiously.

Heavy drinking has been shown to raise mortality risk — but at lower levels, what’s in your glass may also matter, a new study suggests.

In recent research of data from 340,924 participants in the UK Biobank, wine was linked to lower mortality, while beer and spirits were tied to higher death risk.

Data were collected between 2006 and 2022, with more than 13 years of average follow-up. The findings were presented at the American College of Cardiology’s Annual Scientific Session in New Orleans, Louisiana.

WINE EXPERT SAYS ONE COMMON HABIT COULD BE SABOTAGING EVERY SIP

In the study, participants reported their alcohol intake as never/occasional, low, moderate or high.

High consumption was defined as >40 grams per day for men (about three standard drinks) and >20 grams per day for women (about 1.4 standard drinks).

Heavy drinking has been shown to raise mortality risk — but at lower levels, what’s in your glass may also matter, a new study suggests. (iStock)

Participants with high alcohol consumption had a 24% higher risk of all-cause death, 36% higher risk of cancer death and 14% higher risk of cardiovascular death when compared to people who never or occasionally drank, according to the study findings.

With low or moderate alcohol consumption, however, the mortality risk appeared to differ according to the type of beverage.

AMERICA HITS MAJOR MARIJUANA MILESTONE AS DAILY WEED USE SURPASSES DAILY DRINKING

Spirits, beer and cider were associated with significantly higher mortality, the researchers found, while the same amount of wine intake was linked to significantly lower mortality. Moderate wine drinkers had a 21% lower risk of cardiovascular death than those who never or occasionally drank.

Conversely, those who drank low amounts of spirits, beer or cider were found to have a 9% higher risk of cardiovascular death.

In new research of data from 340,924 participants in the UK Biobank, wine was linked to lower mortality, while beer and spirits were tied to higher death risk. (iStock)

"These results come from the general population, and in certain high-risk groups, such as people with chronic diseases or cardiovascular conditions, the risks could be even higher," said Zhangling Chen, M.D., Ph.D., a professor at the Second Xiangya Hospital, Central South University in China and the study's senior author, in a press release.

"These findings can help refine guidance, emphasizing that the health risks of alcohol depend not only on the amount of alcohol consumed, but also on the type of beverage."

"Not everybody should have daily consumption of an alcoholic substance, whether it's wine, beer or certain liquors."

One potential reason for wine’s lower mortality association could be that it contains compounds such as polyphenols and antioxidants, which could have beneficial effects on blood vessels, inflammation and cardiovascular health, the researchers noted.

Jessica Steinman, a Los Angeles addiction specialist and chief clinical officer for No Matter What Recovery, said the study’s information is "helpful," but cautioned against broadly applying the findings to individuals, particularly those with a history of substance misuse.

HOME COCKTAIL MAKER SAYS GEN Z ISN'T GIVING UP ALCOHOL — THEY'RE CHANGING HOW THEY DRINK

While certain ingredients or substances might help someone with a very specific issue, she expressed her concern when it comes to mental health issues and addiction.

"When we hear these stories or get this research, it becomes a ‘black and white’ larger generalization for the population, and we want to be careful with that," Steinman, who was not involved in the research, told Fox News Digital.

Different substances have different levels of alcohol in them, and each person metabolizes alcohol differently, the expert noted. (iStock)

"Not everybody should have daily consumption of an alcoholic substance, whether it's wine, beer or certain liquors … if there's someone who’s struggling with substances, then they really shouldn't be having it at all."

Different substances have different levels of alcohol in them, and each person metabolizes alcohol uniquely, the expert noted.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"All those kinds of things are so specific to one person or a small sect of people," she said. "So we want to make sure anytime there's research given about something, that we're not taking it as a society and saying, ‘Let's do this,’ and not keeping it as black and white."

"Overall, more is not better, but also the higher potency of alcohol and higher percentages of alcohol is going to affect people negatively as well."

Steinman recommended consulting with a medical professional for individual guidance.

There was the chance that wine drinkers may have different dietary or other lifestyle habits that could impact their health outcomes, the researchers noted. (iStock)

The researchers acknowleged some limitations of the study. As it was observational in design, the study could not prove that drinking wine led to lower mortality or that other alcoholic beverages directly caused higher mortality.

Also, the participants reported their baseline alcohol intake at the start of the study, which means any changes in drinking patterns during the follow-up period were not recorded.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

There was also the chance that wine drinkers may have different dietary or other lifestyle habits that could impact their health outcomes, the researchers noted.

The UK Biobank participants also tend to be healthier than the overall population, which could limit the ability for the finding to be generalized to wider populations.

The authors called for high-quality randomized studies to confirm the impact of differences in drinking habits reflect on mortality risk.

Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

articles.title: 'Look at me!' Justice fires back at critics who dare question his Blackness
articles.excerpt: Clarence Thomas shared during a discussion with Peter Robinson hosted by the Hoover Institute that people have questioned his political beliefs because he is Black. (Credit: YouTube/Hoover Institution...
articles.body_text:
Clarence Thomas shared during a discussion with Peter Robinson hosted by the Hoover Institute that people have questioned his political beliefs because he is Black. (Credit: YouTube/Hoover Institution - Aug. 11)

Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas said his views on race and politics have led critics to question his Blackness.

"I mean, how stupid is that? Look at me," Thomas said, grabbing his arm. "You know, then they say things like, ‘Oh, black is a state of mind.’"

Thomas made the remarks during a Hoover Institution conversation with Peter Robinson that included a discussion about the role of Black Americans in politics. The conservative justice reflected on how economist Thomas Sowell, a Black conservative, helped transform his thinking on race and politics and gave him the confidence to challenge prevailing expectations about Black Americans' political views.

CLARENCE THOMAS WARNS AMERICA: LIBERTY DIES WHEN WE CHOOSE COMFORT OVER COURAGE

U.S. Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas speaks during a special lecture celebrating the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence at Hogg Memorial Auditorium at the University of Texas on Wednesday, April 15, 2026. (Jay Janner/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images))

Thomas said that as a young man, he felt pressure to embrace certain political beliefs because he was Black and faced resistance when he began questioning them.

"You have these views, you have these instincts, but you are getting inputs from the media, from the politicians, the people who have the megaphone, the people who have the loudest voices, that tells you you’re wrong, that tells you you’re bad, that there’s something awful about you," Thomas said.

While at Yale Law School, Thomas said he bucked the push for school busing, questioning why Black families would want their children sent across town to unfamiliar schools and neighborhoods.

"I remember saying those things at Yale and people — the bottom line was, well, you shouldn’t believe that because you’re black," Thomas said.

KEY TRUMP AGENCY PUTS TOP UNIVERSITIES IN CROSSHAIRS OVER ALLEGED RACE-BASED DORM PROGRAMS

Thomas argued there was often a disconnect between positions championed by Black political leaders and the views of ordinary Black Americans, pointing to debates over school busing and racial preferences.

"If you ask the leaders, they thought one thing. If you ask the people, they thought another," Thomas said.

It was Sowell’s work, Thomas said, that helped him make sense of views he had already begun developing on his own.

A friend introduced Thomas to Sowell’s Race and Economics, which Thomas said helped free him from the isolation he had felt over his own views.

THE WELFARE STATE BROKE BLACK FAMILIES. WORK CAN HELP RESTORE THE DREAM

Economist Thomas Sowell unleashed on the current state of the U.S. education system, arguing it is keeping students and families trapped in a cycle of failure. (Fox News)

"It was literally like a drink of water," Thomas said. "Here’s someone who’s thought it through and it makes sense. What your instincts were have been now demonstrated in a logical, analytical way. You’re not alone." He later sought out a friendship with Sowell.

But Thomas had not always embraced Sowell’s ideas.

As a Yale student in 1972, Thomas said he "reflexively" rejected Sowell’s Black Education: Myths and Tragedies, believing that "no black man" should think that way.

Thomas said Sowell’s example helped give him the confidence to voice his own beliefs even when doing so brought criticism.

THOMAS LEAVES NOTHING LEFT UNSAID ON RACIAL GERRYMANDERING DECISION: ‘GO FURTHER’

"If they can prove you wrong, fine," Thomas said. "But if they call you names or say you’re not black, I mean, how stupid is that? Look at me."

He tied those attacks to what he described as a broader pressure on Black Americans to conform to certain views.

"There’s this overriding public view that you’re not supposed to think this way, therefore you’re not black, therefore you’re discredited," Thomas said. "Nothing you say matters."

The U.S. Supreme Court as seen on February 20, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Heather Diehl/Getty Images)

But for Thomas, the biggest lesson he took from Sowell was to think for himself.

"He always says what he thinks, but he never tells you to say what he wants you to think," Thomas said of Sowell. "That is yours."

"There seems to be this overwhelming pressure for us to agree with the prevailing notions which I consider almost illusory in a sense," Thomas said.

Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

articles.title: Scramble for Karoline Leavitt's replacement ensues with just weeks until Trump's spokesperson exits
articles.excerpt: Former Trump campaign deputy communications director Caroline Sunshine and independent journalist Lyndsay Keith discuss Karoline Leavitt’s departure as White House press secretary on ‘Fox News @ Night...
articles.body_text:
Former Trump campaign deputy communications director Caroline Sunshine and independent journalist Lyndsay Keith discuss Karoline Leavitt’s departure as White House press secretary on ‘Fox News @ Night.’

The impending departure of President Donald Trump's top spokeswoman has speculation swirling in Washington, D.C., on who will be selected to replace Karoline Leavitt behind the press briefing room podium.

The 28-year-old White House Press Secretary, fresh off maternity leave, dropped a bombshell announcement on Wednesday that she will end her tenure at the end of August to spend more time with her two young children.

Now, with just two weeks left in the month, the race is on to find the next press secretary — and some predict the briefing room will see a rotating line of Trump administration officials briefing the White House press corps rather than a permanent replacement, like what happened during Leavitt's maternity leave earlier this summer.

WHITE HOUSE PLANS GUEST HOSTS FOR PRESS BRIEFINGS WHILE KAROLINE LEAVITT TAKES MATERNITY LEAVE

President Donald Trump and White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt stop to speak to the media as Trump departs on Marine One on the South Lawn of the White House on Feb. 27, 2026 in Washington, DC. (Heather Diehl/Getty Images)

Secretary of State Marco Rubio held the first news conference while Leavitt was on leave, followed by Vice President JD Vance, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz.

"The next press secretary will undoubtedly be someone who has a strong existing relationship with President Trump," former Trump Press Secretary Sean Spicer told Fox News Digital.

"He values and understands the importance of this role in communicating his positions on policy, personnel and key issues so I can’t imagine it not being someone currently in his orbit," Spicer added.

Spicer, known for his very short tenure as White House Press Secretary, withdrew his name for consideration a second time around.

Alina Habba, who serves as senior advisor to the Attorney General for U.S. Attorneys, was viewed as a frontrunner after Trump won re-election and is once again being floated for the role.

TRUMP SAYS KAROLINE LEAVITT WILL LEAVE WHITE HOUSE PRESS SECRETARY ROLE, BECOME OUTSIDE ADVISOR

President Donald Trump, accompanied by White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, speaks to reporters as he departs the White House, on July 15, 2025 (AP)

At the time, Habba said she was "flattered" by the consideration but believed she would "be better served in other capacities."

She then served three months as Counselor to the President before leaving Washington, D.C. for a very controversial and turbulent position as interim Attorney for the District of New Jersey. After her appointment was deemed unconstitutional, she resigned and was made Senior Advisor to the Attorney General for United States Attorneys.

Habba, who was Trump's personal attorney and a high-profile surrogate on the 2024 campaign trail, was the early favorite on Kalshi to replace the press secretary, but now ranks third behind conservative political commentator Scott Jennings and Leavitt's deputy Anna Kelly.

Trump's Principal Deputy Press Secretary has been seen in an outward facing role. Kelly filled in for Leavitt in media hits while she was on maternity leave, but has yet to take the podium for a briefing.

Jennings, a CNN contributor and former aide to President George W. Bush, was also reportedly considered for the press secretary role when Trump retook office in 2024 before he selected Leavitt. Trump has touted Jennings’ recent book and has referred to him as a "patriot" who "gets it."

TRUMP’S DC LAW-AND-ORDER BLITZ MARKS ONE YEAR WITH EYE-POPPING HAUL OF SUSPECTS

Trump's senior advisor Stephen Miller and his wife, Katie Miller, have been floated on social media as potential replacements.

Stephen was asked Wednesday for his thoughts on his wife, former Vice President Mike Pence press secretary and communications director, filling Leavitt’s role. In lieu of commenting, he shot a smile in the direction of the questioner.

White House communication director Stephen Cheung is one of Trump’s most forceful defenders, wielding significant influence but largely operating behind the scenes.

Stephen Miller, White House deputy chief of staff, and his wife, Katie Miller, an aide for DOGE, attend the White House Easter Egg Roll on Monday, April 21, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Other names floated as potential contenders include Breitbart's Washington Bureau Chief Matthew Boyle and former White House deputy chief of staff Taylor Budowich.

Leavitt is Trump’s second-longest-serving press secretary, with 19 months in the role. She comes in second to first-term Press Secretary and now Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders’ 23-month tenure.

After Huckabee's departure, Stephanie Grisham stepped into the role for nine months, but was famous for not holding a single press briefing during that time. She was eventually replaced with Kayleigh McEnany who served through the end of Trump's first term.

Ashley J. DiMella reports on politics for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Top Republican says El-Sayed may be 'full-blown communist' despite socialist denial
articles.excerpt:
House GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain spoke with Fox News Digital about the midterm match-ups in her home state of Michigan.

Michigan’s highest-ranking House Republican is crying foul on Abdul El-S...
articles.body_text:
House GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain spoke with Fox News Digital about the midterm match-ups in her home state of Michigan.

Michigan’s highest-ranking House Republican is crying foul on Abdul El-Sayed's claim that he is not a socialist.

"If it looks like a duck and walks like a duck and quacks like a duck, it's a duck," House GOP Conference Chairwoman Lisa McClain, R-Mich., told Fox News Digital. "So maybe he's not a socialist. Maybe he's a full-blown communist."

El-Sayed, a former public health official, scored an upset victory for Democrats' leftmost flank in Michigan's Senate primary earlier this month. He defeated Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., a House lawmaker who was heavily favored by the Democratic establishment, including Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y.

It was part of a larger wave of victories by candidates aligned with the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), several of whom have toppled sitting House Democratic lawmakers in primaries in New York and Colorado in addition to Michigan.

2026 MIDTERMS STATE OF PLAY: KEY RACES UNFOLD AS STEVENS, EL-SAYED BATTLE IN MICHIGAN

House GOP Conference Chair Lisa McClain accused Dr. Abdul El-Sayed of having communist ideals. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc. via Getty Images; Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

And while El-Sayed himself is not a DSA member, some of the biggest names to campaign alongside him — including Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich. — are self-proclaimed democratic socialists.

El-Sayed told CBS News in an interview posted to YouTube last week that he was working on building a broad coalition that included supporters of President Donald Trump as well as DSA members, even though he is neither.

"Folks who come here, like, with two weeks left in the election, really, really want to label me a socialist. I don't know why, except for maybe it fits into a nice telling of a broader national story. But I'm a scientist, right? And I like solutions that solve problems," El-Sayed said. "I don't do ideology. I'd rather think of myself as a capitalist who actually read about capitalism, in the sense that the biggest risk to capitalism was always going to be corporate consolidation and monopoly, rather than government regulation."

McClain, meanwhile, argued that El-Sayed's platform is inherently socialist.

"He wants to take money out of your pockets. He wants free everything. Well, at the end of the day, if everything is free, someone has to pay for it," McClain said. "Are the farmers not gonna get paid? Are the teachers not going to get paid? He wants higher taxes, and he wants to take money out of your pockets so you can pay for your neighbors. To me, that's socialism. That's borderline communism."

MICHIGAN SENATE CANDIDATE ABDUL EL-SAYED DODGES QUESTION ON WHETHER HE STILL SUPPORTS DEFUNDING THE POLICE

El-Sayed's policy platform includes promises to fight for Medicare for all, raising taxes on millionaires and billionaires, using "wage insurance and basic income" programs to counter artificial intelligence automating industries, and abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), according to his website.

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., join hands following a campaign rally on July 18, 2026, in Detroit. (Jose Juarez/AP Photo)

Republicans have argued that the majority of policies supported by the progressive and socialist left will amount to higher taxes for everyday Americans. But Democrats have insisted that their plans will lead to more affordable living for working- and middle-class people.

Traditionally, the party in power in the White House tends to lose seats in Congress during the midterms. That, combined with low approval numbers for President Donald Trump, means Republicans have an uphill battle to buck past political trends to keep control of the House and Senate.

But McClain pointed out that El-Sayed failed to clinch an outright majority in Michigan Democrats' Senate primary and predicted it would mean Republicans running up and down the ballot in the Wolverine State will see big gains with the far-left progressive at the top of the ticket.

BIDEN-WORLD VETERAN ISSUES STARK WARNING ABOUT ABDUL EL-SAYED AS HE CROSSES PARTY LINES

"I think it's gonna help us tremendously, right? Because if you look at El-Sayed's numbers, 50%, over 50% — the majority didn't vote for him. So what are those voters gonna do?" McClain posed. "How is El-Sayed and his crazy progressive, socialist, communist party going to bring those Democratic voters over to the Democratic side of the ticket? I don't think they are. I think those voters are going to look for a common-sense candidate, and I think those voters are either going to one, stay home or two, vote for Mike Rogers."

Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers speaks before then-Republican vice presidential nominee Sen. JD Vance, R-Ohio, arrives during a campaign rally at FIM Capitol Theatre, Nov. 4, 2024, in Flint, Mich. (Paul Sancya/AP Photo)

Mike Rogers, a former House Republican and FBI agent, is the Republican nominee in Michigan.

He made an appeal to Democrats days after the matchup became official, stating in a video, "If you're among the majority of Democratic voters that woke up on Wednesday feeling, well, hopeless, because the person who won does not represent your values, well, just know, there is still hope."

Fox News Digital reached out to El-Sayed's campaign for comment.

Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

Follow on Twitter at @liz_elkind and send tips to elizabeth.elkind@fox.com

articles.title: Europe swelters in latest wave of extreme heat
articles.excerpt:
Millions of people across Europe, including in France, Italy, Spain and the United Kingdom are sweltering through another wave of extreme temperatures as the continent’s latest heatwave intensifies.

...
articles.body_text:
Millions of people across Europe, including in France, Italy, Spain and the United Kingdom are sweltering through another wave of extreme temperatures as the continent’s latest heatwave intensifies.

Weather agencies recorded temperatures of above 35C (95F) in several European countries on Thursday, where more than 135 million people had been forecast to endure more scorching weather.

The UK recorded its hottest day of the year as the temperature in west London soared to 38.1C (100.5F), surpassing the previous high of 38C (100.4F) in June.

Europe is the planet’s fastest-warming continent and in some places, is ill-equipped to deal with hot weather.

A series of heatwaves and drought have fuelled a summer of wildfires and been linked to thousands of deaths so far.

Scientists blame ever hotter and more frequent heatwaves on climate change caused by human activity.

In Britain, nurses have collapsed from heat exhaustion while working in hospitals that lack adequate cooling, the Royal College of Nursing said on Thursday.

“The heat has been unbearable here, honestly,” pharmacist Bailey Williamson told the AFP news agency. Patients in hospital were also hard-hit, said NHS worker Williamson.

“People in beds are really, really sick and they can’t even breathe because of the heat problem – so it’s really bad.”

Hospitals had recorded an increase in heatstroke cases and the NHS was struggling to keep up, he added.

“It’s scary, it’s scary,” Williamson said of the summer’s heatwaves. “I think it’s a real sign about how bad climate change has really got.”

The France Meteo weather service recorded 38C (100.4F) in Paris and much of the country has been put on heatwave alert.

Similar temperatures were forecast to affect 29 million Italians, particularly along the west coast, in the Po Valley, the “heel” of the boot of Italy, as well as on the islands.

Large parts of the Iberian Peninsula were also likely to be affected, including some 25 million people in Spain.

Spain’s Aemet weather agency recorded temperatures as high as 37C (98.6F) in the centre of the country on Thursday.

articles.title: Carrick urges Manchester United to sign more transfers to boost title bid
articles.excerpt:
Manchester United coach Michael Carrick has urged his club to splash the cash to keep pace with their Premier League title rivals.

United have spent about 85 million pounds ($114m) on Andrey Santos, ...
articles.body_text:
Manchester United coach Michael Carrick has urged his club to splash the cash to keep pace with their Premier League title rivals.

United have spent about 85 million pounds ($114m) on Andrey Santos, Youri Tielemans and Karl Darlow since the end of last season.

But that outlay pales in comparison to some of United’s fellow title contenders, with Manchester City, Arsenal and Chelsea all paying huge fees for high-profile signings.

Carrick knows United need more quality and depth if they are to challenge for a first English title since 2013, while also competing in the Champions League.

Remarkably, United have never spent more than 89.5 million pounds ($120.7m) on a single player – the fee paid for Paul Pogba in 2016.

And in advance of his first season as permanent United boss after a successful interim spell last term, Carrick called on the club’s hierarchy to push for more new recruits.

“I think we’ve done really good business and we’ve got really some top, top, top players,” Carrick told reporters on Thursday.

“We’re delighted with that. We always want to improve. We want more, we need more, we keep looking for how we can do that. That never stops.”

Carrick led United to a third-place finish in the Premier League after he replaced the sacked Ruben Amorim.

But with United so far spending less than promoted sides Coventry and Ipswich, some fans are becoming restless as their Premier League opener at Hull on August 22 looms into view.

“Money’s money, I get that. It’s still about the football, and that’s where the competition lies,” Carrick said.

“Certainly, the situation is what it is as well, whether that’s finances or whatever. For now, we’ve got to make the most of it, but we’ve got to keep pushing and push everything and every boundary that we can to be able to win again.”

Asked why United were not spending on the level of other clubs, Carrick added, “To be honest, I haven’t got the answers for that. We’re working with pushing everything that we can to make the best of it.”

Having spent last season on loan with Barcelona, Marcus Rashford is back at United this week after returning from the World Cup.

Barcelona declined their option to buy the 28-year-old England forward, and questions remain over his United future.

“He’s our player, and he’s a good player, and he gives us something a little bit different in the group,” he said.

“Marcus can offer us so much. He has done, and he can do again, so in that respect it’s quite exciting.”

Several United players have backed the team to dethrone Arsenal as champions, and the understated Carrick would not rule out a title push.

“We’ve definitely got the potential to achieve something really special,” he said.

“I’m not hiding from the fact, and we should aim to do that, but I can’t give you a definite answer on that.

“It’s certainly what we’re pushing to do because we have to, because that’s the club we are.”

articles.title: Police seize cocaine bricks with stickers of Norwegian soccer star Erling Haaland all over them
articles.excerpt: Anti-narcotics agents in Ecuador seize just over 1,000 pounds of cocaine bricks bearing stickers of Norwegian soccer star Erling Haaland from a false bottom in a truck bed (Credit: Ecuador National Po...
articles.body_text:
Anti-narcotics agents in Ecuador seize just over 1,000 pounds of cocaine bricks bearing stickers of Norwegian soccer star Erling Haaland from a false bottom in a truck bed (Credit: Ecuador National Police/AP Newsroom).

Norwegian soccer star Erling Haaland was already a big star, seeing as he plays for Manchester City in the Premier League, but his profile rose even more thanks to a strong World Cup showing and the way he embraced American culture.

You'd think that would be enough to say, "Yeah, this dude has made it," but I think a more recent incident is proof that he has "made it."

Is anyone really a global superstar until their face winds up plastered all over a seized shipment of cocaine somewhere in South America?

Police in Ecuador uncovered just over 1,000 pounds of cocaine, all of it plastered with stickers of Norwegian soccer star Erling Haaland. (Ecuador National Police via AP)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

But Erling Haaland has hit the big times after police in Ecuador seized over a thousand pounds of packaged cocaine that had stickers with his face on it.

The 370 packages of Haaland-faced booger sugar were found in the false bottom of a truck that anti-narcotics agents pulled over on the Pan-American Highway.

According to The New York Post, the driver of the vehicle carrying the drugs was arrested (probably a good call), but he didn't explain why Haaland's mug had been plastered all over his shipment.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON’T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Anti-narcotics agents haul bricks of cocaine out of a truck bed's false-bottom. (Ecuador National Police via AP)

However, it is known that criminal organizations slap the famous names and visages of celebrities and athletes on their "stuff" as a way of making it known which criminal network it came from and who the client is.

Also, maybe they do it so they have something else aside from drugs to talk about. If they hand someone a brick of cocaine with an R2-D2 sticker on it, they could be like, "Hey, what did you think of the sequel trilogy? It sucked, right?"

Hey, it can't just be all drug talk all the time. Even these guys have to have interests outside of work.

Criminal networks have been known to use names and images of celebrities and athletes to mark shipments. (Ecuador National Police via AP)

So being deemed famous enough to be on an illicit drug shipment? That's big.

Haaland is not the only World Cup star to get the drug-packaging treatment. Argentine captain and global superstar Lionel Messi has also wound up on packaging.

articles.title: Several homes ablaze as firefighters try to contain West Midlands grassfire
articles.excerpt:
About 60 crew responding to blaze covering about 16 hectares near Stourbridge golf course

Several homes were ablaze and two people were receiving treatment as firefighters attempted to contain a gras...
articles.body_text:
About 60 crew responding to blaze covering about 16 hectares near Stourbridge golf course

Several homes were ablaze and two people were receiving treatment as firefighters attempted to contain a grassfire in the West Midlands on Thursday.

The region’s fire service was alerted to an extensive grassfire near Stourbridge golf course just before 1.30pm on Thursday.

About 60 firefighters were responding to the blaze covering about 16 hectares (40 acres).

“Some local rail services have been stopped for safety reasons,” a fire service spokesperson said.

Images released by the fire service showed the fire spreading into nearby woodland and homes.

The fire service spokesperson said two people had been affected by heat and smoke, but did not give details about their condition.

Six homes were directly affected by the blaze, and others in the area reported power problems.

Stourbridge town hall was opened up to receive those forced to leave their homes.

“Transport is also being arranged for those who can’t make their own way,” West Midlands fire service said in a social media post.

“If you must drive, take extra care if you are driving, avoid areas of dense smoke and please don’t head to areas where fires are taking place to watch.”

Care home residents have also been evacuated as a result of the fire, a local councillor, Andrew Southall, said.

The UK recorded its hottest day of the year on Thursday, with the Met Office giving a provisional reading of 38.1C (100.6F) at Kew Gardens in west London.

Forty locations across central and southern England recorded temperatures of 36C or above.

articles.title: Judge nixes Trump lawsuit alleging Harvard did not protect Jewish students
articles.excerpt:
A federal judge in the United States has thrown out a lawsuit filed by the administration of US President Donald Trump claiming Harvard University did not do enough to protect Jewish students.

The le...
articles.body_text:
A federal judge in the United States has thrown out a lawsuit filed by the administration of US President Donald Trump claiming Harvard University did not do enough to protect Jewish students.

The legal filing was one of many actions taken by the Trump administration in response to how top universities responded to pro-Gaza protests amid Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza.

The administration has repeatedly claimed administrators did not adequately protect students against anti-Jewish actions during the demonstrations.

Protest organisers have long rejected the premise, saying the administration has willfully conflated criticism of Israel with anti-Semitism while using isolated anti-Jewish actions to justify crackdowns on pro-Palestinian speech.

The lawsuit filed in March by the Department of Justice charged that Harvard’s “faculty and leadership turned a blind eye to antisemitism and discrimination against Jews and Israelis”.

It said Harvard’s actions were not in compliance with Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which bans discrimination ‌based on race, colour and national origin in programmes that receive federal funding.

But Judge Richard Stearns said on Thursday the Trump administration’s lawsuit had ‌not shown evidence of the claimed violation.

Stearns said the incidents highlighted in the legal filing were “too isolated and episodic” to support the claim of ongoing civil rights violations.

Trump had previously moved to freeze $2.2bn in federal funding to Harvard, in what the university’s lawyers have called an effort to leverage research money in exchange for allowing the administration to “micromanage” the institution.

A federal judge last year ruled that the freeze was unlawful.

Harvard, which has an endowment valued at more than $56bn, has stood apart from other top universities for its defiant approach to the administration.

Several others, including Columbia University, Northwestern University, and Cornell University, chose to reach multimillion-dollar settlements with the Trump administration to preserve funding in response to a series of allegations, including their response to pro-Palestine protests, as well as hiring and admissions practices.

Critics have noted the emphasis on anti-Semitism comes as the administration has used immigration enforcement to crack down on pro-Palestine advocates.

In July, Columbia University protest leader Mahmoud Khalil, who has been targeted for deportation, in part, for his involvement in the demonstrations, filed a civil rights lawsuit alleging a “public-private” partnership to silence pro-Palestine voices.

The lawsuit pointed to the conservative Heritage Foundation’s “Project Esther” report, which appears to have laid out a blueprint similar to the Trump administration’s approach. The lawsuit further alleges the Trump administration has relied on outside groups, including the Canary Mission and Betar, to identify student and faculty members to target.

A November 2025 report published by the American Association of University Professors accused the Trump administration of weaponising civil rights law to stifle free speech on college campuses.

It noted that “while reprehensible acts of antisemitism have occurred on campuses” since 2023, the association’s analysis found the majority of federal civil rights complaints came not from students, but from “people and organisations who have no relationship with the schools under investigation”.

“A longstanding ‘Palestine exception’ to the First Amendment now threatens to give way to a new reality,” the report said.

“Palestine is less an exception to academic freedom than it is a pretext for erasing the norm altogether, as part of an authoritarian assault on the autonomy of higher education and on the very idea of racial and gender equity.”

articles.title: Poland arrests Russian allegedly hired to kill Ukrainian-American who was 'inconvenient to the Putin regime'
articles.excerpt:
Assassination attempts, car bombings and alleged spy plots put drone bosses in the crosshairs in Ukraine war, expert says.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk revealed Thursday that his country arreste...
articles.body_text:
Assassination attempts, car bombings and alleged spy plots put drone bosses in the crosshairs in Ukraine war, expert says.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk revealed Thursday that his country arrested a Russian man hired by Moscow to kill a Ukrainian-American citizen who was "inconvenient to the Putin regime."

Tusk said the suspect was taken into custody Friday, with the alleged target being a man in Poland’s capital of Warsaw, according to a report from Reuters.

"Thanks to the truly brilliant action of our services ... we detained a Russian citizen recruited by Russian intelligence services," Tusk was quoted saying, adding that the target held both Ukrainian ‌and ⁠U.S. passports. "At the last minute, thanks to the action of the Internal Security Agency and the police, we managed to ⁠prevent this execution, this attack."

Fox News Digital has reached out to the State Department for comment.

MOSCOW, KYIV ASSASSINS HUNT WEAPONS BOSSES AS UKRAINE WAR SPILLS BEYOND THE BATTLEFIELD

FILE - Russian President Vladimir Putin chairs a meeting aboard the missile cruiser Varyag in Russia's far eastern Sakhalin region on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. Putin previously said Russia is not waging a sabotage campaign against Europe. (Reuters)

Tusk also said Thursday that it was the first time that "someone on the order of Russia" sought to attack an American citizen on the territory of another NATO country, The Associated Press reported.

The operation was carried out in cooperation with U.S. services, Tomasz Siemoniak, Poland’s minister overseeing intelligence services, told the AP.

The news agency reported that it has mapped about 200 acts of sabotage, arson and other disruption across Europe since the start of the Ukraine war that officials have linked to Russia. President Vladimir Putin claimed to the AP in May that Russia is not waging a sabotage campaign against Europe.

RUSSIA LINKED TO ARSON ATTACKS ON PROPERTIES CONNECTED TO UK PM KEIR STARMER, POLICE SAY

FILE - Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk speaks to the media at the site where an unidentified flying object, believed to be a Russian missile, fell after violating Polish airspace in a field near Tarnawa Kolonia, near Lublin, Poland, on July 30, 2026. (Jakub Orzechowski/Agencja Wyborcza.pl/Reuters)

In June, a Russian artist who was critical of Putin was shot and killed at close range near his home in eastern Poland. Tusk said at the time that the killing had the hallmarks of a political assassination. He suggested it was possible Russia was behind it, but Polish officials have not yet attributed it to Moscow.

Last year, French officials disrupted a plot which they believe was aimed at killing Vladimir Osechkin, a Russian exile who lives under police protection and works to help military defectors flee Putin’s war.

Lithuanian officials also disrupted a plot last year to kill a Lithuanian supporter of Ukraine and another against a Russian activist.

FILE - Tusk said the alleged target was a citizen in Warsaw, Poland. (dpa/picture alliance via Getty Images)

Officials in Germany have similarly broken up two plots: one to target the head of a German weapons company supplying Ukraine, the other against a Ukrainian military official.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Greg Norman is a reporter at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Little League World Series coach divides fans with his 'Jesus' message during mound visit
articles.excerpt:
Little League players find success on the field after their coach implements a strict no-phone policy before games.

An Arizona baseball coach sent the internet into a tizzy this week when he gave his...
articles.body_text:
Little League players find success on the field after their coach implements a strict no-phone policy before games.

An Arizona baseball coach sent the internet into a tizzy this week when he gave his pitcher a sermon on the mound during a Little League World Series regional game.

Drew Breivogel went viral Wednesday night when an ESPN hot mic caught his faith-filled message to his pitcher in the fourth inning. With the game hanging in the balance and two runners on, Breivogel called time, walked to the mound and gave his player some simple advice to help calm the nerves.

Fans watch from the hill overlooking Lamade Stadium during Day 2 of the Little League World Series on Friday, Aug. 21, 2015, in Williamsport, Pa. (MLB via Getty Images)

"I'm so proud of you," he said. "I've known you since you were eight. Remember Zacchaeus in the Bible? Someone planted that tree, 30, 40 years prior, so he could climb up into it. Salvation. We're talking salvation. It's a baseball game, right?

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

"If you walk the next five guys Jesus is still Lord. If you strike out the next five guys, guess what? Jesus is still Lord. I love you. Have some fun."

Nothing like a little church on a Wednesday night! Brings me back to my childhood.

Social media, shockingly, was all over the place on this video. Some loved the message. Others were confused by it, given it didn't include any real strategy on how to work out of the jam.

Nothing about mechanics, or 'buckling down,' or throwing strikes, or hitting spots.

A quick check of the box score says that Hawaii would score four runs in the inning en route to a 5-2 win to stave off elimination. Not great.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Garrett Gallegos #19 of the Mountain Region from Las Vegas, Nevada reacts before the sixth inning against the Asia-Pacific Region team from Taoyuan City, Chinese Taipei during the 2025 Little League World Series Championship at Howard J. Lamade Stadium on Aug. 24, 2025, in South Williamsport, Pa. (Getty Images)

"How about a scouting report?" one fan commented on the now-viral video. "Some advice about mechanics? Something that may actually help the kid learn baseball? If I was the pitcher I would of pushed my coach away."

"If I’m struggling on the mound on national tv and my coach comes up to me and starts this BS instead of advice or mechanical changes, I’m quitting," added another.

Said a third: "Then the next 3 hitters reached base safely because there was no gameplan instilled during the mound visit. This was a coach using TV to make himself look good he knew he was Mic’d up, that was his BIG moment."

All fair points. But it's also Little League. A big spot? Absolutely. But these are 12-year-old kids. How much of a scouting report do they really have on them? Little League baseball is the Wild Wild West. I grew up in. I've seen it all. I've heard it all. Admittedly, I was never part of a mound meeting quite like that.

So, again, I see both sides here. That little sermon did remind me of a great quote my old Little League coach used to tell us when we were nervous before a game:

"If you strike out, there are a billion people in China who won't care tomorrow."

Makes sense. Made us feel a little better.

But, we also never got close to reaching Williamsport or the Little League World Series.

So perhaps we could've used a different approach.

articles.title: Government could pay higher rents to spread asylum accommodation across UK
articles.excerpt:
Greater use of private rental properties would form part of PM’s plan to spread accommodation more evenly across UK

Ministers are considering paying higher prices for housing asylum seekers in privat...
articles.body_text:
Greater use of private rental properties would form part of PM’s plan to spread accommodation more evenly across UK

Ministers are considering paying higher prices for housing asylum seekers in private rental properties as part of Andy Burnham’s plan to spread accommodation more evenly across the country.

The shift towards more private rental accommodation, known as “dispersal”, and the use of former military barracks, are cheaper than expensive hotels for asylum seekers.

However, officials believe it may be necessary to raise the strict caps on how much the Home Office can pay landlords in rent so that the accommodation is not concentrated heavily in the most deprived areas.

The move would fit with Andy Burnham’s plea this week for more areas to “play their part” in housing those seeking asylum, instead of accommodation most often falling in areas where rents are the cheapest.

A Downing Street source said the biggest priority was reducing the need for accommodation for people seeking asylum overall.

The policy of national responsibility for asylum seekers is broadly supported by refugee charities but they said local councils must take the lead and people should not be sent to places without sufficient means of supporting them.

Imran Hussain, director of external affairs at Refugee Council, said: “Ever since the policy of dispersing asylum seekers away from London and the south-east was introduced, we have been clear that supporting refugees should be a national responsibility and that people should not be sent to places without adequate housing, legal advice, support services or established refugee communities.

“That’s why local authorities should take the lead on asylum accommodation, using their local knowledge. Local councils should be given the powers and resources they need to provide people seeking asylum with housing, working with their local residents and also providing value for money to the taxpayer.”

He added: “Poor-quality decision-making by the Home Office is keeping a large number of people in the asylum system while they wait for the courts to overturn flawed decisions. The new government’s priority should be ensuring decisions are made quickly and are right the first time.”

Karen Bradley, the Conservative chair of parliament’s home affairs watchdog, pointed to her committee’s report which said “asylum accommodation has been heavily concentrated in areas with high levels of deprivation … that is where accommodation is cheapest and the old asylum contracts prioritised cost above ensuring a fair spread across the country”.

Some critics of the proposal to raise private rental payments for asylum accommodation said it would cost more but government sources said it was cheaper than using hotels, with the closures so far since the last Conservative administration having saved £1bn. They suggested the government’s aim was to ensure no single area carries a disproportionate burden, rather than decisions being driven solely by cost.

A government spokesperson said: “We are already working to fairly house asylum seekers across the entire country, working closely with local authorities and listening to local concerns to help reduce the impact on communities.

“The number of hotels in use has fallen from 213 in July 2024 to fewer than 160 today. Before the general election, hotel use peaked at 400 sites, costing £9m a day.

“The number of asylum seekers staying in hotels has fallen by 35% over the past year and is down 63% from the peak in 2023, while overall asylum support costs have fallen by £1bn since the general election.”

Joe Robertson, a Conservative MP on the Isle of Wight, told the Telegraph, which first reported the policy proposal, that Burnham “needs to choose locations which offer the most cost-effective accommodation in the best interest of taxpayers” and that “self-serving political choices which cost more would be wrong on every level”.

The policy of more “dispersal” of asylum accommodation was pursued under the last Conservative government by Robert Jenrick as immigration minister, now a Reform UK MP and finance spokesperson.

Marley Morris, a researcher on migration at the IPPR thinktank, pointed out on Thursday that Jenrick had pursued the policy to allow more equitable distribution of asylum seekers across the UK and also argued it would be cheaper. “This is because it helps to reduce use of hotels, which are far more expensive than dispersal accommodation,” Morris said.

articles.title: Nearly 100 children detained as adults under UK-France migration deal
articles.excerpt:
Figures emerge in critical letter to Home Office from organisation appointed to scrutinise detention facilities

Nearly 100 children have been wrongly identified and detained as adults under Shabana M...
articles.body_text:
Figures emerge in critical letter to Home Office from organisation appointed to scrutinise detention facilities

Nearly 100 children have been wrongly identified and detained as adults under Shabana Mahmood’s “one in, one out” deal with France, the Guardian can disclose.

Home Office staff said that of 304 age-disputed cases arising from the scheme over nine months, 94 (31%) – were ultimately found to be minors. Children are supposed to be excluded from the scheme, while government policy limits immigration detention of unaccompanied children to 24 hours.

The figures have emerged in a letter sent to the Home Office minister Anna Turley from Jane Leech, the interim chair of independent monitoring boards (IMBs), which scrutinise prisons and immigration detention facilities.

In the highly critical letter, Leech also said some people detained under the scheme:

Had been awaiting deportation for more than six months, despite being supposed be held for up to 28 days only “in exceptional cases”.

Were being readied for removal to France despite having TB or requiring hospital treatment.

Faced removal after being separated from family members with whom they had travelled, which she said had a “particularly damaging impact”.

The “one in, one out” initiative, launched last August, allows the UK to send somepeople who arrive by small boat back to France while agreeing to take the same number of people from France if they are judged to have a legitimate claim.

Leech said the deal was “placing highly vulnerable, newly arrived individuals, including children and survivors of abuse, in detention”.

In the letter to Turley, she wrote: “Your officials have informed the IMB that 304 age disputes have taken place between 15 August 2025 and 1 May 2026, of which 94 (31%) were assessed to be children.

“The IMB is therefore concerned that child safeguarding mechanisms are ineffective, and believes more should be done to ensure that those whose age is under dispute are not detained in the first place.”

Leech criticised the length of time it took for officials to complete age assessments. “In two cases observed by the Heathrow Board, it took 40 days or more from arrival at the IRC [immigration removal centre] to age assessment,” she wrote.

Referring to the deal as Operation Hillmore, its official name within the Home Office, Leech said she had “significant concerns” about the vulnerabilities of those detained under the scheme.

She wrote: “Many of those who have recently arrived present as psychologically distressed, and Boards have observed records and heard testimonies showing that many are survivors of torture and abuse.”

There was evidence of poor health screening at Manston among the Hillmore detainees, Leech wrote. “Gatwick IRC recently received one individual from Manston with tuberculosis, while a second was refused admission to Brook House because of the critical state of their health, and referred directly to hospital.”

She said people were being held for lengthy periods despite the scheme being intended to operate at pace, with one man detained for 27 weeks.

Government figures covering 4 August 2025 to 30 June 2026 show that 1,087 people were returned to France under the deal. During the same period, 27,920 people arrived in the UK on small boats.

Imran Hussain, the executive director of external affairs at the Refugee Council, described the figures as “disturbing” and said they were the latest example of children being wrongly treated as adults by the Home Office.

“Too often refugee children are being treated as adults and put into unsafe situations, at risk of abuse and neglect, and exposed to significant safeguarding risks,” he said.

“We call on the government to prioritise professional assessments led by trained social workers, which has been found to be the most accurate way to determine age and therefore avoid these risks.”

A Home Office spokesperson said: “Robust age assessments are essential to maintaining the integrity of our border and ensuring migrants receive appropriate safeguarding and access to services.

“We will continue to strengthen and modernise this process, including through the rollout of cutting-edge AI technology from next year to support age assessment.”

articles.title: Mystery surrounds Little League coach's ejection during championship game after ESPN cuts his mic
articles.excerpt:
Little League players find success on the field after their coach implements a strict no-phone policy before games.

Was this a quick trigger or was the Little League umpire well within his rights to ...
articles.body_text:
Little League players find success on the field after their coach implements a strict no-phone policy before games.

Was this a quick trigger or was the Little League umpire well within his rights to kick this coach out of the game?

During Wednesday's Great Lakes regional finals game, with a trip to the Little League World Series on the line, Team Kentucky assistant coach Matthew Teague was ejected by the home plate umpire.

Down 6-0 in the top of the 4th and running out of time for a comeback, Teague was seen meeting with one of his hitters and turning his attention to the umpire who had just called out a Kentucky hitter on a tough strike three call for the second out.

IDAHO TEEN UMPIRE DELIVERS ULTIMATE REALITY CHECK TO COACH COMPLAINING ABOUT WALK-UP MUSIC

"Oh boy, Matthew Teague has (been) ejected from the game," the ESPN announcer said while adding that the umpire warned Teague not to come closer to the batter's box.

Were there words exchanged between Teague and the umpire? If so, ESPN didn't let fans hear what was said. The network failed to play the audio from Teague, who was mic'd up.

According to Little League observers on Facebook, coaches "receive a blanket warning" at the start of tournaments that there is a zero tolerance policy on arguing with umpires. Add in the fact that coaches are mic'd up and it's extremely rare for a Little League coach to be ejected from the World Series or regional tournaments.

A general view before the game between Mountain Region and Metro Region at Howard J. Lamade Stadium in Williamsport, Pa., on Aug. 23, 2025. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

In the Little League rule book, Rule 9.02(b) states: If a manager believes a decision conflicts with the written rules (a misapplication of a rule, not a judgment call), the manager may request "Time." Once the home plate umpire grants time, the manager (and only the head manager) may approach the umpire who made the call to politely ask for clarification or appeal.

Based on the ejection, the umpire seems to have applied this exact rule to give Teague the boot. How did fans react online? About as you'd expect. It was a mixed bag of people arguing it was soft to kick the coach out of a meaningful game while others argued that Teague was foolish for thinking he could push the envelope.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

"They were down 6-0 was tossing him even worth it? No. Umpire try to show off....nothing more," one fan wrote on Facebook in support of Teague.

Meanwhile, on the opposite side, a fan took a shot at the coach and his shorts, writing, "Balls & Strikes arguments = zero and non-starter. Already warned- he can take his Ralph Lauren shorts to the BUS."

You get the idea. Emotions are high this time of year. We're talking about 12-year-old baseball, TV, glory and fame. Add it up and you have a powder keg of emotions just waiting to boil over.

Joe Kinsey is the Senior Director of Content of OutKick.

articles.title: Cruz sounds alarm over $400M Hamas-era provision in Board of Peace plan — issues blunt warning
articles.excerpt: Ret. Four-Star Gen. Jack Keane breaks down the next phase of President Donald Trump's Gaza peace deal on 'Fox & Friends.' Keane explains how the historic agreement mandates the complete disarmament of...
articles.body_text:
Ret. Four-Star Gen. Jack Keane breaks down the next phase of President Donald Trump's Gaza peace deal on 'Fox & Friends.' Keane explains how the historic agreement mandates the complete disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups, leading to the withdrawal of Israeli forces and the transition of power to a new Palestinian government.

U.S. officials have for years warned that Hamas has exploited ostensibly civilian and humanitarian funding streams to support its terrorist infrastructure, fueling concerns over whether money entering Gaza can be kept out of the terror group's hands as a new U.S.-backed governing structure prepares to take control.

The Treasury Department has repeatedly targeted what it describes as Hamas financing networks, including a secret investment portfolio, sham charities and organizations that raised money under the guise of humanitarian work while supporting Hamas' military wing.

Those concerns resurfaced this week after Israel's Kan News reported that a provision in the Board of Peace's Gaza roadmap could allow up to $400 million to address unpaid obligations accumulated during Hamas' rule, including money owed to public-sector workers, suppliers and contractors.

The dispute is over whether a successor government can settle legitimate obligations inherited from nearly two decades of Hamas rule without indirectly benefiting the terrorist group. Critics warn that doing so could relieve financial burdens associated with Hamas' rule or create opportunities for the group to siphon off resources while it retains influence on the ground. Board officials argue the mechanism is instead designed to allow a successor government to preserve essential services and relationships with legitimate workers and suppliers — with each claim individually vetted and any payment that could benefit Hamas rejected.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROBES UNRWA OVER ALLEGED EMPLOYMENT OF 1,500 TERRORISTS

U.S. President Donald Trump takes part in a charter announcement for his Board of Peace initiative aimed at resolving global conflicts, alongside the 56th annual World Economic Forum (WEF), in Davos, Switzerland, Jan. 22, 2026. (Jonathan Ernst/Reuters)

Nickolay Mladenov, the Board of Peace's high representative for Gaza, sharply rejected the characterization that the provision amounted to a financial agreement with Hamas.

"The claims that there is a financial agreement between the Board of Peace and Hamas are false," Mladenov wrote in Hebrew on X Wednesday, adding that no such proposal had been "discussed, negotiated, or considered." He said the Board's objective remained the complete disarmament of Hamas and the establishment of civilian governance backed by an international security presence.

Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, told Fox News Digital that he remained alarmed by the provision.

"I'm deeply concerned about these reports. Terrorists use money as fungible and they build credibility by having international donors finance their debts, which is why Congress long ago banned money from going to Palestinian governments in the West Bank," Cruz said.

"We also know that international donors paid for Hamas to build terrorist infrastructure across the Gaza Strip in the first place, and shouldn't be trusted to direct reimbursement money," Cruz continued. "Hamas should be utterly eradicated before new resources flow into Gaza."

HAMAS AGREES TO COMPLETE DISARMAMENT UNDER 'HISTORIC' GAZA AGREEMENT: TRUMP

Palestinian Hamas terrorists stand guard on the day of the handover of hostages held in Gaza since the deadly Oct. 7, 2023, attack, as part of a ceasefire and a hostages-prisoners swap deal between Hamas and Israel, in Rafah in the southern Gaza Strip, Feb. 22, 2025. (Hatem Khaled/File Photo/Reuters)

A senior Board of Peace official, speaking to Fox News Digital on background Thursday, pushed back on the premise that the roadmap commits $400 million to paying Hamas' debts.

"There's really just a commitment to analyze when we get the data. There's no commitment to fund anything. We don't have an obligation to even do $400 million," the official said.

The official described the provision as a three-year review process, capped at $400 million, under which the successor Gaza administration could determine whether particular unpaid obligations need to be resolved in order to maintain essential services and relationships with legitimate suppliers.

HILLARY CLINTON BREAKS WITH DEMOCRATIC CRITICS BY BACKING TRUMP’S GAZA PLAN AS THE 'ONLY GAME IN TOWN'

Palestinians shop at a crowded Eid al-Adha market in Gaza hours after Israel announced the killing of Mohammed Odeh, the newly appointed head of Hamas’ military wing, in an airstrike in Gaza. (Credit: Jusoor News)

"This notion that there's, like, a $400 million payoff vehicle, Hamas kind of has a commitment for it — none of that is true," the official said. "If anybody's gonna start running with a narrative that a $400 million committed tab is beginning now ... that would just be incorrect reporting. That's not the deal."

"No one's picking up a tab right now," the official added, saying any review would take place only after the new Gaza administration gains access to financial records allowing it to determine who the creditors are, what services they provided and whether those relationships are needed going forward.

"Even the first dollar of the $400 million, we're going to evaluate that first dollar," the official said. "It's not going to be a blank check handed to Hamas. It's going to be evaluated, rigorously analyzed."

The official compared the process to a corporate restructuring, arguing that while Hamas is being permanently removed from government, the successor administration cannot necessarily walk away from every legitimate obligation accumulated during the previous government's rule.

HAMAS SAYS IT WILL DISSOLVE GAZA GOVERNMENT, BUT ISRAEL WARNS GROUP STILL SEEKS HEZBOLLAH-STYLE CONTROL

Displaced Palestinians gather with pots and containers to receive hot meals distributed by charities ahead of iftar in Khan Yunis, Gaza Families, including children, wait in line amid difficult living conditions. (Abed Rahim Khatib/Anadolu via Getty Images)

He offered the example of a European pharmaceutical company that supplied medicine to Gaza hospitals but was never paid. If the new administration needs that company to continue supplying medicine, he said, resolving some of its unpaid invoices could be necessary to maintain the relationship.

"The theme here, really, is continuity of services," the official said.

The official did not say that Hamas would have to be fully disarmed across the entire Gaza Strip before the first claim could potentially be paid.

"The reality is that this is going to be community by community," the official said, explaining that the successor administration is expected to move into individual areas as Hamas disarms there.

IRAN REAFFIRMS SUPPORT FOR HAMAS AS TRUMP PUSHES TO DISARM TERROR GROUP

Al-Hayya, Hamas' longtime chief negotiator in indirect ceasefire and hostage talks with Israel, will now lead its political bureau. (LOUAI BESHARA / AFP) (Photo by LOUAI BESHARA/AFP via Getty Images))

Asked whether Hamas would have to be completely removed from Gaza before the new administration could resolve an outstanding liability — for example, involving a hospital in Rafah — the official said a payment could occur even if Hamas had not yet been fully removed elsewhere in the Strip.

"The idea is that where those decisions are made, Hamas is not gonna be there," he said.

When Fox News Digital asked specifically whether it was accurate to say money would not be transferred into areas where Hamas remained in control, the official said: "It's accurate to say."

The official acknowledged that more complicated cases could arise if the same supplier operates in both Hamas-free and Hamas-controlled portions of Gaza. Officials might then have to determine whether to reimburse only the portion associated with the area controlled by the successor government or negotiate some other arrangement necessary to maintain the service.

US URGES DONORS TO ABANDON UNRWA FUNDING AS UN DEFENDS AGENCY'S MISSION

Hamas terrorists stand guard on the day of the handover of hostages held in Gaza since the deadly October 7 2023 attack, as part of a ceasefire and a hostages-prisoners swap deal between Hamas and Israel, in Rafah in the southern Gaza Strip, Feb. 22, 2025. (Hatem Khaled/Reuters)

Cruz's central criticism is that money is fungible: if international donors satisfy obligations accumulated under Hamas rule, resources that might otherwise have been needed to cover those liabilities could theoretically be used elsewhere.

The Board official rejected that argument, saying Hamas is insolvent and was never going to pay many of the outstanding creditors in the first place.

"It's not as though we're alleviating them from, like, their budget that they actually were gonna actually go pay that $100 and now they get to save it," the official said.

"They were never paying it in the first place," he continued. "We're making a decision separate and apart from Hamas, whether this fits into our budget and our relationships."

HAMAS TAPS 'ULTIMATE INSTITUTIONAL SURVIVOR' AS TERROR CHIEF, SENDING MESSAGE TO ISRAEL: EXPERT

Hamas terrorists take security measures as preparations are completed at Nasser Hospital to welcome Gazans to be released under the ceasefire and hostage-prisoner exchange deal between Israel and Hamas in Khan Yunis, Gaza, on October 13, 2025. (Doaa Albaz/Anadolu via Getty Images)

The official described Hamas as "dead insolvent right now" and "financially, completely, completely in shambles."

Fox News Digital also pressed the official on a separate concern: even if money is never transferred directly to Hamas, could the group extract taxes, payments or other benefits from suppliers or employees receiving funds while it remains armed elsewhere?

"If there's a risk that some of the money is going to still end up in the hands of Hamas, then we're gonna shut it down," the official said.

He said officials would examine each recipient, the services provided and where the money ultimately would go.

"If Hamas is not fully disarmed ... can it end up in their hands? If the answer to that question is yes, then they're not gonna get money," he said. "Like, that is crystal clear."

The official also disclosed that the Board intends to try to recover assets it believes Hamas stole and use those assets, where possible, to satisfy legitimate obligations.

"We are going to make a real effort to go and try to recover those assets and use some of those assets, where we have found theft ... to satisfy some of these obligations," he said.

If recovered assets are insufficient, the official said outside funding would come from countries in the region rather than Washington.

Palestinians inspect the site of an overnight Israeli strike on a medicine warehouse, according to medics, next to tents sheltering displaced Palestinians, in Deir al-Balah, in the central Gaza Strip, August 1, 2026, residents had been pre-warned by the Israeli military to evacuate. (Mahmoud Issa/Reuters)

"This is coming from regional partners. This is not coming from the United States," he said.

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

articles.title: BAE Systems to pay $36m penalty after 104 violations of US arms export rules
articles.excerpt:
State department says it has reached administrative settlement with company’s US arm to resolve breaches

The UK defence company BAE Systems is to pay a $36m (£26.7m) civil penalty after breaching US ...
articles.body_text:
State department says it has reached administrative settlement with company’s US arm to resolve breaches

The UK defence company BAE Systems is to pay a $36m (£26.7m) civil penalty after breaching US arms exports regulations more than 100 times.

The US Department of State announced on Thursday that it had reached an administrative settlement with the US arm of BAE to resolve 104 violations of the Arms Export Control Act and the International Traffic in Arms Regulations.

The breaches included the unauthorised exports of technical data to multiple countries, including China, and violations of directorate of defense trade controls authorisations involving various countries.

BAE voluntarily disclosed all but one of the alleged violations, which helped it avoid a higher penalty. It also persuaded the state department to suspend half of the penalty, on the condition that the $18m was used to strengthen BAE’s compliance programme.

BAE Systems said it remained committed to ensuring full compliance with all applicable export control laws, and had “thoroughly cooperated” with the state department’s review.

“We have been working diligently to implement improvements to our BAE Systems Inc compliance programme over the last several years, and we will continue to do so. We take seriously our responsibility to protect critical information and support all our customers’ security,” the company added.

The state department said the settlement highlighted “the importance of exporting defence articles pursuant only to appropriate authorisation from the department”.

BAE was accused of sending technical data related to printed wiring boards for use in global positioning system (GPS) to a manufacturer in China in December 2023. According to the state department, the company “recognised its supply chain team did not fully understand the export control and compliance regulations” and that its secure file transfer networks did not highlight export control warnings before the data was sent.

The company also sent data related to printed wiring boards for use with military GPS to Canada in September 2021, after a licence agreement had expired, and the technical specification of an “explosive mixture” to the UK. In another breach, technical data related to a US navy guided-missile destroyer were sent to Germany.

A BAE subcontractor also “furnished defence services without authorisation” on more than 17 separate occasions in Italy and France, and also in Indonesia, according to the state department.

The company also accidentally exported without authorization a control system for a military gas-turbine engine to Switzerland.

articles.title: Luigi Mangione expected to plead guilty in federal case: reports
articles.excerpt: A surprise federal court hearing for Luigi Mangione, the suspect accused of killing UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, fuels speculation of a potential plea deal. National correspondent Bryan Llenas...
articles.body_text:
A surprise federal court hearing for Luigi Mangione, the suspect accused of killing UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, fuels speculation of a potential plea deal. National correspondent Bryan Llenas breaks down what this development means for both the federal and state prosecutions.

Accused UnitedHealthcare CEO assassin Luigi Mangione is expected to plead guilty to the federal charges against him at a surprise pretrial conference Friday, according to local reports, a move that could upend his state-level murder trial just weeks before it's supposed to begin in New York City.

State and federal prosecutors and Mangione's legal team have not responded to requests for comment from Fox News Digital.

But two of the city's major newspapers, the New York Post and New York Times, both reported Thursday that the 28-year-old former Ivy Leaguer is expected to plead guilty in his federal stalking case.

LUIGI MANGIONE HEARING SET FOR FRIDAY STIRS PLEA DEAL SPECULATION IN HIS FEDERAL CASE

Luigi Mangione attends a pre-trial appearance at Manhattan Criminal Court, in New York City, U.S., August 11, 2026. REUTERS/

Mangione is accused of following UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson to a Manhattan Hilton hotel on the morning of Dec. 4, 2024, and shooting him in the back hours before a business conference was supposed to take place there. Surveillance video shows a man in a hoodie approach Thompson from behind and open fire with a handgun — the same weapon authorities allege Mangione had in his backpack when he was arrested in a Pennsylvania McDonald's five days later.

Mangione has pleaded not guilty to all charges in both cases previously. His defense team has had some success already, convincing judges in both cases to dismiss the most serious charges. As a result, he no longer would face capital punishment if convicted in a federal trial, and would not face life without parole if convicted in New York state.

UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson pictured in an undated portrait provided by UnitedHealth. The executive was shot from behind and killed on his way to an investor conference in New York City in what prosecutors have described as a politically motivated assassination. (AP Photo/UnitedHealth Group via AP)

SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE

He could still face a maximum sentence of life without parole in federal prison if convicted in that case — but experts say he would probably avoid the stiffest possible sentence even if convicted by a jury.

Luigi Mangioni is escorted from an NYPD helicopter in New York City, NY, Thursday, December, 19, 2024. Mangione is the prime suspect in the murder of United Healthcare CEO, Brian Thompson. (Rashid Umar Abbasi for Fox News Digital)

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

"Rarely somebody with no background, who’s educated, gets the maximum sentences," said Donna Rotunno, a Chicago criminal defense attorney and Fox News contributor. "Is he looking at minimum sentences? No. But at the end of the day, he’s benefiting from more serious charges being dismissed."

He is still likely looking at decades behind bars, and any legal issues arising from a potential plea deal could also delay the start of his state trial, which is supposed to begin with jury selection on Sept. 8, she said.
