articles.title: 10 House incumbent lawmakers who saw their 2026 re-election bids end in primary defeat
articles.excerpt:
Laura Ingraham, Sean Hannity and Greg Gutfeld bring Fox News viewers their fresh takes on the top news of the day.

So far during the 2026 election season, 10 incumbent House lawmakers have lost prima...
articles.body_text:
Laura Ingraham, Sean Hannity and Greg Gutfeld bring Fox News viewers their fresh takes on the top news of the day.

So far during the 2026 election season, 10 incumbent House lawmakers have lost primaries, including three Republicans and seven Democrats.

The three Republican incumbents who fell short include Dan Crenshaw of Texas, Thomas Massie of Kentucky, and Andy Ogles of Tennessee.

The seven incumbent House Democrats who lost include Al Green of Texas, Julie Johnson of Texas, Dan Goldman of New York, Adriano Espaillat of New York, Diana DeGette of Colorado, Shri Thanedar of Michigan, and John Larson of Connecticut.

The failed Texas and Tennessee U.S. House incumbents grappled with redistricting in their states that applied to this cycle.

Rep. Dan Crenshaw, R-Texas, arrives to a meeting of the House Republican Conference in the U.S. Capitol on Wednesday, January 10, 2024 (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Crenshaw, the only U.S. House Republican incumbent seeking re-election in Texas who did not get President Donald Trump's endorsement, lost the GOP primary for Texas' 2nd Congressional District to state Rep. Steve Toth.

While Trump did not endorse either of the men ahead of the primary, he has since endorsed Toth.

Crenshaw has served in the House since 2019.

Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., leaves the U.S. Capitol after the last votes of the week on Thursday, June 25, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

MTG SAYS GOP'S FUTURE 'DESTROYED' AFTER TRUMP-BACKED PRIMARY CHALLENGER DEFEATS THOMAS MASSIE

Massie lost the Republican primary for Kentucky's 4th Congressional District to Trump-backed challenger Ed Gallrein, a former Navy SEAL.

The race made history as the most expensive U.S. House primary contest ever, reports indicate.

Massie has served in the U.S. House of Representatives since late 2012.

Rep. Andy Ogles, R-Tenn., at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, Feb. 25, 2025. (Kent Nishimura/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Despite having Trump's endorsement, Ogles lost the GOP primary for Tennessee's 5th Congressional District to former state Agriculture Commissioner Charlie Hatcher.

Ogles has served in the House since 2023.

Trump backed Hatcher last week after he defeated Ogles in the primary.

"Last night was another good night for Endorsements, 8-1, and the 1 was a person who I remained loyal to even though he had virtually no chance of winning, and was running against a Great 'Trump' Candidate, and former Agricultural Commissioner of Tennessee, named Charlie Hatcher. Good luck Charlie! Run tough and hard. You have my Complete and Total Endorsement!" Trump declared in a Truth Social post.

Rep. Shri Thanedar, D-Mich., arrives for the vote on the budget resolution in the U.S. Capitol on Thursday, April 10, 2025. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

DSA-BACKED CANDIDATE TOPPLES MILLIONAIRE DEM INCUMBENT

Thanedar, who has served as a lawmaker in the lower congressional chamber since 2023, lost the Democratic U.S. House primary in Michigan's 13th Congressional District this year to state Rep. Donavan McKinney, a Democratic socialist.

Thanedar declared in October 2023 that he was renouncing Democratic Socialists of America membership, though then-Detroit DSA co-chair Mikal Goodman declared at the time in a post on X that Thanedar "was expelled as a member on September 17th, by 91% of vote the general membership. He no longer had a membership to renounce."

Rep. Dan Goldman, D-N.Y., during a canvass launch on the final weekend of early voting ahead of a primary election at Brooklyn Borough Hall in the Brooklyn borough of New York, on Saturday, June 20, 2026. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Goldman, who took office in 2023, lost the Democratic U.S. House primary in New York's 10th Congressional District to former New York City Comptroller Brad Lander.

Big Apple Mayor Zohran Mamdani, a Democratic socialist, had backed Lander ahead of the primary contest.

"He’ll bring principled leadership to Washington and make sure Congress works for the many, not just the few," Mamdani wrote in part of a post on X.

U.S. Rep. Adriano Espaillat, D-N.Y. walks through the U.S. Capitol on Feb. 10, 2026 in Washington, D.C. (Heather Diehl/Getty Images)

MAMDANI-BACKED SOCIALIST WITH HISTORY OF ANTI-AMERICAN RHETORIC WINS VICIOUS DEM PRIMARY RACE

Espaillat lost the Democratic U.S. House primary for New York's 13th Congressional District to Democratic socialist Darializa Avila Chevalier, who was also endorsed by Mamdani.

The congressman has served in the U.S. House chamber since 2017.

He is chair of the Congressional Hispanic Caucus.

Rep. Diana DeGette participated in a League of Women Voters Congressional District 1 candidate forum at Montview Presbyterian Church on May 28, 2026, in Denver, Colo. (RJ Sangosti/MediaNews Group/The Denver Post via Getty Images)

DeGette lost the Democratic U.S. House primary for Colorado's 1st Congressional District to Democratic socialist Melat Kiros.

The congresswoman has served in the House for nearly two decades since taking office in 1997.

Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, joins Texas House Democrats for a press conference at the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers union hall on Aug. 4, 2025 in Warrenville, Ill. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

Green, who has served in the House since 2005, lost the Democratic U.S. House primary runoff for Texas' 18th Congressional District to U.S. Rep. Christian Menefee.

Rep. Julie Johnson, D-Texas, speaks during a news conference outside the U.S. Capitol with the Democratic Women's Caucus on Equal Pay Day to call for "equal pay for equal work," on Thursday, March 26, 2026 (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Johnson, who has only served in the House since last year, lost the Democratic U.S. House primary runoff for Texas' 33rd Congressional District to former Rep. Colin Allred.

LONGTIME ANTI-TRUMP DEM OUSTED AFTER TOUGH PRIMARY FROM UPSTART PROGRESSIVE MAYOR

Rep. John Larson, D-Conn., leaves the U.S. Capitol after the last votes before August recess, on Wednesday, July 23, 2025. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

Larson, who has served in the House since 1999, lost the Democratic U.S. House primary in Connecticut's 1st Congressional District to former Hartford Mayor Luke Bronin.

Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: DR Congo Ebola outbreak spreads to a sixth province
articles.excerpt: The latest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has spread to a sixth province after a death was recorded in previously unaffected Bas-Uele, said the head of the Africa Centres for Disea...
articles.body_text:
The latest Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo has spread to a sixth province after a death was recorded in previously unaffected Bas-Uele, said the head of the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention.

Jean Kaseya said on Thursday that the man died in Buta, the capital of Bas-Uele province, after travelling from Haut-Uele province.

“If we do not stop this outbreak, it will last more than a year and will be the largest in the world,” Kaseya warned. That would also increase the risk of the outbreak spreading to other countries, he added.

The World Health Organization (WHO) says it is spreading faster than any previous one.

The latest outbreak began in the northeastern Ituri province and infections have also been recorded in North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele and Tshopo provinces.

It has killed 2,128 people out of 4,566 cases recorded, according to government figures. There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus responsible for this outbreak.

WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said on Wednesday that “at its current pace”, the outbreak was on track to surpass the deadliest on record, which started over a decade ago and killed more than 11,000 people.

The current outbreak was formally declared on May 15 but the virus had begun circulating in February, health officials said this week.

The WHO hopes to reverse the spread of the virus within three months, but warned that the outbreak would not end by then.

Ebola is rare but highly contagious and can be contracted from bodily fluids and contaminated surfaces and materials, such as bedding and clothing. The disease it causes is severe and often fatal.

Clinical trials of two possible treatments for this type of Ebola began last month in Ituri.

Two vaccines developed specifically for the Bundibugyo virus are being tested in people for the first time, the WHO said on Wednesday.

The UN health agency also plans to test whether an existing Ebola vaccine could protect people against the latest virus after studies in animals showed promising results.

articles.title: Judge dismisses Trump lawsuit that claimed Harvard failed to protect Jewish students
articles.excerpt:
Federal court rules administration failed to plausibly show ongoing violation of civil rights law

A US federal ⁠judge ⁠has dismissed ​the Trump administration’s lawsuit that ⁠claimed ​Harvard ‌Univer...
articles.body_text:
Federal court rules administration failed to plausibly show ongoing violation of civil rights law

A US federal ⁠judge ⁠has dismissed ​the Trump administration’s lawsuit that ⁠claimed ​Harvard ‌University failed ‌to protect Jewish ‌and Israeli students from harassment in the aftermath of the war in Gaza.

In a ruling on Thursday morning, US district ‌judge Richard Stearns in ​Boston said the administration’s lawsuit – ⁠filed in March – failed to plausibly ​show ​an ongoing ​violation ‌of ​federal ​civil rights law on Harvard’s campus.

The administration’s complaint focused largely on a handful of incidents alleged ‌in March 2025, Stearns said, saying these were “too isolated and episodic” to support a claim of ​ongoing civil rights violations by Harvard.

Thursday’s ruling deals a blow to Donald Trump and his officials, and their ongoing push to force the elite university to bow to its will – not only on the response to antisemitism, but to a range of race-in-admissions, diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) and other issues.

In its original complaint, the Trump administration painted a dystopian picture of Harvard life in the wake of Hamas’s 7 October 2023 attack. Department of Justice (DoJ) lawyers said that Jewish and Israeli students were “harassed, physically assaulted, stalked, and spat upon” while the response of the university administration had been to “do nothing”.

That, the DoJ argued, was a violation of Title VI of the 1964 Civil Rights Act that prohibits discrimination in federally funded programs on grounds of race or national origin.

In a brief, but pointed, four-page ruling, Stearns said he was not “diminishing any concern arising” from campus events in the immediate aftermath of the Hamas attacks. But he said that the DoJ’s complaint had misconstrued the remit of Title VI.

In framing the 1964 legislation, the judge ruled, Congress intended not to penalize a “wayward funding recipient but instead to incentivize it to bring itself into compliance with Title VI”. It was in essence forward looking, rather than backward looking, while the examples of alleged discrimination that the Trump administration had provided in its complaint were almost entirely restricted to the 2023-24.

The Trump administration’s later amended complaint was “devoid of any factual allegations” and evidence of noncompliance after it had put Harvard on notice under Title VI in June 2025. As a result, what the judge dismissively described as “the government’s fevered forewarning of potential havoc” failed to meet the purpose of the enforcement action.

Matthew McConaughey is a Texas boy at heart.

During Wednesday...
articles.body_text:
Country star Riley Green told Fox News Digital he won't abandon his Alabama farm even though he has "every reason" to move to Nashville.

Matthew McConaughey is a Texas boy at heart.

During Wednesday's episode of "The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon," the 56-year-old actor embraced his Southern roots by performing Ella Langley's hit song, "Choosin' Texas," alongside Fallon and indie folk band The Last Bison. The cover quickly drew attention on social media and even earned a response from Langley herself.

"I don't think I'll ever recover from this," Langley wrote on her Instagram Stories alongside a video of McConaughey and Fallon jamming to her hit song.

KOE WETZEL AND ELLA LANGLEY RELEASE NEW COUNTRY SONG 'JADED' AND IT'S ALREADY GOING VIRAL

Matthew McConaughey covered Ella Langley's "Choosin' Texas" during an appearance on "The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon." (Getty Images)

"POV me driving singing this with my whole chest," one fan commented.

"The cover we didn’t know we needed," another wrote.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

Host Jimmy Fallon and actor Matthew McConaughey appear during "Audience Suggestion Box" on Wednesday, Aug. 12, 2026. (Todd Owyoung/NBC via Getty Images)

The performance unfolded during a new installment of "Tonight Show Audience Suggestion Box," when Fallon read a submission that combined Langley’s hit with McConaughey’s latest movie, "The Rivals of Amziah King."

"I love that song ‘Choosin’ Texas’ by Ella Langley," Fallon read. "And I’m really excited to see Matthew McConaughey’s new movie ‘The Rivals of Amziah King,’ where he performs in a bluegrass band. If there was only a way to combine those things, that would be a dream come true."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"This is ‘The Tonight Show,’ where dreams become reality," Fallon quipped.

Moments later, the curtain opened to reveal McConaughey with a mandolin in hand alongside The Last Bison, while Fallon joined in on the washboard. The group then launched into a bluegrass rendition of Langley's chart-topping hit.

Matthew McConaughey is a Texas native.  (Getty Images)

McConaughey's cover comes as "Choosin' Texas" continues to make history for Langley.

ELLA LANGLEY'S 'CHOOSIN' TEXAS' SPENDS 15 WEEKS AT NUMBER ONE ON THE BILLBOARD HOT 100

The country anthem recently scored its 17th nonconsecutive week at No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100, making it the longest-running non-holiday No. 1 by a solo female artist in the chart's history.

The milestone pushed Langley past Whitney Houston's "I Will Always Love You" and Mariah Carey's "We Belong Together," which each spent 14 weeks at the top of the chart.

For McConaughey, the song choice was particularly fitting.

The Oscar-winning actor has long been outspoken about his love for the Lone Star State, where he was born and later returned to raise his family.

‘SOPRANOS’ STAR JAMIE-LYNN SIGLER FLED HOLLYWOOD FOR TEXAS WHERE SHE NO LONGER FEELS ‘WATCHED’

McConaughey left Malibu, California, for Austin, Texas, with his wife, Camila Alves McConaughey, and their three children in 2014. He previously explained that returning to Texas was always part of his plan once he started a family.

McConaughey and his wife, Camila Alves, share three children together.  (Rick Kern/Getty Images)

"This has always been home, there are multiple reasons for that," McConaughey previously said during an appearance on "Today."

The "Dallas Buyers Club" star said his mother and two older brothers were also in Texas and explained that he wanted his children to experience some of the same values he grew up around.

"I wanted them to have what I grew up around," he said, adding that there is a certain amount of "common sense" that comes with life in Texas.

Christina Dugan Ramirez is an entertainment journalist with more than 15 years of experience, including a decade at PEOPLE writing high-profile cover stories, covering Hollywood's biggest events, and interviewing many of the industry's most influential stars before joining Fox News Digital in 2024.

articles.title: Ukraine ‘offering Russia deal to halt attacks on civilian ships in Black Sea’
articles.excerpt:
Kyiv reportedly suggested mutual agreement in attempt to reopen crucial grain corridor

Ukraine has proposed a deal with Russia for both sides to halt their attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea ...
articles.body_text:
Kyiv reportedly suggested mutual agreement in attempt to reopen crucial grain corridor

Ukraine has proposed a deal with Russia for both sides to halt their attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea in an apparent attempt to reopen a crucial grain corridor, Reuters reports.

Kyiv is said to have made the offer through a third party. Moscow has yet to respond, the news agency added. The busy waterway is a key export route for both Russia and Ukraine, used to transport grain and other vital foodstuffs worldwide.

Since July Ukraine has effectively closed the route for commercial Russian shipping. Its drones have hit nearly 220 vessels in the Sea of Azov and Black Sea, including oil tankers, grain cargo ships and passenger ferries.

The campaign has forced Russia to suspend shipping through a canal that connects the Caspian Sea with the Sea of Azov via a Russian river network. The route goes through the Kerch strait between occupied Crimea and Russia, and leads on to the Bosphorus strait in Turkey.

During the same period, Russia has escalated its attacks on Ukraine’s southern ports, dealing a severe blow to the country’s agricultural sector. About 90% of grain and sunflower shipments leave from Odesa, and the neighbouring harbours of Chornomorsk and Pivdenne.

In July Russian drones killed 10 sailors soon after their Turkish-owned grain carrier, the Golden Leo, set off from Odesa. Many of the victims were from Syria and India. Another 16 port workers and sailors have died in other recent strikes.

Kyiv’s reported overture appears to be pragmatic, allowing both sides to resume shipments that are crucial to international food security. It comes as the country’s harvest season begins and with shipping from Ukrainian ports at a virtual standstill.

The offer also follows a report in the FT that the US vice-president, JD Vance, had asked Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy to cease some attacks on the Russian Black Sea port of Novorossiysk.

In a phone call on 31 July, Vance complained that Ukrainian strikes on tankers carrying oil from Kazakhstan were hurting US companies and destabilising oil prices. He told Zelenskyy to stop them, the newspaper said, citing unnamed Ukrainian officials.

Zelenskyy’s office has not commented, but Kyiv is in the middle of delicate negotiations with the Trump administration. It is seeking US-manufactured Patriot interceptors to defend Ukrainian cities from rampant Russian ballistic missile and drone swarms.

Since the phone call, Ukraine’s unmanned systems forces have not attacked ships carrying oil from Kazakhstan via the Caspian Pipeline Consortium terminal. But they have continued to pound other targets in Novorossiysk, which is home to Russia’s Black Sea naval fleet.

On Wednesday Zelenskyy hailed a “massive” combined attack on the port, featuring rockets, jets and sea drones. He said Ukraine had taken out Russian warships, including two frigates, a large landing ship, a corvette and other vessels. They had been “hiding” in Novorossiysk Bay, he wrote on Telegram.

Other targets included two major grain export terminals, it was reported. Russian officials said three people, including a child, were killed. “It is entirely justified that Ukraine is responding to Russia’s war, and it is Russia that can and must bring this war to an end,” Zelenskyy posted.

The two sides have previously signed an agreement, brokered by Turkey and the UN, to stop maritime attacks. The Black Sea grain initiative lasted from July 2022 to July 2023. It ended when the Kremlin refused to renew it, complaining that western sanctions were damaging Russia’s agricultural sector.

Ukraine subsequently reopened the route unilaterally, using sea drones to sink Russian ships using the north-west part of the Black Sea. Most vessels in Russia’s Black Sea fleet were forced to relocate from the exposed occupied Crimean port of Sevastopol to Novorossiysk.

articles.title: Bride serves McDonald's customer in wedding dress while tying knot at restaurant: 'Handing out extra sauces'
articles.excerpt: Jamie Callicoat tells Fox News Digital how she ended up celebrating her marriage to George Callicoat at the Akron, Ohio, restaurant where they work and even helped a customer while still wearing her w...
articles.body_text:
Jamie Callicoat tells Fox News Digital how she ended up celebrating her marriage to George Callicoat at the Akron, Ohio, restaurant where they work and even helped a customer while still wearing her wedding dress.

A Northeast Ohio McDonald's restaurant was transformed into a wedding venue last Saturday as two co-workers said "I do" in front of friends, family, fellow employees and the occasional customer.

"We had people trying to come in the lobby the whole time," despite the dining room being closed to the public for the ceremony and reception, bride Jamie Callicoat, of Akron, Ohio, told Fox News Digital this week after marrying co-worker George Callicoat.

"I was handing out extra sauces to an actual customer in my wedding dress."

'MCDONALD'S CHANGED THE COURSE OF MY LIFE': CONGRESSMAN SELLS BUSINESS HE BUILT SINCE HIS TEEN YEARS

Some customers made it to the kiosks inside to order, and the drive-thru remained open throughout the celebration. Everyone — including unsuspecting customers — "rolled with the punches," Jamie said.

"It's still work, if you're there off the clock, on the clock, whatever," she said. "We were there interrupting to have our personal wedding."

George and Jamie Callicoat pose with members of their wedding party outside the McDonald's where they work and were married. (Jamie Callicoat)

The intimate ceremony has since gone viral online.

"Social media content surrounding the wedding has already generated more than 20 million impressions across Instagram and Facebook, with the story continuing to spread," McDonald's of Northeast Ohio said in a news release.

MCDONALD'S NEWEST MENU ITEM HAS FANS BEGGING FOR ONE DISCONTINUED FAVORITE

"We kind of figured it would get some attention, but this is just unreal," Jamie said of the reaction.

The newlyweds were back at work on the Tuesday after their wedding as customers and others who frequent the restaurant began congratulating them.

"Our co-workers are amazing, our bosses are amazing and McDonald's is amazing for allowing us to do this."

"Our Brinks guys, who come and pick up our money, came in and they both walked right up to us and said, 'Oh my gosh, we've seen the video. Congratulations!'" Jamie said.

Jamie is a manager at the McDonald's where she wed George, the restaurant's crew trainer.

McDonald's provided the venue and helped decorate the restaurant. (Jamie Callicoat)

The pair met through mutual friends at Cedar Point in Ohio in June 2025 and went on a few dates. When Jamie moved to Akron and began working at the McDonald's in October 2025, George trained her.

Jamie said George's personality drew her to him.

"We just get along very well," she said. "I love everything about George. He's a great guy."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"I love everything about her," George told Fox News Digital. "She is a wonderful person, very caring, very kind."

The pair became engaged at Cedar Point and initially planned to get married there, too. Then a district manager jokingly suggested they tie the knot at the McDonald's where they both work.

"We thought about it for a day or so and went back and were like, 'Well, were you guys serious?'" Jamie recalled. "And one thing kind of led to another, and here we are."

Jamie Callicoat said her bosses planted the idea of getting married inside the McDonald's. (Dana Dershaw)

The celebration became a team effort, McDonald's said in its news release.

"Crew members and managers came together to help make the couple's wedding day special, providing dinner, a wedding cake and other touches for the celebration," McDonald's said. "Even the officiant had a McDonald's connection: the husband of the restaurant's general manager performed the ceremony."

McDonald's provided the venue, and despite ultimately holding a larger celebration than the destination-style wedding they had originally envisioned, Jamie said the ceremony was "cost-effective."

The couple handled some of the decorations and food themselves. Guests were served pulled barbecue chicken, buffalo chicken dip, homemade rigatoni and fried chicken, while the kids ate fresh McDonald's food.

Even the flower girl got a McDonald's touch, tossing petals from a Happy Meal box.

"That was my decision, mostly," Jamie said. "I mean, we work at McDonald's. I thought it was cute."

George Callicoat trained his future bride when she started working at the McDonald's restaurant in Akron, Ohio. The husband of the location's general manager officiated the wedding ceremony. (Dana Dershaw)

The official Instagram account for McDonald's commented on a video of the ceremony, writing, "A modern day love story."

"Congrats to them on their McMarriage!" wrote another well-wisher. "'Forever After All' and we're McLovin' it."

One commenter even joked about McDonald's notoriously finicky soft-serve machines, but George said theirs wasn't a problem.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"Ours is always working, unless it's being cleaned," he said.

Tammy Snider, the location's general manager, said it was "so much more than a wedding at a McDonald's."

"It's a story about two people in love and a restaurant team that wanted to make sure they felt celebrated," Snider said. "Our restaurants are places where friendships are made, milestones are celebrated and communities come together. George and Jamie's wedding is such a beautiful example of that."

"We had a great time," she said. "Our co-workers are amazing, our bosses are amazing and McDonald's is amazing for allowing us to do this."

Teresa Mull is a freelance writer with the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

The 18-year-old Georgia angler made the decision earlier this year to skip his graduation ceremony and compete in the Phoenix Bass Fishing League All-American on Lake Murray. Looking back now, it doesn’t sound like he lost much sleep over it.

Jack Story, 18, skipped his high school graduation and became the youngest-ever winner of the 43rd annual Phoenix Bass Fishing League (BFL) All-American Championship. (Photo courtesy of Jack Story)

During a recent interview with OutKick Outdoors, Story said he originally qualified through a regional tournament and "never really expected" to make it to the All-American. But once he found out the tournament landed on the same day as graduation, the choice was pretty simple.

"I was going fishing, and they could either be accommodating or not," Story said. "Thankfully, they were very helpful with it."

His school wasn’t completely thrilled, though. Story said the headmaster and others at the school "handled it about as well as they could have," even if they would have preferred to see him in a cap and gown.

Still, some tried to make him reconsider.

"One of my teachers kind of hinted that I should be at graduation," Story said. "But it just wasn’t even an option."

Watch Jack Story's full interview with OutKick Outdoors here:

Story went on to win the All-American and the $100,000 prize that came with it. He also qualified for REDCREST 2027 and the Toyota Series Championship — a pretty strong consolation prize for missing a graduation ceremony.

Still, even weeks later, he said the whole thing feels surreal.

"It was so stressful during the tournament that I think it was a huge relief, but I also didn’t even know what to do," Story said. "The feeling of accomplishment doesn’t even register. Looking back on it, it doesn’t feel real."

The win also came with a little family bragging rights.

Story’s dad previously fished the All-American and finished 34th. So yes, beating him was somewhere on the checklist.

"I thought that was going to be pretty easy given the lake it was on," Story said.

A 7 pound largemouth bass is held against a backdrop of cypress trees. (Getty: JLFCapture)

But that wasn’t the only goal. Story said he wanted to beat the other two anglers from his regional and keep advancing. Instead, he ended up winning the whole thing.

His dad’s advice has always been simple: If you’re going to do something, go all in. That applied to fishing, too.

"If I wanted to skip school to go fish, I was at least going to actually fish," Story said. "His thing was, if you’re going to fish, you’re going to fish all day. Just dedicate yourself to it."

That mindset mattered at Lake Murray. Because Story’s victory was anything but smooth.

The final day came down to 10 ounces, and Story said he knew it was going to be close. What made it worse was the fact that he had already been hit with penalties after issues with his livewells and oxygen tank.

"I was really stressed out about the fact that I could lose because of penalties," Story said. "I’d rather lose by 10 pounds than lose by any sort of penalty."

In other words, this was not some easy stroll to a giant check.

DENNY HAMLIN CHASES MONSTER LARGEMOUTH BASS IN TEXAS WITH BASSMASTER PRO CHRIS ZALDAIN

There was also the added pressure of chasing history. Now the tournament's youngest winner ever, Story broke a 15-year record previously held by Jacob Wheeler — one of the biggest names in the sport.

Unfortunately, Story found out about the record before the tournament was over.

"I honestly wish I would have figured that out after, rather than the night of day two," Story said. "Somebody texted me, and I was like, ‘Dude, that is not what I needed.’ It made it more stressful because instantly, that became my goal."

Since the win, Story said life has included more interviews, podcasts and attention. But mostly, it has included more fishing.

He had a rough finish in a high school tournament shortly after the All-American, and that did not sit well with him.

"I hate losing in fishing, especially when it’s to one of my friends," Story said. "I’ve got to get my get-back, if that makes sense. I want to go beat them again the next day. I just want to fish, and I want to win."

Story is headed to Carson-Newman, where he plans to fish in college. He is also considering fishing the Tackle Warehouse Invitationals if he can make the schedule work.

For other kids who want to get into competitive fishing, Story said persistence matters. So does helping parents understand that fishing can create real opportunities, including scholarships.

"I don’t think people really realize that you can get a scholarship for fishing," Story said. "If you dedicate yourself and put in the constructive work to get there, I think it’s easier than people make it seem. You just have to know how to do it."

A fisherman holds a fishing rod by a lake during sunset in an outdoor setting. (scyther5 / Getty Images)

More than that, Story said fishing gave him something positive to pour himself into.

"I’m out of trouble because I fish," he said. "It keeps you out of trouble. You’re doing something outdoors. It’s good."

And even after winning $100,000 at 18 years old, Story is already thinking about helping more kids get on the water.

STAY "FEARLESS" ON THE GO! TAKE TOMI LAHREN WITH YOU. DOWNLOAD THE TLIF PODCAST NOW!

"I really enjoy taking the younger generation fishing," Story said. "I think every kid deserves the opportunity to fish, and that’s that."

articles.title: Conditions on US aircraft carrier at sea for more than 250 days raise alarms
articles.excerpt: Concern about living conditions on a US aircraft carrier that has been deployed in the Middle East for more than 250 days is leading a US senator to demand answers from the military about the vessel a...
articles.body_text:
Concern about living conditions on a US aircraft carrier that has been deployed in the Middle East for more than 250 days is leading a US senator to demand answers from the military about the vessel and putting more pressure on the Trump administration over the Iran war.

Reports suggest US military members aboard the USS Abraham Lincoln are living with food shortages and broken plumbing and that there have been suicide attempts.

Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth on Thursday called the reports "completely misrepresented".

The carrier left San Diego in November for the South China Sea and was then sent to the Middle East ahead of the attacks on Iran in February. No return date has been announced.

Connecticut Senator Richard Blumenthal, a Democrat, listed the reported hardships on the carrier,  where about 5,000 people are on board, in a letter to Hegseth:  "Shortages of basic supplies, water contamination, plumbing issues, deteriorating mental health, deck safety concerns, and disruptions in the mail system, which have caused many care packages in route to the ship to be lost in transit for months."

"These reports warrant immediate attention," he wrote, "but they also raise a broader question: whether the Navy can sustain the operational tempo now being demanded of its carrier force."

The Military Times and Stars and Stripes reported on Tuesday that multiple sailors on the carrier had considered suicide or attempted to jump overboard, according to their family members.

CBS News, the BBC's US partner, has reported that last month a sailor went overboard and was recovered safely, citing two unnamed officials. The circumstances are currently under investigation.

The deployment was originally set to end in May, but has been repeatedly extended with no date publicly announced for when the carrier will return.

Hegseth, while speaking to reporters in Panama on Thursday, said the government makes sure "every ship, every crew, every captain has everything we can provide them at every single moment".

"Some deployments are longer than others, and I have more respect and gratitude for those sailors than anybody," he sid. "What they do in those high seas in those austere conditions with less port calls - it's incredible."

On Thursday, the Wall Street Journal reported that the US is preparing to replace the Lincoln with the aircraft carrier USS George Washington as part of a previously scheduled rotation plan. The BBC has contacted the Pentagon about the report.

Taylor Sheridan attends the black carpet event for the "Yellowstone" Season 5 Fort Worth premiere at Hotel Drover on Nov. 13, 2022, in Fort Worth, Texas. (Omar Vega/Getty Images)

I've never thought about how the shows could cross over, but I have told Taylor, I'm like, 'Bro, anything you ever want me to do, I'll do. I love being in Texas. I love saying your words.' I think he's truly a standalone talent. There's nobody who's doing or has ever done what he's doing. It's incredible what he does. And he's just one of the smartest dudes you'll ever meet. Air India is to test all of its pilots for banned substances, starting immediately.

It comes after an incident las...
articles.body_text:
The airline said in a memo that the move would reassure passengers and stakeholders

Air India is to test all of its pilots for banned substances, starting immediately.

It comes after an incident last week in which its Phuket to Delhi flight suddenly lost altitude, with a preliminary report saying the senior pilot had to retake their substance test. Reports say they had tested positive for marijuana.

Pilots at the airline's budget arm, Air India Express, will also be subject to the tests from Thursday.

Existing rules require at least 10% of pilots to be tested at random.

Seventeen passengers and crew were injured when the Airbus lost about 91 metres (300 feet) in height shortly after departure on 4 August.

It is being investigated by Indian authorities working alongside Airbus and France's air safety agency.

Both pilots of the flight have been removed from duties until the investigation is complete.

In a memo seen by the BBC, Air India said it was "important to go further" in its testing.

"This initiative, which goes beyond regulatory requirements, reflects our determination to uphold the highest standards of safety and professionalism, and to provide reassurance to our passengers, stakeholders and the community at large," it said.

The airline has already been under scrutiny after a June 2025 flight from Ahmedabad to London crashed shortly after take-off, killing 241 people on board and 19 on the ground. Only one passenger survived.

The tests - for substances as well as medications prohibited under aviation regulations - are being carried out alongside training sessions at Air India's academy, as well as other locations including briefing centres and offices.

Last week, former Ethiopian Airlines boss Tewolde Gebremariam became Air India's new chief executive.

articles.title: Mark Consuelos confesses what would keep him in 'loveless marriage' with Kelly Ripa

articles.body_text:
Dana Perino discusses the anticipated Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce wedding, offering her perspective on marriage. She stresses that happiness in a marriage is built on mutual trust rather than extravagant costs or prenups. Perino emphasizes a commitment-first approach for couples considering long-term unions.

Mark Consuelos revealed that he’d rather stay in a "loveless marriage" with Kelly Ripa than risk losing their dog Lena in a divorce.

"How do we fight over pets in a divorce?" Ripa asked in the opening segment of Tuesday's episode of "Live with Kelly and Mark," a prerecorded episode from before she was out for oral surgery.

"I mean, listen. Let’s just put it this way," Consuelos responded. "I would stay in a loveless marriage just to make sure I could be with Lena every day. That’s how much I love Lena."

KELLY RIPA'S PAINFUL SURGERY LEAVES HER UNABLE TO SPEAK

Mark Consuelos joked that he would rather stay in a "loveless marriage" than risk losing their dog, Lena. (FilmMagic)

Ripa asked him sarcastically, "Is that all you’re asking for is a loveless marriage? Because that can be arranged."

Consuelos added that if he ever lost Lena in a divorce, he would "stay up at night, wondering what she is doing."

Ripa quipped that he would be "wondering if there was some other man petting her."

They were discussing a new bill in Pennsylvania that would change pets from being considered property to members of the family in a divorce, according to People.

The couple rescued Lena, a Maltese and Shih Tzu mix, in 2021 after she was featured in a pet adoption segment on the show.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Mark Consuelos is seen balancing his dog, Lena, on his head. (Kelly Ripa/Instagram)

Ripa said her main worry when she adopted Lena was that she wouldn’t get along with Chewie, a Shih Tzu she adopted from a 2007 segment on the show.

The two dogs got along right away, she said — but her children wanted Lena to be named after a "Star Wars" character.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"My kids want her to be named Leia, as in Princess Leia, because we have Chewie," she said on the show soon after adopting the pup, according to People. "I don't know. I need guidance."

Kelly Ripa and Mark Consuelos have been married since 1996. (Disney General Entertainment Content via Getty Images)

Ripa talked about the importance of rescuing pets on the show in 2022.

"Adopt your dogs if you can, because they’re the best," she said to applause from the audience. "They’re like, ‘We’ve been in the system, we don’t want to go back. We’re going to be extra good. We’re hardly going to poop anywhere we’re not supposed to, and we’re rarely going to chew things that aren’t meant to be chewed.'"

Ripa and Consuelos have been married for 30 years and they share three children.

Brie Stimson is a Los Angeles-based entertainment and breaking news writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Mangione lawyers to meet federal prosecutors amid reports of plea deal
articles.excerpt: Attorneys for Luigi Mangione, who is accused of killing United Healthcare CEO Brian Thompson in New York in 2024, are meeting federal prosecutors on Friday amid US media reports about a potential plea...
articles.body_text:
Attorneys for Luigi Mangione, who is accused of killing United Healthcare CEO Brian Thompson in New York in 2024, are meeting federal prosecutors on Friday amid US media reports about a potential plea agreement.

Mangione faces two federal stalking crimes that carry a maximum penalty of life in prison without parole, but it was not immediately clear which charges are under discussion.

"There's a conference scheduled for 11 am on Friday, and that's all we can say at this time," Jamie McDonald, the US Attorney for the Southern District of New York (SDNY), said this week.

Mangione also faces a separate state trial in the case. He has pleaded not guilty to all charges in both cases.

Discussion of a plea deal does not guarantee one will be reached, and such arrangements can fall apart. Any deal must also be approved by the court.

Federal prosecutors brought the stalking charges against Mangione for allegedly travelling, and using surveillance, to kill Thompson.

A federal judge threw out two other charges in January, one of which carried the death penalty as a possible sentence.

Mangione's attorneys, the SDNY, and Manhattan District Attorney's office did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

His attorneys have previously argued he should not be tried in both state and federal court. At the moment, the judges presiding over both cases have allowed the trials to proceed.

But if Mangione pleads guilty in his federal case, it could open the door for his attorneys to argue the state case runs afoul of double jeopardy – a constitutional protection that prevents an individual from being prosecuted twice for the same crime.

New York's state constitution has its own prohibition on double jeopardy, which, if invoked here, could have a knock-on effect on Mangione's upcoming state trial.

"If a federal prosecution has been completed on a matter, the state cannot prosecute the matter on those same facts," said Mitchell Epner, a white-collar attorney and former federal prosecutor.

Mangione's state trial is scheduled to begin on 8 September, while the federal trial is listed for January 2027.
