Lucy Davis revealed a devastating Stage 4 breast cancer diagnosis after quietly battling the disease for the past year and a half.

...
articles.body_text:
Fox News Flash top entertainment and celebrity headlines are here.

Lucy Davis revealed a devastating Stage 4 breast cancer diagnosis after quietly battling the disease for the past year and a half.

"The Office" actress said the cancer had metastasized to her spine, right hip and ribs and was now "incurable," with chemotherapy no longer an option.

"The initial lump that I felt, wasn’t a ‘lump’ as such; rather a kind of hard spot. Really tiny," she wrote on Instagram. "I almost didn’t bother getting it checked. So I guess I’m saying don’t ignore anything – get everything checked out."

Rather than dwell on her prognosis, Davis said she was determined to embrace whatever time she had left.

BARRY MANILOW RESCHEDULES CONCERT 45 MINUTES BEFORE START AMID ONGOING LUNG CANCER RECOVERY

‘The Office’ actress Lucy Davis is opening up about her private battle with incurable Stage 4 breast cancer – and the subtle symptom she almost ignored. (Frederick M. Brown/Getty Images)

"As of now, I’m trying to live out whatever might be left of my life in as fun a way as I possibly can," she explained. "I always like to find the teachable moments in anything negative that happens. And cancer has not disappointed in that regard; there’s a lot I have learned from it, and I’m grateful for that."

Davis said maintaining that outlook had not made the physical realities of cancer any easier.

"As some of you will know, the pain can really be something else," Davis wrote. "Standing and walking for too long a time can be hard, and I need to use a wheelchair sometimes (so if you see me toddling around in one, feel free to give me a push!)"

Despite the pain, Davis said she had found peace with what could come next.

"The Office" star Lucy Davis says she’s choosing joy, purpose and peace as she continues acting and advocating for animal rights amid her cancer diagnosis. (Kevin Winter/Getty Images)

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR THE ENTERTAINMENT NEWSLETTER

"I’m not scared of whatever comes next," she said. "I’m at peace with it. I’ll see my Gracie sooner than expected, and for me, leaving my physical body just means going home. Any and all grieving is for my family; it’s far harder for them than for me."

But Davis made clear she had no plans to stop pursuing the work and causes she loved.

"I’m still going to keep up all my work for animal rights," Davis noted. "It’s so important to me. And I still would like to keep working. I’m perfectly able to do so, and acting is one of the biggest joys in my life."

After an 18-month battle kept largely out of the public eye, Lucy Davis shared an emotional update on cancer’s physical toll and the outlook keeping her going. (Dave Benett/Getty Images)

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Simon Pegg, Lucy Davies and Nick Frost attend the U.K. premiere of "Shaun of the Dead" on March 30, 2004. (Dave Benett/Getty Images)

Davis began acting in the 1990s, with an early role as Maria Lucas in the BBC’s acclaimed 1995 adaptation of "Pride and Prejudice." Her major breakthrough came as receptionist Dawn Tinsley in Ricky Gervais and Stephen Merchant’s original British version of "The Office," which ran from 2001 to 2003 and became an international comedy phenomenon.

Davis later built a career spanning British comedy and major Hollywood productions including, "Shaun of the Dead," "Wonder Woman," "Chilling Adventures of Sabrina" and "The Villains of Valley View."

articles.title: Paramount escalates threat to leave California as Dem AG's antitrust lawsuit stalls Warner Bros merger
articles.excerpt: NewsBusters executive editor Tim Graham tells Fox News Digital that Paramount CEO David Ellison’s recent essay about making CNN "straight down the middle" didn’t do him any favors with the network’s l...
articles.body_text:
NewsBusters executive editor Tim Graham tells Fox News Digital that Paramount CEO David Ellison’s recent essay about making CNN "straight down the middle" didn’t do him any favors with the network’s liberal staffers.

Paramount's new chief is threatening to move his studio out of California if the Golden State's attorney general doesn't come to the table to resolve the high-stakes antitrust lawsuit.

Puck News reported Tuesday that Paramount CEO David Ellison is serious about relocating his headquarters to a more business-friendly state like Georgia, Tennessee or Texas if California AG Rob Bonta, who is leading 11 other states to block Paramount's $111 billion merger with Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD), doesn't negotiate a settlement by Oct. 1. According to the report, Ellison is "in contact" with multiple states.

Ellison, who will soon be forced to pay WBD a multimillion-dollar "ticking fee" if the merger stays in limbo, remains convinced that Paramount would be victorious in court — except the antitrust trial isn't taking place until March 2027, meaning his company will have to likely fork over at least $650 million quarterly to WBD if nothing is settled until next spring.

PARAMOUNT-WARNER BROS DISCOVERY ANTITRUST TRIAL DATE SET; MERGER PUT ON PAUSE OVER LEGAL BATTLE

Paramount became the first major film studio to speak out against a widespread boycott of Israeli film institutions on Thursday. (Erik McGregor/LightRocket)

According to the report, Ellison could move Paramount — and potentially Warner Bros. if he ultimately merges both companies — out of California "regardless of the eventual outcome of the case." Ellison has even developed a five-year plan that would relocate the vast majority of jobs out of the state while still maintaining a footprint in Hollywood.

Bonta slammed the latest Paramount buzz, renewing his accusation of attempted "blackmail" by the studio.

"In a span of weeks, Paramount agreed to halt the merger until a court decision or until June 2027, asked for a November trial, and is now back with another attempt to blackmail the state into letting an illegal deal through. Paramount has lost the plot as it continues to lose in court," Bonta wrote on X. "It didn't work the first time — on the eve of our July lawsuit — and it won't work this time."

"This illegal merger will result in higher costs, fewer options, and fewer people making movies. My office remains committed to stopping illegal consolidation and protecting a vibrant California economy for businesses that play by the rules," he added.

CALIFORNIA AG ROB BONTA FACES ‘POLITICAL FAVOR’ CLAIMS OVER NETFLIX-LINKED $1M TRAIL IN PARAMOUNT SUIT

Attorney General Rob Bonta speaks during a news conference in Sacramento, Calif., Tuesday, Sept. 26, 2023. California's attorney general will not seek criminal charges against a police officer who in 2020 fatally shot a man outside a pharmacy in the San Francisco Bay Area amid national protests over the police killing of George Floyd, his office announced on Dec. 19. (AP Photo/Rich Pedroncelli,File)

However, while speaking at a Politico conference later in the day, Bonta did signal a willingness to negotiate with Paramount if "structural remedies" are implemented by the company.

Bonta's lawsuit claims the merger would "lead to higher prices, lower quality, and less content for film and television, harming movie theaters, basic cable distributors, and ultimately, audiences on every sofa and movie theater seat in the U.S."

The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District for the Northern District of California, claims the merger violates Section 7 of the Clayton Act, which holds that mergers that may substantially lessen competition or tend to create a monopoly are illegal. Both sides argued their case last week but Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín waited until Monday to temporarily delay the merger.

The merger, which was set to close this year, is now being delayed until at least June 2027.

Bonta has faced accusations of a conflict of interest from his Republican challenger for California attorney general, Michael Gates, who questioned whether a financial connection to Netflix co-founder Reed Hastings' family influenced Bonta's decision to bring the lawsuit.

"Rob Bonta has turned his taxpayer-funded office into a favor factory for his political bosses and donors. He's pursuing politically-motivated litigation against a competitor for a company that's bankrolled his PAC," Gates told Fox News Digital.

Campaign-finance records reviewed by Fox News Digital show Hastings' wife, Patty Quillin, contributed $1 million to Smart Justice California Action Fund on March 16, 2022. The independent committee was working to boost Bonta and other progressive prosecutors.

Netflix was previously in negotiations to purchase Warner Bros. Discovery before Paramount made its offer.

CNN STAFFERS SEE PARAMOUNT MERGER AS 'INEVITABLE' DESPITE LEGAL BATTLE DELAYING ELLISON TAKEOVER

(Noam Galai/Getty Images for Paramount) (Noam Galai/Getty Images for Paramount)

CLICK HERE FOR THE LATEST MEDIA AND CULTURE NEWS

Paramount's bid to buy Warner Bros. Discovery would be a historic deal merging two major Hollywood studios under one corporate umbrella as well as all of their television networks, including CBS and CNN. Critics of the deal believe such a merger would crush the entertainment industry and lead to mass layoffs. Some have also been vocal against Ellison and his billionaire father, Larry Ellison, who is heavily financing the deal and is a close ally to President Donald Trump.

Liberal critics in particular also claim that, as a result of the deal, CNN would be given a MAGA-bent to its coverage, and it would be run by current CBS News editor-in-chief Bari Weiss, who has been harshly criticized by some media liberals. The Paramount CEO has previously assured that CNN would maintain editorial independence following the merger.

In an op-ed published in The New York Times, Ellison addressed the "speculation" about what would happen to CNN under his ownership.

"I have regularly voted for candidates of both parties; I hold some views that would be called conservative and others that would be called liberal, just like most Americans; and when it comes to our news operations, I do not aspire to lead these companies to bend their newsrooms to my views. I believe that news should be based on facts and truth," Ellison wrote.

"Great news organizations like CNN and CBS News are here to tell it straight down the middle," he added. "That requires newsrooms that reflect the whole world, not one side of it. And it requires independence."

The deal would follow Ellison's $8 billion purchase last year of Paramount, merging the studio with Skydance Media.

Fox News Digital reached out to Paramount and Bonta's office for comment but did not immediately receive a response.

Fox News' CJ Womack contributed to this report.

Joseph A. Wulfsohn is a media reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to joseph.wulfsohn@fox.com and on Twitter: @JosephWulfsohn.

articles.title: Fever coach Stephanie White launches fiery defense of herself after Sophie Cunningham hit
articles.excerpt:
DiJonai Carrington went to Threads to claim "white privilege" following her takedown flagrant foul of Sophie Cunningham despite her intentionally clotheslining her in the face.

When Chicago Sky guard...
articles.body_text:
DiJonai Carrington went to Threads to claim "white privilege" following her takedown flagrant foul of Sophie Cunningham despite her intentionally clotheslining her in the face.

When Chicago Sky guard DiJonai Carrington hit Sophie Cunningham on Saturday, pundits predictably turned on Cunningham. Meanwhile, Fever coach Stephanie White stayed quiet.

White has stayed similarly quiet when Caitlin Clark has absorbed physical hits and media fire. Heading into Tuesday's game against the New York Liberty, White took the podium and suddenly found plenty to say.

DiJonai Carrington of the Chicago Sky was ejected after a brutal foul on Sophie Cunningham of the Indiana Fever. (Kamil Krzaczynski/Imagn Images)

"You know, this isn't necessarily for those people that are in this room. This is more for an online community that's trying to create narratives that simply don't exist. Trying to create a fabrication or distortion of who I am, of what I'm about. Our players' success, our players' health and wellness, our players' safety is always a top priority for me. One of the things I pride myself on is my relationships with players."

SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM SPEAKS OUT AGAINST DIJONAI CARRINGTON AFTER FLAGRANT FOUL AND 'WHITE PRIVILEGE' POST

White brushed off criticism as a fabricated narrative while Cunningham absorbed the heat.

Sophie Cunningham #8 and head coach Stephanie White are shown during a game against the Toronto Tempo at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Ind., on June 16, 2026. (Getty Images)

"For those who have anything to say about the play in the last game? I didn't see the play in real time. I went straight to a press conference. I thought the play got called right. Thankfully, Sophie's okay. Was it egregious? Absolutely. When you have a chance to watch that over and over and over on replay, you can see that. I didn't have that in real time."

Missing the hit live explains Saturday night. It doesn't explain the silence that followed.

FEVER COACH STEPHANIE WHITE DODGES QUESTION ON GOP LETTER ABOUT CAITLIN CLARK’S TREATMENT IN WNBA

"I take personally any suggestions that I don't 100% always have my players' back. I ride with them 10 toes down all the time, all of the time. They know that. It's a shame that we can't have an opportunity to talk about what great basketball they're playing because they are f***ing playing."

Riding "10 toes down" rings hollow when Cunningham was left to absorb the backlash after Carrington's hit. Clark has faced similar moments before her. Then came the moralizing.

White added, "The reality is with me, I will always lead with love. I will also lead with grace. I will always lead with humility. And I will always lead with integrity. Doesn't mean I'll always get it right. I'm also human."

Nobody attacked her humanity; they called out her passivity. White then framed the criticism as something more sinister.

LET'S HAVE AN HONEST CONVERSATION ABOUT CAITLIN CLARK, RACISM, AND MEDIA COWARDICE

She continued, "The hate, the fear-mongering, the divisiveness, the stuff that's trying to hijack our league will not win. It won't win. We are united. We are connected. We will not be divided. Every day, these women put their a** on the line. Every day. When they go low, we go high. Love will win, grace will win. Humility will win and kindness will win. I stand by them, I will always stand by them. Everybody else can go to hell."

After the news conference, Fever president Kelly Krauskopf soon issued a statement backing White.

"Coach White has done a tremendous job leading the Fever and for the second-consecutive season, has us in great position for a playoff push. She has kept our team focused and united, all while under the brightest spotlight our team and our league have ever experienced. She has the full support of leadership."

The statement backs White. But it doesn't answer the criticism.

Cunningham took the hit and the backlash that followed. By the time White finally called Carrington's play "egregious," much of her response was spent defending herself.

That's not riding 10 toes down. That's showing up after the fight is over.

Head coach Stephanie White and Caitlin Clark of the Indiana Fever meet during the second quarter against the Connecticut Sun at Gainbridge Fieldhouse in Indianapolis, Indiana, on June 17, 2025. (Dylan Buell/Getty Images)

Send us your thoughts: alejandro.avila@outkick.com / Follow along on X: @alejandroaveela

Alejandro Avila is a longtime writer at OutKick, living in Southern California.

articles.title: CBS Sports president says 'no timetable or final decision' on Tony Romo's future after OWI arrest
articles.excerpt:
Fox News national correspondent Kevin Corke reports on Tony Romo’s refusal to take a breathalyzer test on ‘The Will Cain Show.’

Tony Romo’s status with CBS remains a fluid situation, but the presiden...
articles.body_text:
Fox News national correspondent Kevin Corke reports on Tony Romo’s refusal to take a breathalyzer test on ‘The Will Cain Show.’

Tony Romo’s status with CBS remains a fluid situation, but the president of CBS Sports said "there is no timetable or final decision" following his OWI arrest last month.

CBS Sports president David Berson spoke at "NFL on CBS" Media Day on Tuesday, where he was asked about Romo, who was placed on indefinite leave by the network. J.J. Watt was named as CBS Sports’ top analyst alongside play-by-play legend Jim Nantz on gamedays ahead of the 2026 NFL season.

The announcement came after Romo was arrested by Milwaukee County Sheriff’s Office deputies after showing signs of impairment while driving in Wisconsin on his way back from a golf event.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Tony Romo speaks to police on bodycam footage during traffic stop that led to arrest. (Milwaukee County Sheriff's Office)

"It’s an evolving situation and we are still assessing," Berson replied to the question about Romo. "There is no timetable or final decision at this time.

"I hope you can respect and appreciate this is a personal matter and a legal one for Tony."

A follow-up question asked Berson why he was placed on leave as the legal situation played out.

"We have to consider the impact on our image and our brand," he replied. "That’s very important to us. The focus should be and needs to be on our presentation and this great product and not on any others.

"Fortunately, we have a deep bench and everybody is stepping up."

Romo was charged with operating while intoxicated after performing poorly during field sobriety tests. He was also charged with having an open bottle of alcohol in his vehicle and with unsafe passing.

CBS Sports play-by-play announcer Jim Nantz (left), analyst Tony Romo (center) and sideline reporter Tracy Wolfson at press conference at the Super Bowl LVIII Media Center at the Mandalay Bay Resort and Casino on Feb. 6, 2024. (Kirby Lee/USA TODAY Sports)

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Romo is in the middle of his massive 10-year, $180 million deal with CBS as their top NFL analyst, and he is reportedly still owed $72 million after signing the deal in 2020.

OutKick reported in late July that Romo’s future with CBS is in jeopardy beyond his leave, as there were doubts prior to his arrest about whether the network would keep him as its lead analyst after the 2026 season. It’s also worth noting CBS will be airing the Super Bowl in 2028.

Debate about Romo’s preparation has come up in recent seasons, especially among critics saying he hasn’t gelled with Nantz like in years past.

It’s also been reported that Romo’s contract has an industry-standard morals clause, which CBS could invoke to fire Romo over the arrest video. His legal team, though, would almost certainly fight that with millions still owed.

Tony Romo on "The Drew Barrymore Show" ahead of Super Bowl LVIII. (Gail Schulman/CBS via Getty Images)

Romo’s court date has been set for Sept. 21, which comes eight days after CBS Sports’ first NFL broadcast.

Follow Fox News Digital’s sports coverage on X and subscribe to the Fox News Sports Huddle newsletter.

Scott Thompson is a sports writer for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Colombia scrambles to find survivors after deadly earthquake
articles.excerpt:
At least 254 deaths have been reported so far as rescuers continue to sift through collapsed buildings in western Colombia.

Cali, Colombia – A day after a magnitude 7.4 earthquake shook western Colom...
articles.body_text:
At least 254 deaths have been reported so far as rescuers continue to sift through collapsed buildings in western Colombia.

Cali, Colombia – A day after a magnitude 7.4 earthquake shook western Colombia, rescue teams are frantically fighting through the rubble of collapsed buildings to find survivors and recover bodies.

The powerful quake has caused at least 254 deaths nationwide, most of them concentrated in the cities of Pereira and Cali, according to government figures.

“For me, the earthquake felt eternal,” recalled Luis Saenz, a 22-year-old journalism student from Cali.

Saenz was at home enjoying his morning coffee when the quake struck at 7:34am (12:34 GMT) on Monday. He remembers his cat darting under the bed, then chaos as his family fled into the street.

Some 5,000 homes suffered damage, according to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, while dozens of buildings – many of them residential – collapsed entirely.

In Cali, Colombia’s third-largest city, at least 95 people died, and 45 structures have fully or partially collapsed, according to local government statistics.

“I never thought I would see my city like this,” resident Maria Isabel Cumbal said between sobs, as she watched rescue efforts unfold at the Vanessa Building in the south of the city.

The seven-storey residential apartment block was reduced to wreckage in Monday's earthquake.

Rescuers now wield hammers, shovels and heavy machinery in an attempt to pierce through thick slabs of concrete and rescue the estimated 20 people trapped underneath.

On and around the collapsed residence, hundreds of volunteers help to clear the rubble by forming a human chain to pass buckets from atop the mound of debris down to dump trucks.

Every so often, a rescuer will hold up a fist to call for silence, so that emergency responders can listen for signs of life.

When the building collapsed, it fell onto a neighbouring building that housed a nursery, according to multiple volunteers at the site.

“There are approximately 17 children trapped under the rubble,” explained Maximiliano Herrera, 32, a local volunteer coordinating rescue efforts.

The nursery was part of a nearby Adventist Church. Herrera, a member of the congregation, knows many of the families whose children are stuck under the rubble.

“It’s very sad to know that the kids of friends and acquaintances are most likely under here,” Herrera told Al Jazeera.

He added that two children, Samuel and Sara, have shown signs of life but are located “in the most out-of-reach corner of the entire site".

Some onlookers wait for news about loved ones who were at home when the Vanessa Building crumbled.

Samir Valencia lived in the apartment block until 2022, when he moved down the road. Many of his former neighbours remain missing.

Valencia tried to help clear the debris, but he found it too painful to see his old home in ruin.

“I wanted to stay, but no, I couldn't,” said Valencia, as he watched a mobile phone video he took last week from a friend's apartment inside the Vanessa Building. “I was helping, but I couldn't continue. Believe me, my heart just couldn't take it.”

Valencia’s new home was also severely damaged by the earthquake. Thick cracks now creep across the facade of his apartment block, and large chunks of concrete lie at the foot of the building.

His neighbours continue to make risky expeditions into their flats to retrieve their valuables. When an aftershock triggered an earthquake siren on Tuesday morning, several residents ran out of the tottering apartment block, at least three cradling flatscreen TVs.

Such retrieval missions come amid fears of looting in a city with one of the country’s highest crime rates.

Prior to the earthquake, officials estimated that Cali, the capital of the Valle de Cauca province, accounted for more than 8 percent of the homicides in Colombia, with 1,067 recorded last year.

Fearing an uptick in crime, the mayor of Cali, Alejandro Eder, announced the “militarisation” of the city on Monday, imposing a curfew from 8pm to 6am – with the exception of rescue teams, medical staff and other essential workers.

Many rescuers have not slept since the earthquake struck, working through the night to try to save lives.

“We haven’t stopped. We’ve been doing this all night,” Cristian Nieves, a weary volunteer who sat perched on a paint bucket, said on Tuesday morning.

Local authorities have received support from their counterparts in Colombia’s capital, Bogota, and its second-largest city, Medellin, with firefighters and rescue teams arriving from major metropolises.

Much of the aid has also come from citizens and private companies, according to organisers on the ground.

All the heavy yellow machinery – including the cranes and diggers – operating at the Vanessa Building were donated by private construction firms, according to Yhoshua Jafet Arles, who works with the mayor’s office.

The crisis represents the first major test for President Abelardo de la Espriella, who was inaugurated on Friday in Cali.

De la Espriella chose the city for his oath of office as a sign of his commitment to fighting crime in Colombia. Normally, inaugurations take place in Bogota.

Since Monday's earthquakes, the right-wing leader has pledged support for survivors and met with local leaders in Cali and Quibdo, the capital of the department of Choco.

But people in hard-hit cities like Buenaventura – which is historically more impoverished than Cali and Pereira – have said they feel neglected by the government.

Valencia moved to Cali from Buenaventura, and he worries government assistance will not reach his hometown.

“We've always been forgotten in Buenaventura,” said the 42-year-old. “All the help is centred around the city of Manizales, in Armenia and Bogota, which were hardly affected at all.”

Others have said the government response has been disorganised, with multiple agencies responding to the crisis without centralised leadership.

“It's not a lack of support. It's a lack of organisation. Because it's unbelievable that such a large city has no control over its agencies,” said Herrera.

But for now, residents are most concerned about saving lives. Saenz, the journalism student, was among the survivors donning a hard hat and face mask to sift through the destruction in Cali.

“We’re all tired and everything, but we’re trying to keep going,” said Saenz.

articles.title: Federal judge blocks Trump administration from restricting mail-in ballots ahead of midterms
articles.excerpt: Postmaster General David Steiner indicated that under a proposed rule, if a state declines to provide the federal government with its absentee voter list, USPS would not mail ballots for those states....
articles.body_text:
Postmaster General David Steiner indicated that under a proposed rule, if a state declines to provide the federal government with its absentee voter list, USPS would not mail ballots for those states. (Credit: Senate Homeland Security Committee)

A federal judge in Massachusetts on Tuesday blocked the U.S. Postal Service (USPS) from implementing part of President Donald Trump's executive order tightening mail-in voting rules ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.

U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani granted a preliminary injunction preventing the USPS from implementing or enforcing Section 3 of Executive Order 14399 for the Nov. 3 midterm elections, or any earlier federal election.

The ruling prevents USPS from refusing to transmit mail-in or absentee ballots under the challenged section and blocks rulemaking to implement certain regulations outlined in the executive order for the November elections.

The injunction does not prevent the federal government from providing nonbinding USPS guidance on ballot-mail envelopes.

JUDGE HANDS TRUMP MAIL-BALLOT WIN FOR NOW AS DEMOCRATS’ NEXT MOVE LOOMS

A federal judge on Tuesday blocked the U.S. Postal Service from implementing part of President Donald Trump's executive order tightening mail-in voting rules ahead of the 2026 midterm elections. (John Roark/The Idaho Post-Register via AP, File)

Talwani held a hearing Friday on the plaintiffs' renewed request for a preliminary injunction. The Trump administration is expected to appeal Tuesday's ruling to the 1st U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Boston.

Trump signed the executive order in March as part of his election integrity agenda.

It directs the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) to compile lists of confirmed U.S. citizens eligible to vote and provide them to states, instructs the USPS to establish new standards for mail-in ballots, and directs the Department of Justice (DOJ) to prioritize investigations into state and local election officials who issue federal ballots to people deemed ineligible to vote.

"Cheating on mail-in voting is legendary. It’s horrible. Democrats want to use it for cheating," Trump said.

Tuesday's ruling comes weeks after the 1st Circuit rejected the administration's attempt to enforce other provisions of Trump's executive order while a separate legal challenge proceeds.

OBAMA-APPOINTED JUDGE BLOCKS TRUMP'S ELECTION ORDER AS SAVE AMERICA ACT FIGHT INTENSIFIES

President Donald Trump signed an executive order tightening mail-in voting rules in March. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images, File)

In a 2-1 decision July 25, the appeals court denied the DOJ's request to pause a June ruling blocking several provisions of Trump's order in 23 Democratic-led states and the District of Columbia.

That lawsuit was led by California, Massachusetts, Nevada and Washington. The states argued that the Constitution gives states primary responsibility for administering federal elections and that Trump exceeded his authority by directing federal agencies to impose new voting requirements.

Talwani had previously blocked several provisions of the executive order in June, finding they likely exceeded the president's authority. The appeals court left that injunction in place July 25, while the administration's appeal proceeds.

The DOJ previously told the appeals court it could seek emergency relief from the U.S. Supreme Court if it did not prevail.

A federal judge on Tuesday blocked the U.S. Postal Service from implementing part of President Donald Trump's executive order tightening rules for mail-in ballots ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.

The League of Women Voters of Massachusetts praised Tuesday's ruling, saying it protects voting rights for people who rely on voting by mail.

"The League of Women Voters of Massachusetts commends the court for upholding one of our most sacred constitutional rights: the right to vote," a representative for the organization wrote in a statement shared with Fox News Digital. "We are pleased to see this ruling and are committed to remaining in the fight to protect voting rights – not just for the Bay Staters who rely on mail voting, but for every American who utilizes this safe, secure, and trusted tool."

The White House, DOJ and USPS did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's requests for comment.

Talwani ordered the plaintiff organizations in Tuesday's ruling to post a nominal $100 bond by Aug. 18.

Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

articles.title: ICE to spend up to $20m on gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks
articles.excerpt:
According to manufacturer,  shock ‘is usually effective in bringing individuals into compliance in less than three seconds’

ICE plans to spend up to $20m (£15m) to purchase thousands of gloves that c...
articles.body_text:
According to manufacturer,  shock ‘is usually effective in bringing individuals into compliance in less than three seconds’

ICE plans to spend up to $20m (£15m) to purchase thousands of gloves that can deliver painful electric shocks for officers and agents by March, according to a notice published Monday by the Department of Homeland Security.

The devices, called Glove (Generated Low Output Voltage Emitter), are manufactured by Compliant Technologies LLC of Lexington, Kentucky.

According to the manufacturer, “the discomfort associated with the stimulation is usually effective in bringing individuals into compliance in less than three seconds and leaves no burns, marks or scars”. The company has advertised the device as a “humane, low-optics, de-escalation solution for many situations facing our men and women in uniform”.

The gloves have previously been used in settings such as jails in the US.

Compliant Technologies says the devices function as a normal pair of patrol gloves until officers press a switch to activate their electrical mode. The gloves must be applied directly to someone’s skin to deliver a pain stimulus that typically helps an officer gain compliance within seconds, according to the company.

“It’s immediate and sharp, and it will distract you. I call it like a bee sting,” said John Peters, president of the Institute for the Prevention of In-Custody Deaths, who is studying how the device has been used. “If the officer is getting any type of resistance from the person, this is certainly an effective tool.”

Civil rights advocates expressed alarm at the plan, saying ICE officers already face criticism for their use of force with little oversight or accountability while enforcing Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown.

Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy project director on policing at the American Civil Liberties Union, told the Associated Press that she questioned the use of the devices for civil immigration enforcement.

“ICE spent the last year showing this country they are too quick to use force. Now they will be able to deploy electric shocks with the slight push of a button that maybe nobody else can see them do,” she said. “Introducing gloves that can so easily be used to deliver terrible pain in encounters is a recipe for harm to the public.”

Peters said he believed ICE’s planned purchase would likely be the largest from the company to date. He said he could envision ICE officers using the gloves to help remove uncooperative subjects from cars and houses and in and out of detention facilities.

The manufacturer warns the device should not be used as punishment, against people merely exhibiting “verbal defiance or belligerence” or on high-risk populations such as children, pregnant women or elderly or disabled people.

Jeff Niklaus, the founder and CEO of Compliant Technologies, wrote in an email: “Unfortunately, we are unable to speak on this subject.”

articles.title: These seaside apartments were a ghost city - then police say scammers moved in
articles.excerpt:
Scammers busted in Southeast Asia's biggest ghost town

From a distance, Malaysia's Forest City looks 3D-printed: a bristle of identical white blocks clustered on an otherwise unremarkable coastline.
...
articles.body_text:
Scammers busted in Southeast Asia's biggest ghost town

From a distance, Malaysia's Forest City looks 3D-printed: a bristle of identical white blocks clustered on an otherwise unremarkable coastline.

When it was unveiled by Chinese developers in 2016, the $100bn mega-project was pitched as "a dream paradise for all mankind": a special financial zone that could house some 700,000 residents. But a decade later, this 14-sq-km (3,400-acre) artificial island on Singapore's doorstep is thought to be inhabited by less than 1% of that.

Rows of eerily vacant skyscrapers loom over quiet streets. Inside empty apartments, benchtops and windows are filmed with dust.

"In 2016 they described it here like the golden city; very, very beautiful," says Jason Deng, a 56-year-old investor who was among the first to buy in Forest City, paying "a lot of money" for five properties.

"If I had known it was not so good I would not have bought so many apartments," he says now. "I thought it would be much, much better."

As it turns out, this is only a golden city for some people – and they're not the ones developers had hoped to attract.

In mid-July, Malaysian police raided two alleged scam operations spread across 32 premises in Forest City, arresting 335 people ‌and seizing assets worth about one million ringgit (£181,810; $245,000), including 313 computers, 1,557 mobile phones, 17 laptops and 10 modems.

From these two call centre hubs – one occupying 27 apartments across five storeys of a residential tower, the other spread between five bungalows – cryptocurrency syndicates ran investment and love scams targeting victims abroad, according to police.

Those arrested include 309 Chinese nationals, 19 Indonesians, three Malaysians and four Myanmar nationals. Johor police chief Ab Rahaman Arsad said authorities were working with Interpol to track down the mastermind behind the operations.

The BBC reached out to Forest City and Johor police for comment, but did not receive a response.

Experts and locals tell the BBC this is likely to be the tip of the iceberg – and a symptom of a global scam industry that is spreading, evolving, and professionalising.

Forest City was meant to house some 700,000 residents - but the current population is thought to be less than 1% of that

"The reality is that many of these organisations now resemble multinational corporations more than a traditional organised crime network or gang," says John Wojcik, an analyst at TRM Labs, which investigates crypto-facilitated crime. "They have dedicated recruitment teams, IT departments, money-laundering specialists and infrastructure."

Authorities and experts agree that the Forest City operations were probably staffed by criminals who had been driven out of Cambodia, a global nerve centre for transnational scams.

Over the past five years, this criminal sector has ballooned into a multi-billion-dollar industry, built on the forced labour of brutalised trafficking victims who work under threat of torture and abuse.

Since late last year, the Cambodian government has stepped up efforts to stamp out these operations. Authorities recently estimated that 300,000 people had left the country within a few months as raids on industrial-scale compounds intensified.

But these Malaysian offshoots do not appear to have been scam "compounds" in the traditional sense.

Compared to more infamous walled complexes in places like Sihanoukville or the Myanmar borderlands, the alleged scam hubs in Forest City appear almost white collar, reportedly staffed by local residents and sitting wall-to-wall with the homes of unsuspecting neighbours.

Forest City's sales gallery features a gigantic diorama of the complex in miniature

Kevin, a tenant who also works in property sales for Forest City, believes scammers are still operating in "condominiums or serviced apartments" in the complex. He asked for his name to be changed for fear of repercussions.

"We know what they're doing," he says. "This is actually a very common issue in Johor city and Kuala Lumpur, but especially in Forest City. Forest City is very special."

Part of what makes Forest City "special", according to Kevin, Wojcik and others, is the very thing that has gained it so much notoriety: its reputation as a semi-abandoned "ghost city".

"When we speak to clients or customers, the company teaches us to say 'we already have 23,000 residents living in this area'," says Kevin – but the reality, he quietly adds, is there are "less than 5,000".

"That's the reason" scammers have chosen Forest City to set up shop, he suggests.

"They have their own privacy... Nobody comes here."

Shuttered buildings and dilapidated infrastructure are a common sight in Forest City

There are several factors which precipitated what many see as the downfall of Forest City.

Spearheaded by Country Garden, one of China's largest property developers, and Danga 88, a private company controlled by Malaysian Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar, the project was initially dreamed up as an eco-friendly metropolis for well-heeled Chinese clients. Featuring a high-end hotel, golf course and water park, the resort-style city's seafront offices and apartments were expected to be in high demand.

But the combined weight of the Covid pandemic, China's spiralling property slump and constricted borrowing limits for its citizens have sunk those sky-high ambitions, and all but ground the project to a standstill.

The lights are still on, but almost no-one is home.

And that appears to  have made the complex a honeypot for scammers.

"Forest City reflects the conditions organised crime have been targeting for years - a flagship location marketed as a prestigious, luxury, master-planned smart city that never came close to fulfilling that vision," Wojcik says.

"Developments like this offer precisely what these syndicates look for: modern infrastructure, large numbers of vacant properties, and international connectivity all wrapped around the veneer of legitimate economic activity to ensure that the criminal nature of what goes on inside remains unnoticed."

With this in mind, the glittering facade of Forest City echoes a more infamous metropolis 1,800 kilometres (1,120 miles) to the north: Shwe Kokko, the so-called resort city on Myanmar's Thai border, which is one of the world's most notorious scam hubs.

Built by the private Chinese conglomerate Yatai, Shwe Kokko markets itself as a safe holiday destination for Chinese tourists and a haven for the super-rich. But behind its tree-lined streets and luxury villas is a nexus of fraud, money-laundering and human trafficking.

The complex sits on Malaysia's southernmost tip, less than five kilometres (three miles) from Singapore

For all its headwinds, and despite the fact that only 15 to 20% of the originally proposed project has been completed, Forest City similarly still markets itself as an up-and-coming hotbed for property investment, tech innovation and tax-free business ventures.

Such entrepreneurial packaging serves as a Trojan horse for scammers wanting to set up shop without drawing unwanted attention – and allows them to perpetrate their fraud more effectively.

Wojcik explains that "when scam syndicates can embed themselves behind seemingly legitimate businesses in ordinary commercial developments, they not only become more difficult to detect and disrupt, they become capable of exerting serious amounts of power and influence through the massive profits they generate".

Such power and influence in turn allows scammers to professionalise in other ways.

Though human trafficking still largely fuels much of the scam industry's labour force, there is now a noticeable trend of syndicate operators recruiting and retaining experienced scammers with higher pay and better working conditions.

Meanwhile, in the same Telegram groups where scam jobs are being advertised, career scammers are also now posting detailed resumes, outlining their experience in fraudulent activities and emphasising their eagerness to work.

"It's a sign the industry is maturing into a more professionalised criminal enterprise," Wojcik explains, "while coercion and exploitation still remain widespread".

The Forest City raids highlight a transnational scam industry that is shifting in size and shape. But this is far from the first time such operations have been detected in Malaysia.

Throughout 2022, before the industry gained widespread global attention, Malaysian authorities raided several scam centres operating out of bungalows and condominiums in the southern state of Johor, the northern state of Penang and the capital city of Kuala Lumpur.

Yet while these and other major crackdowns sent a message of zero tolerance to fraud syndicates, Wojcik notes that Malaysia has remained home to influential criminal networks - and that "any signs of large-scale re-emergence deserve close attention".

The $100-billion dollar complex's quiet streets and deserted beaches have earned it a reputation as a "ghost city"

In Forest City, such signs may already be emerging.

Kevin says it's long been an "open secret" that scams are happening here, and that "the only shocking thing is that the police were effective".

He's certain there are more, too – but is unperturbed at the idea that his neighbours might be defrauding people out of hundreds of thousands of dollars.

"For me, I don't care," he says. "It's not my business... I work here just for the salary."

Phillip, whose name we have also changed, moved to Forest City from Singapore last year, attracted by the relatively cheap property market and the idea that he could get more value for his money. He works in tech, and says he is "very focused" on the topic of cyber protection.

"Yes they [the scammers] might be on my doorstep, they might be my neighbours... [they] could be one of the ones that's running one of these syndicates. At the end of the day, it doesn't matter where you go – this is going to happen."

He says he was "not surprised" to hear about the reports of scam centres in his complex. What has surprised him is the fact that "more and more people are moving" to Forest City.

One of the reasons he chose the development where he lives is because of the peace and quiet, he says – but he's pleased to see that it is evolving from a "ghost town" into a place where people seem to want to be.

"So many people have lost money on these developments," he points out. "But the last three months, you see the lights on in the condos. You've gone from one in 20 to maybe one in five."

Inside Malaysia's Chinese-built 'ghost city'

Fake Australian, Chinese and Brazilian police stations: BBC goes inside a seized scam compound

The Chinese mafia's downfall in a lawless casino town

Casinos, high-rises and fraud: The BBC visits a bizarre city built on scams

articles.title: How a 97-year-old escaped deadly Indian floods on a banana raft
articles.excerpt:
A woman wades through floodwaters outside her inundated house at a village in Assam's Sivasagar

Well past midnight on 19 July, as floodwaters surged through a village in India's northeastern state of...
articles.body_text:
A woman wades through floodwaters outside her inundated house at a village in Assam's Sivasagar

Well past midnight on 19 July, as floodwaters surged through a village in India's northeastern state of Assam, Bornali Baruah and her husband were trying to save his 97-year-old mother.

Almost bedridden, Lokada Duarah could not walk. There was no boat, no rescue team and no neighbour available to help. So they lifted her onto a makeshift raft made of banana trunks, and carried her through the rushing water towards safety.

"Everyone was trying to save themselves," Baruah says.

An hour later, she says, the three of them reached a shelter camp on a national highway some distance away from their house in Charing village in Sivasagar district, one of the worst flood-affected districts.

The water was three to four feet deep and the current so strong that they had to move slowly, holding each other's hands and using sticks to steady themselves.

By then, Baruah's home was disappearing beneath the flood. The water would eventually rise to about five feet inside it.

Baruah quit journalism to concentrate on animal husbandry

The scene in Charing was part of a much wider disaster unfolding across Assam.

The latest figures put the death toll from floods at 100, with 10 districts and 456 villages affected and about 140,000 people impacted. Fifty-two relief camps have been set up. Overall, the floods have affected nearly 1.2 million people across 25 districts, damaged more than 19,000 houses and left more than 75,000 people in 252 relief camps.

The floods have been particularly severe in parts of Upper Assam, where villages like Charing that do not usually flood have been inundated.

For Baruah, 40, the shock is especially profound.

"This is the first flood we have experienced in this area in our lifetime," she says.

Baruah has lived in Charing since birth, and her ancestors lived here before her. She recalls hearing about a major flood in 1950, long before she was born, but nothing like this had happened during her lifetime.

Her home sits in a landscape criss-crossed by rivers, though none runs immediately beside it. The single-storey, eight-room house is about 25km (15 miles) from Sivasagar town; the Brahmaputra is roughly 20km away, the Dikhow 12km, the Jhanji 10km and the Mitong just 5km.

A 97-year-old Lokada Duarah was carried onto a banana tree trunk and taken to safety after floodwaters rose around her home

A boy uses a makeshift banana raft to navigate floodwaters in Assam

She had never imagined the water would reach her doorstep. But when it did, the flood threatened not only her home, but the livelihood she had spent years building.

Baruah was once a full-time journalist. In 2016, she left the profession to take up animal husbandry, and three years later was named Assam's 'Best Livestock Farmer'.

Her farm grew to around 300 goats, 500 ducks and 1,000 chickens, along with fish. The flood destroyed much of it.

She says she lost most of her goats, 300 ducks, 300 chickens and a sizeable amount of fish, as well as the machine she used to make animal feed. Furniture, laptops, vehicles and the family's collection of books were also destroyed.

None of her livestock was insured. "There is no insurance system here for livestock, especially goats," she says.

The first warning came on 17 July, when the Jhanji river began to rise. Two days later, the Dikhow and Mitong spilled into surrounding areas as the Brahmaputra and its tributaries swelled rapidly.

Several rivers breached their embankments, Baruah says, sending powerful currents through towns and villages.

About a day after the water began rising, she and her family abandoned their home. By then, the water inside the house was four feet deep. They spent the next 10 days in a relief camp.

Baruah and her family abandoned their home nearly a day after the water began rising

For five days in the camp there was no electricity or mobile connectivity and Baruah could not even charge her phone. The government provided the family with a relief kit containing rice, lentils and cooking oil.

Help also came from strangers at the camp. A young woman whom Bornali had never met, helped with food, cleaning and looking after her 60 surviving goats.  Another took responsibility for treating and feeding animals that had fallen ill.

But why did the water reach a place that Baruah says had never flooded before?

Dhrubajyoti Sahariah, a professor of geography and director of the Centre for Brahmaputra Studies at Gauhati University, says flooding itself is natural in the Brahmaputra Valley,  a lowland region in Assam. What has changed is the "frequency, intensity and severity of floods well beyond historical norms".

The Brahmaputra, one of the world's largest multi-channel rivers, ranks among the top five globally for both water discharge and sediment load. Much of that sediment comes from Tibet, where the river originates.

A family shelters inside a tent in Sivasagar district, among more than 5,000 people lodged in 252 relief camps

Amit Giri holds a photo of his father, Siv Sankar Giri, who died in the floods, outside their damaged home in Sivasagar. He is among 100 people killed in the floods.

As it enters Assam's vast floodplains, home to some 28 million people and hemmed in by hills, it slows and deposits sediment, fuelling erosion and floods. Flooding is an annual feature of life in Assam, but some years are far worse: the 2004 floods alone affected 12 million people and killed 251.

In the recent floods, Sahariah says, continuous heavy rainfall in Upper Assam and neighbouring Nagaland's Mon district triggered severe flooding and large-scale silt deposition in Sivasagar, Charaideo and Jorhat.

Sahariah says floods are reaching areas once spared because more people have settled on active floodplains, forests have been cleared, mining and hill-cutting have increased sediment in rivers, and roads, bridges and other infrastructure have been built without adequately accounting for the region's hydrology.

Yet Assam cannot manage the Brahmaputra on its own. Many of its tributaries originate in the surrounding hill states, while flood-control measures are largely planned within Assam.

"What is needed is basin-scale planning," Sahariah says, along with greater coordination between states and better understanding of the rivers' changing geography.

For Baruah, however, the science has become painfully personal.

Only 60 of Baruah's goats survived the floods

She has returned to the area around her flood-damaged home. For now, she and her family are staying at a neighbour's house nearby, hoping to move back into their own home within a week.

Baruah says she does not intend to leave Charing. Moving away, she says, requires economic and social circumstances that her family simply does not have.

So she is beginning to think about how to live with a threat that was, until now, largely absent from her life.

She says that if heavy rain comes again, she would need to raise the house higher, perhaps by building up its foundation. She is not yet sure how she would manage it or pay for it. The family would also need a raised platform where they could retreat to safety, and they would stock food and drinking water in advance.

Baruah is learning to live with the possibility of more floods – and to prepare for them. Did she feel like a climate refugee?

"No. If we regain our economic and mental strength, life will return to the way it was before."

"We will have to learn to coexist with the floods."

articles.title: Babylon Bee sues New Mexico officials over law requiring AI disclaimers on political satire
articles.excerpt: Alliance Defending Freedom counsel Jim Campbell says New Mexico’s HB 182 crosses a dangerous line by penalizing political humor, calling forced disclaimers unconstitutional government coercion that th...
articles.body_text:
Alliance Defending Freedom counsel Jim Campbell says New Mexico’s HB 182 crosses a dangerous line by penalizing political humor, calling forced disclaimers unconstitutional government coercion that threatens core political speech.

FIRST ON FOX — Should political satire come with a warning label?

A New Mexico law requiring disclaimers on certain AI-generated political content, including parody and satire, is being challenged in court by Christian satire news site The Babylon Bee.

HB 182, passed in 2024, amended New Mexico’s Campaign Reporting Act to add disclosure requirements for political advertisements containing what the law defines as "materially deceptive media." The law mandates that relevant images, video or audio manipulated or created through artificial intelligence must display a prominent AI disclaimer identifying the content as created or manipulated by artificial intelligence.

The Bee, which frequently pokes fun at political candidates and issues, argues the state law violates fundamental free speech rights and due process.

On Tuesday, the humor site filed a lawsuit against state officials, with the help of the legal organization Alliance Defending Freedom ("ADF"), arguing that the law chills their speech and destroys the intent of comedy.

TENNESSEE MAN JAILED 37 DAYS OVER FACEBOOK MEME MOCKING CHARLIE KIRK'S DEATH WINS $850K SETTLEMENT

A man is seen casting a vote at a New Mexico polling site. (Nicholas Roberts/AFP/Getty Images)

"This disclaimer alters the content of the satire and parody The Bee wants to express by alerting the viewer to the satirical or parodical nature of the communication and thereby depriving the expression of its rhetorical force," the complaint states. "Put simply, HB 182 spoils the joke as it begins, each and every time." The website says it is not willing to publish content with the mandated label because it would alter its message.

Seth Dillon, CEO of The Babylon Bee, told Fox News Digital that the law's disclosure requirement imposes a "deeper problem" of compelled speech.

"New Mexico is stuffing words into our mouths, forcing us to say things we wouldn’t say otherwise," he explained.

Just this past week, the Bee posted a satirical AI-generated travel advertisement mocking the Democratic "utopia" of New Mexico and the state's Supreme Court justice David K. Thomson, who will appear on the November ballot. In the fake advertisement, an AI-generated video of Thomson announces the court rules "against the Second Amendment, the First Amendment or any other amendment that lets people do things."

THOMAS, GORSUCH TARGET LANDMARK RULING TRUMP SAYS PROTECTS THE 'FAKE NEWS'

The Bee argued it intends to create content with AI that parodies or satirizes other candidates or ballot questions in the state's elections. Dillon said, though they have not faced penalties yet, they are suing preemptively to protect their rights.

"The concern is real, but we don't censor ourselves," Dillon told Fox News Digital. "If a joke we want to tell is likely to violate the law, we'll tell it, anyway — both because we have a right to, and we refuse to do the tyrant's work for him. If penalties are imposed, we'll sue to defend our rights. In this case, we're suing preemptively to settle the matter before it escalates to that point."

The Babylon Bee is fighting a New Mexico state law with the backing of Alliance Defending Freedom. (Getty Images)

AI CHATBOTS TAKE HEAT OVER LEFT-WING BIAS: ‘NO LONGER BE CONSIDERED NEUTRAL’

The Bee and ADF also argue the law discriminates based on content, by giving a blanket exemption for content appearing in news stories or editorials while entertainment, satire, parody, cartoons and memes are restricted.

The complaint names the seven members of the New Mexico Ethics Commission, which enforces the challenged provisions, as defendants, and calls on the court to issue injunctions preventing enforcement. The filing also claims that individual violations of the law can draw fines up to $1,000 and those can total up to $20,000 with additional violations.

"The government cannot decide which political speech is allowed and which is forbidden," ADF Chief Legal Counsel Jim Campbell told Fox News Digital. "Whenever government officials determine what political speech is acceptable, dissent disappears and democracy suffers. So what we're arguing here is that the First Amendment ensures that the Babylon Bee and anyone else in New Mexico can continue to post political ads and political messages — including satire and parody, addressing some of the most important political questions facing the people of New Mexico."

Campbell noted that concerns about the legislation also came from Democratic state officials.

New Mexico Governor Michelle Lujan Grisham speaks at a rally hosted by the Democratic Party of New Mexico at Ted M. Gallegos Community Center in Albuquerque, New Mexico, on November 3, 2022. (Saul Loeb/AFP via Getty Images)

Upon signing HB 182, Democratic Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham wrote that portions of the bill were ambiguous and could "pose legal issues."

The complaint also cites an advisory opinion issued by Attorney General Raúl Torrez in July 2025, concluding that HB 182's disclaimer requirement on satire and parody was "likely unconstitutional on its face."

Fox News Digital reached out to Grisham's office for comment but did not immediately hear back.

The New Mexico Ethics Commission called the lawsuit "baseless" in a statement to Fox News Digital.

"Babylon Bee’s pre-enforcement lawsuit is baseless," a spokesperson said. "The Commission has never taken action to enforce the AI-disclaimer requirements in Section 1-19-26.4 of the Campaign Reporting Act, much less for political parody and satire. While the Babylon Bee has a First Amendment right to mock New Mexico, it does not have a right to extract attorneys’ fees from the State."

A sign welcomes motorists to New Mexico at the state's border with Colorado near Antonito (Robert Alexander/Archive Photos/Getty Images)

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Alliance Defending Freedom has represented the Babylon Bee in other lawsuits challenging similar censorship laws in Hawaii and California against deepfakes and political satire. The laws were struck down after courts ruled in each case that the state laws were unconstitutional.

Campbell said they will continue to fight similar legislation as it crops up around the country.

"We're trying to ensure that political debate remains robust and that the government doesn't tell its citizens which political speech is allowed," Campbell said.

"We need for people to be allowed to express their views and, ultimately, we need political debate and discourse to be open and free so that the American people can determine what's best for our country moving forward," he added.

Kristine Parks is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Read more.

articles.title: US military fires on cargo vessel it said sought to break Iran blockade
articles.excerpt:
The United States military has said it fired on a ship attempting to break its blockade of Iranian ports in the Gulf of Oman.

The attack on Tuesday comes amid a period of relative calm in the US-Isra...
articles.body_text:
The United States military has said it fired on a ship attempting to break its blockade of Iranian ports in the Gulf of Oman.

The attack on Tuesday comes amid a period of relative calm in the US-Israeli war with Iran, with attacks mostly paused since a 13-day escalation in July. That came after a ceasefire as part of a memorandum of understanding (MoU) signed by the US and Iran in June appeared to collapse.

In a statement, US Central Command (CENTCOM), which oversees the Middle East, said a Navy helicopter fired two Hellfire missiles at the Panama-flagged Vela Nova cargo vessel.

It said the vessel “attempted to transit the Gulf of Oman and violate the U.S. blockade against Iran by sailing toward an Iranian port”.

The attack targeted the ship’s engine room and disabled its steering gear, CENTCOM said, alleging the crew “ignored repeated warnings from American forces”.

It did not say if any crew members were wounded in the attack. In its statement on Tuesday, CENTCOM said US forces had disabled 55 commercial vessels throughout its blockade on Iranian ports, disabled three “non-compliant vessels”, and boarded two.

The US reimposed its naval blockade of Iranian ports amid the recent return to fighting, with Iran again reasserting its control over the Strait of Hormuz. Both of those conditions had been lifted as part of the June MoU, which was meant to launch renewed negotiations on a more lasting peace, as well as the future of crippling sanctions on Iran and its nuclear programme.

Efforts to return to an agreement have so far yielded little progress, with Trump on Monday appearing to up the ante as he called for reparations from Iran for “50 years” of damage. Tehran has previously called for reconstruction funding to be part of any deal, with the June MoU containing a preliminary plan for a $300bn fund.

The conflict has been further complicated in the latest bout of fighting by attacks by the Yemen-based Houthis on ships in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait, another key trade route in the region.

Iran, for its part, has largely focused its diplomatic efforts on direct talks with Oman to determine new shipping lines in the Strait of Hormuz, an arterial waterway through which 20 percent of the world’s maritime fossil fuel trade transited prior to the war launched by the US and Israel on February 28.

Iran’s semi-official Tasnim news agency on Tuesday quoted Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council, saying the Strait of Hormuz “will not be opened until the United States changes its behaviour and accepts Iran’s conditions”.

He maintained that any agreement with Oman would be “separate” from the issue of the strait’s closure.

Pakistan’s Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi, meanwhile, arrived in Tehran on Tuesday for talks with Iranian officials, in the latest effort towards wider mediation of the war.

articles.title: Jets player taken off field in ambulance during training camp joint practice with Buccaneers
articles.excerpt:
Shawne Merriman details why he believes NFL training camps now are not preventing more injuries due to players not being in football shape.

A scary moment occurred in New Jersey on Tuesday when a joi...
articles.body_text:
Shawne Merriman details why he believes NFL training camps now are not preventing more injuries due to players not being in football shape.

A scary moment occurred in New Jersey on Tuesday when a joint training camp practice between the New York Jets and Tampa Bay Buccaneers was halted due to an apparent medical emergency.

A Jets player, later revealed to be cornerback Qwan'tez Stiggers, was taken off the practice field at the team's facility in Florham Park in an ambulance.

According to ESPN, Stiggers was given an IV while on the turf.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Cornerback Qwan'tez Stiggers of the New York Jets celebrates a stop during a game against the Washington Commanders at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, N.J., on Aug. 10, 2024. (Getty Images)

Head coach Aaron Glenn said Stiggers came to the bench after a play and "passed out" but was conscious. Glenn then praised the medical staff.

Glenn added that Stiggers is "able to talk" and is "for the most part...good."

Temperatures in Florham Park were reaching 85 degrees on Tuesday and had approached triple-digits over the weekend.

Cornerback Qwan'tez Stiggers and linebacker Charles Surratt of the New York Jets make a stop against the Washington Commanders at MetLife Stadium in East Rutherford, N.J., on Aug. 10, 2024. (Getty Images)

CAM NEWTON BACKS AARON RODGERS, CLAIMING NFL 'PLAYERS, COACHES AND EXECUTIVES' USED FAKE COVID VACCINE CARDS

It was quite an eventful practice, as at least three fights broke out, one of which even included Stiggers.

Stiggers did not attend college but instead played for the Fan Controlled League out of high school. From there, he spent a season in the Canadian Football League playing for the Toronto Argonauts.

Geno Smith No. 7 of the New York Jets stretches during a joint practice between the Tampa Bay Buccaneers and New York Jets at Atlantic Health Jets Training Center in Florham Park, N.J., on Aug. 11, 2026. (Getty Images)

He was drafted by the Jets in the fifth round of the 2024 NFL Draft and appeared in 15 games last year, becoming the first person since 1999 to be drafted straight out of the CFL. He made 27 tackles and recovered two fumbles this past season.

Follow Fox News Digital’s sports coverage on X, and subscribe to the Fox News Sports Huddle newsletter.

articles.title: Taliban wipes out decades of progress as 2.4M Afghan girls remain locked out of school, UN agency says
articles.excerpt: UConn international student Sadaf Zarei discusses the plight of the Iranian women's soccer team, whose captain dropped her asylum bid in Australia fearing for her family's safety from the oppressive I...
articles.body_text:
UConn international student Sadaf Zarei discusses the plight of the Iranian women's soccer team, whose captain dropped her asylum bid in Australia fearing for her family's safety from the oppressive Iranian regime. Zarei highlights the pervasive digital blackouts and human rights abuses, advocating for an end to the "criminal terrorist entity" currently in power.

Five years after the Taliban reclaimed reclaimed Afghanistan, 2.4 million girls remain locked out of secondary school, wiping away decades of progress and leaving a generation of young women without access to the classroom.

Afghanistan is now the only country in the world that formally prohibits girls and women from receiving an education beyond the primary level, according to UNESCO, which issued a new call Tuesday for the "immediate and unconditional" restoration of their right to education.

The United Nations agency warned that the consequences of the Taliban's policies now reach far beyond the classroom, with women barred from most paid jobs and public-facing professions and facing restrictions on their ability to travel without a male guardian.

MOSCOW, TALIBAN FORGE MILITARY ALLIANCE IN POWER GRAB AFTER US AFGHANISTAN EXIT: REPORTS

Afghan girls participate in a lesson at Tajrobawai Girls High School, in Herat, Afghanistan, Thursday, Nov. 25, 2021. (AP Photo/Petros Giannakouris)

"Women have been erased from public life, and as a new generation of girls grows without an education, their future becomes increasingly dark," UNESCO said in a statement.

The Taliban swept back into power on Aug. 15, 2021, as U.S. and NATO forces withdrew from Afghanistan after two decades of war.

The Taliban soon barred girls from secondary schools and later expanded the restrictions to universities, employment and other areas of public life.

Despite years of pressure from the United Nations, humanitarian groups, human rights advocates and several Islamic countries, the Taliban has refused to lift the education restrictions and has maintained that the issue is a domestic matter, according to The Associated Press.

IRAN AGREES NOT TO EXECUTE EIGHT WOMEN TIED TO ANTI-REGIME PROTESTS AFTER TRUMP'S PUBLIC APPEAL

The Taliban has refused to lift its education restrictions on girls and women despite longstanding international pressure. (© UNESCO/Navid Rahi)

The impact has been a dramatic reversal of the educational gains made by Afghan girls during the previous two decades.

While girls had severely limited access to schooling in 2001, nearly 1 million were enrolled in secondary education by 2021, according to UNESCO.

Five years later, an estimated 2.4 million girls are excluded from secondary education.

"Five years is not a temporary interruption in a child's education," Hoda Jaberian, UNESCO's program coordinator for education in emergencies, said during a video news conference Tuesday, according to The AP. "It is clearly almost an entire secondary school cycle."

UNESCO warned that denying education to girls while restricting women's ability to work could deepen Afghanistan's already severe economic problems.

Nearly half of Afghanistan's population lives below the poverty line, according to UNESCO, which said preventing women from studying and working further limits their ability to support their families and contribute to the country's economy.

The agency also warned that excluding girls from school can damage their mental and physical well-being and increase the risk of early marriage.

The effects could also reach Afghan boys.

UNESCO said the Taliban's ban on female teachers teaching boys is worsening teacher shortages and undermining the quality of education across Afghanistan.

TRUMP BETS ECONOMIC PRESSURE CAN SQUEEZE IRAN AS REGIME’S OWN FAILURES DEEPEN THE PAIN

Women wear burqas in Kabul, Afghanistan on May 7, 2022. (Sayed Khodaiberdi Sadat/Anadolu Agency via Getty Images)

With formal secondary and higher education closed to women and girls, UNESCO says it has turned to community-based education, literacy and skills development programs and psychosocial support to keep them learning.

Nearly 70,000 people have participated in UNESCO's programs, with women accounting for 73% of the learners, according to the agency.

Some literacy and skills classes take place in community spaces and in the homes of facilitators with the knowledge of authorities, according to The AP. More than 1,000 literacy facilitators are involved, most of whom have been trained by UNESCO and its partners.

UNESCO said a recent study found evidence that its literacy and skills programs have helped increase household incomes and improve livelihoods.

The agency acknowledged, however, that such efforts cannot replace formal schooling.

"Afghanistan's girls and women have the right to learn, to work, to move freely, and to shape their own futures," UNESCO said, adding that "the world must not look away until their human rights are restored."

UNESCO said it would continue working with local communities and partners to maintain alternative opportunities for Afghan women and girls while pressing for the education ban to be lifted.

"UNESCO continues to call for the immediate and unconditional restoration of girls and women's right to secondary and higher education," Jaberian said Tuesday. "It is not negotiable. It's a basic human right and we reiterate that there is no substitute for this."

The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

articles.title: Male redback spiders invite cannibalism through a ‘self-sacrificial somersault’ during sex – but why?
