Speaking of One Nation’s immigration bill, Ted O’Brien tells News24 that he’s open to working with “anybody who is going to make Australia safer.”

He says the Coalition are working on their own immigration bill, and that the opposition “won’t be political” in dealing with the issue.

double quotation markWe are open to working with anybody who is going to make Australia safer. I don’t particularly care where they come from.

We’re yet to see all the detail, right? So if, at the end of the day, ours is a better bill, of course, we’ll be pursuing ours over it but I think the right thing to do by Australia is not to be overly political on these issues. If somebody wants to genuinely bring forward a bill, absolutely, let’s engage in good faith, have a look at it.

In two separate cases in June 2022 and in November 2023, the high court struck down Coalition-era laws that gave the home affairs minister power to strip dual nationals of Australian citizenship for engaging in suspected terrorist activities.

The shadow home affairs minister, Jonno Duniam, also told News24 this morning that the Coalition would work with One Nation on the bill:

double quotation markWe’ll work with them on that legislation, it is important we get it right. We’d love to see it go off to a Senate committee to make sure that people who know a little more than we in the Senate know, legal experts to make sure it is robust.

We want to shut the door on terrorists, we’ve been trying for years to do this.

Albanese to meet with Vietnam’s president at Parliament House

The president and general secretary of Vietnam, To Lam, is in Canberra today, currently meeting with the governor general, Sam Mostyn.

Lam arrived in Sydney yesterday, in time for the government to announce that VietJet would start flying into the new Western Sydney airport.

The president will then head over to Parliament House to meet with Anthony Albanese and the pair will later provide joint statements to the media.

We can probably expect China and Donald Trump to be on the agenda for the talks.

Malinauskas didn’t consult with federal counterparts on AI royal commission

Yesterday’s announcement that South Australia would hold a royal commission into artificial intelligence would have taken some by surprise yesterday – including the federal government.

The SA premier, Peter Malinauskas, has done his own media rounds this morning plugging the announcement, but says he didn’t give the commonwealth a heads up.

double quotation markNo, this is something that we’re pursuing as a state government because of course within our federation sub-national governments or states are responsible for a whole range of areas of service delivery that are quite separate to considerations of the federal government.

Earlier, independent MP Kate Chaney told RN Breakfast it was good the premier was “realising the magnitude of this issue” but said a royal commission wasn’t the right mechanism.

double quotation markIt’s very slow, takes too long. I wrote a letter to the Coalition and some others a few weeks ago pushing for or seeking support for a joint standing committee on AI because I do think we need parliamentary oversight … But Peter Malinauskas has at least recognised the urgency of this issue.

Speaking of One Nation’s immigration bill, Ted O’Brien tells News24 that he’s open to working with “anybody who is going to make Australia safer.”

He says the Coalition are working on their own immigration bill, and that the opposition “won’t be political” in dealing with the issue.

double quotation markWe are open to working with anybody who is going to make Australia safer. I don’t particularly care where they come from.

We’re yet to see all the detail, right? So if, at the end of the day, ours is a better bill, of course, we’ll be pursuing ours over it but I think the right thing to do by Australia is not to be overly political on these issues. If somebody wants to genuinely bring forward a bill, absolutely, let’s engage in good faith, have a look at it.

In two separate cases in June 2022 and in November 2023, the high court struck down Coalition-era laws that gave the home affairs minister power to strip dual nationals of Australian citizenship for engaging in suspected terrorist activities.

The shadow home affairs minister, Jonno Duniam, also told News24 this morning that the Coalition would work with One Nation on the bill:

double quotation markWe’ll work with them on that legislation, it is important we get it right. We’d love to see it go off to a Senate committee to make sure that people who know a little more than we in the Senate know, legal experts to make sure it is robust.

We want to shut the door on terrorists, we’ve been trying for years to do this.

PM ‘still under the thumb of the gambling companies’: Greens senator

Greens senator Sarah Hanson-Young says she’s sceptical of negotiations between the opposition and government over gambling reforms, worried they won’t go far enough.

She stops by the cameras stationed outside the Senate entrance:

double quotation markWe haven’t seen any details from the government, as to how far they’re willing to go, I am sceptical that the prime minister is still under the thumb of the gambling companies.

She also responds to the bill Pauline Hanson wants to introduce a bill to strengthen powers to cancel or refuse passports and toughen bail laws for terrorism charges. It’s legally tricky territory with the high court previously ruling that a minister could not strip the citizenship of a dual national.

double quotation markPauline Hanson is a one trick pony. She preys on people’s fears and on their grievances … If Pauline Hanson really wants to help people in Australia, become with [the] cost of living crisis, she would focus on that rather than on where people have come from.

Albanese congratulates new ACTU secretary

Anthony Albanese has congratulated Melissa Donnelly, who will replace Sally McManus as secretary of the Australian Council of Trade Unions.

In a statement on Monday night, the prime minister said McManus leaves the job with “the gratitude and well-wishes of the entire Australian labour movement.”

double quotation markMelissa will assume the Secretary role at the end of August after seven successful years leading and growing the Community and Public Sector Union … It is a tremendous honour to lead the Australian union movement on behalf of all working people, and one I know Mel will succeed in.

McManus and the ACTU president, Michele O’Neil, both announced they’d step down after eight years in the job, but the later will finish up a little later this year.

Ted O’Brien says that just because the Japanese government has downplayed melon-gate, doesn’t mean Anthony Albanese’s gaffe isn’t a “national embarrassment”.

We’ve seen reports Japan sent a memo to the government last month suggesting they did not believe the prime minister’s comments about the pair of crown melons he received as a gift were made with “ill intention”.

O’Brien tells RN Breakfast that the fact that he’s speaking about the issue on national radio shows how bad the issue is, even if the Japanese government isn’t fazed.

He also confirms that he held a meeting with the Japanese ambassador to Australia to “express my deep regret about the prime minister’s remarks”.

double quotation markThis is one of our most important partnerships. This is a national embarrassment. Now, we can say, ‘yes, but, you know, some people think it isn’t.’ Well, here we are on national radio talking about it. The Australian prime minister has been inappropriate …

I’m the shadow minister for foreign affairs. I don’t have the authority to apologise on behalf of the government or the prime minister. If I did have that authority, I would have done so.

Opposition working ‘constructively’ with government on gambling

Anthony Albanese and Angus Taylor are still ironing out amendments to the government’s gambling legislation, which we know will involve some changes to inducements – but not much else.

The shadow foreign affairs spokesperson, Ted O’Brien, can’t say whether Coalition party room meeting will today land on a position.

He tells RN Breakfast he personally believes in the “importance of personal choice” but also that footy time should be “family time” and not gambling time.

double quotation markPeople who want to have a punt should be allowed to have a punt. But we should also recognise it comes with harmful effects that need to be addressed … we’ve got to protect children from being exposed unnecessarily to gambling ads when really they should be spending time with family. I also believe in the importance of law and order, which is why we need to ensure that we push back against any predatory illegal behaviour of inducements and whatnot.

Yesterday Taylor also singled out acting on “predatory” inducements – which suggests we might not see a total ban on gambling inducements.

What happened to Tony Burke’s migration speech?

We’re all still pretty baffled in Canberra over what happened to Tony Burke’s National Press Club address.

The home affairs minister had been scheduled to address the press club and announce significant immigration reforms – but the speech was postponed at the 11th hour.

We’re told no one even asked about it at yesterday’s Labor caucus meeting.

Katy Gallagher is asked on RN Breakfast whether the new migration measures were finalised when cabinet also met yesterday, but she doesn’t say.

double quotation markThis is a big piece of work. Obviously we’ve been making a number of reductions. We’ve seen net overseas migration come down about 45% from its peak. There’s some additional work that Minister Burke is undertaking and when that work is complete he will announce what those measures are.

‘It’s not where everyone wants to be’, says Gallagher on gambling reforms

The finance minister says the government is negotiating with the Coalition on gambling inducements as it tries to find a pathway for its reforms through the Senate.

The prime minister in his televised address to caucus yesterday hinted some further action on tackling inducements, while the opposition says it wants to see “predatory inducements” for problem gamblers banned. It suggests we might see a partial ban on inducements, but not a full block.

Katy Gallagher has moved her way down the press gallery corridor and landed in the ABC’s RN Breakfast studio – she doesn’t have any further details on how negotiations are tracking.

She points to Labor’s national conference last month which agreed to explore how to better prevent online gaming and social media platforms from offering “embedded inducements” within video games and social media accounts.

She also defends the government’s response to gambling as a whole, after it took almost three years for the prime minister to respond to the landmark ‘you win some, you lose more’ parliamentary report.

double quotation markI accept it’s not where everyone wants to be, but it’s a very, very strong response to a problem that exists in our community.

‘He did not mean it’ Gallagher dragged into melon-gate

Katy Gallagher has also been asked to weigh in on the PM’s melon comments – you can see a hint of exasperation in her face as she’s asked about it on Channel 9.

I’m sure you don’t need a recap at this point, but just in case you missed it – Anthony Albanese told the Bush Deep podcast last month the Japanese prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, had given him a gift of two Japanese melons, and appeared to make hand gestures in front of his chest.

Gallagher says Albanese “did not mean it in the way that it’s been reported”.

double quotation markI accept that he did not intend those comments to be made the way that some media are reporting them. It’s an important relationship, he has a good relationship with the Japanese.

Earlier this morning Michaelia Cash called the comments an embarrassment and a “diplomatic incident”.

To give you a bit of context on how Japan has taken the comments, News.com.au reported the Japanese government said there had been “sensationalised reporting” over the incident in a memo sent last month, and that they did not believe there was “ill intention” in Albanese’s comments. They said there would be no action taken over the matter.

Government sticks to Treasury advice on cooling housing market

The finance minister, Katy Gallagher, has been tapped on the shoulder to do the media rounds this morning ahead of the RBA’s rates decision.

She’s asked repeatedly on channel nine whether the government takes some responsibility for the decline in the housing market, but says the advise from the Treasury department in the budget showed house prices would continue to grow but slow by 2%.

Yesterday big four bank Westpac said mortgage applications were down 20% between mid-May and the end of July, the period right after the federal budget was handed down.

Gallagher says there’s a range of factors influencing the housing market, not just the government’s changes to negative gearing and the capital gains tax discount:

double quotation markThere are other factors that influence the housing market, including the interest rate increases that we have seen over the last few months … the Treasury advice to us was that house prices would continue to grow slightly slower. Our focus on the housing market is making those tax changes so that first home buyers can get into the housing market, but also focusing on supply to make sure we’re building enough houses for people to buy.

Kate Chaney, who was on the inquiry with the late Labor MP Peta Murphy that handed down the landmark ‘you win some, you lose more’ report on gambling harm, says so far it seems the talks between the Coalition and Labor on a gambling reform package are “disappointing”.

Speaking to the ABC’s RN Breakfast a little earlier, the independent MP says the government has listened to the gambling lobby instead of the evidence.

Part of the government’s proposed reforms limit online gambling ads on television to three per hour between 6am and 8.30pm.

But Chaney says the last time ads were partially banned, the ads didn’t slow down – they just moved to different time slots.

double quotation markIn 2017, when the last round of partial restrictions came in, the money just moved around. And for example, gambling ads after 8.30 more than doubled, increased 131%. And I suspect that that’s what we’re going to see here too: is the money moving around.

I think it is about the government listening to the money and the power, not the people. The gambling companies make big political donations. They are present lobbyists in this building. We’re hearing their talking points coming out of the prime minister’s mouth. And the media companies and the sports codes make a lot of money out of gambling too. Unfortunately, Australians pay the cost for that. And the average Australian household loses more in gambling than they pay for in electricity. So this is our blind spot.

Independent MP Monique Ryan says Anthony Albanese’s now infamous interview with the Bush Deep podcast was “pretty cringe” and has joined critics who say the PM should apologise over his comments about the Japanese’s prime minister’s gift of melons.

Albanese told the podcast Sanae Takaichi had given him a gift of two Japanese melons, and appeared to make hand gestures in front of his chest.

Ryan told the Today Show this morning that “we can probably expect a bit better” from the PM.

double quotation markI think that that whole interview was pretty cringe. Let’s face it, the prime minister didn’t really cover himself with glory with that. And it’s disturbing to hear that the Japanese government has expressed some concerns about it.

We’re talking about a really special gift that the Japanese state has given to the country. And if I was the PM, I’d pick up the phone to the Japanese prime minister and apologise to her on this one.

Cabinet ministers have defended the PM and called it an issue “people are trying to blow up”, while Angus Taylor yesterday said Albanese should pick up the phone to Takaichi and apologise.

Joining the panel with Ryan, shadow cabinet minister Michaelia Cash called it a “diplomatic incident”.

double quotation markWhen the prime minister’s crude and dirty podcast banter is formally raised by the Japanese government. Anthony Albanese just has embarrassed himself. He’s embarrassed Australia. This is now a diplomatic incident because of the appalling behaviour of the prime minister.

The Reserve Bank’s latest interest rate decision is due at 2.30pm today, and the unanimous prediction is that they will hold the cash rate at 4.35% for a second meeting in a row.

Inflation is still running too hot at 3.8% in the year to June – miles above the RBA’s official 2.5% target.

But recent data shows inflation is not as high as had been expected, while unemployment is a touch higher – two signals for the RBA to sit on its hands for now.

While financial markets see virtually no chance of a hike today, they still see a nearly 50% chance of a move higher this year.

A number of economists see a November hike as the most likely next move; others reckon the next move will be down (although not until the second half of 2027).

That means all the attention will be on the statement the RBA board issues at the time of the decision, and whether the decision to hold rates is unanimous.

RBA watchers will also be listening for what message Michele Bullock, the governor, sends at her 3.30pm press conference.

Today the bank will also release its latest set of economic forecasts in the quarterly statement on monetary policy.

Experts reckon it will still show inflation heading back to target in the next 12 months, but any slippage would be a red flag that the bank might need to hike again.

The bank’s rate-setting board meets every six weeks.

Krishani Dhanji here with you, and we’re so back for another sitting fortnight after a winter break.

It’s negotiation city this week in Canberra with the government hunting for deals on its overhaul to the national disability insurance scheme, gambling reforms and news bargaining incentive. The Coalition is in the hot seat for all three of those with Anthony Albanese and Angus Taylor meeting yesterday and will continue to talk over the next couple of days.

Today the Reserve Bank will also make their latest interest rates decision which we’ll all be watching with eagle eyes.

Time to stretch these (slightly) rusty fingers and let’s get cracking!

articles.title: Colombia earthquake live updates: more than 100 dead and buildings collapsed after 7.4-magnitude quake
articles.excerpt:
More than a dozen buildings collapsed in aftermath of earthquake, which has also prompted evacuations

At least 111 have died and 87 people injured after dozens of buildings collapsed following a 7.4 ...
articles.body_text:
More than a dozen buildings collapsed in aftermath of earthquake, which has also prompted evacuations

At least 111 have died and 87 people injured after dozens of buildings collapsed following a 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck western Colombia on Monday morning – the largest to hit the country so far this century. After declaring a state of national disaster, Colombia’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said in an address to the nation that his government had deployed all of its capabilities “to protect lives, assist affected ‌communities and deliver aid wherever it is needed”. “The first priority is rescuing the people trapped under the rubble,” he said after around 1,600 buildings had been damaged, including at least 61 that completely collapsed.

The president declared an emergency to expedite funding for the quake recovery while saying he would visit the disaster zone. “We aren’t going to leave people alone. They are in our hearts and we are going to tend to people with our full determination,” he said.

The quake hit the remote Chocó region around 7.30am local time on Monday morning and was felt as far as the capital Bogotá (250 miles away), as well as neighbouring countries Ecuador, Venezuela and Panama. The epicentre was in San Jose Del Palmar, a community of about 4,800 people, and the initial quake was followed by two 2.8 and 4.8 magnitude aftershocks.

Local officials confirmed deaths across several regions, including the coffee region of Risaralda and in Valle del Cauca, while rescue teams race to free people trapped under debris of collapsed buildings. Among the worst-hit areas was the city of Pereira, where at least 40 people have been killed, according to the mayor. In the department of Chocó, at least 12 people were killed, according to the local governor there, and at least 27 deaths have been reported in the neighbouring Valle del Cauca department, including at least three children and including 15 people in Cali, Colombia’s third-largest city.

The United States and countries across Europe and Latin America offered support. The Trump administration is “closely monitoring” the earthquake, US secretary of state Marco Rubio said earlier, adding that Washington “stands ready to support” the people and the pro-Trump government. Other countries including Ecuador, France, Mexico and Brazil also offered support.

It all comes less than two months after two earthquakes devastated parts of Venezuela, killing more than 6,100 people.

Further to the last post: Mauricio Andrade, a firefighter in Colombia’s third-largest city of Cali, said his team had rescued two adult women and two children from a collapsed building.

As he spoke, his team was preparing to rescue more people from the rubble.

“They are alive,” he told Reuters. “We are making space so we can free them and get them out.”

Juan Carlos Osorio told Caracol Television that the collapse of one building “sounded like a bomb”, as he helped remove debris from a collapsed structure in Cali.

double quotation markAll of us neighbours are working together, forming human chains. We need heavy equipment. There are many people trapped.

Reports from Choco, near the epicentre of the quake, have been slowed by communications outages, with some areas still lacking mobile phone service hours after the earthquake. ‌

Governor Nubia Carolina Cordoba said 12 people had been killed and 84 injured in the largely rural area, as mentioned.

The quake’s heaviest casualties appeared to be concentrated in Risaralda, part of Colombia’s coffee-growing region. Pereira, the department’s capital, suffered extensive damage, with rescue workers continuing to search collapsed buildings for survivors.

A four-story building crumbled in Pereira during the quake, according to Reuters-verified video, while footage from Manizales showed one of the side towers of the city’s landmark neo-Gothic cathedral collapsing and scattering debris onto nearby streets.

Reuters footage showed rescue workers, police and volunteers shovelling debris by hand and loading rubble into trucks as they searched for trapped survivors. ‌Other footage showed damage to residential towers and emergency-service facilities, with debris crashing onto ambulances parked below.

Colombia’s Pacific region around the epicentre of the earthquake lies along the Ring of Fire, the line of seismic faults encircling the Pacific Ocean where most of the world’s quakes occur.

The Pacific, particularly the Choco region where the quake hit, is one of Colombia’s poorest and is nestled in dense jungle. Much of the region is reachable only by boat or plane, which may pose a problem for authorities in assessing the wider toll, as the AP reports.

Northwestern University seismologist Suzan van der Lee said the ​quake’s powerful magnitude, inland location and strike-slip motion may have amplified damage in populated valleys despite its considerable depth.

“This one was ​far below the crust, and in ‌theory it shouldn’t cause as much ​shaking,” she said, quoted by Reuters. “At this magnitude, it did actually ​cause a lot of shaking.”

The Colombia earthquake has left many people trapped under the debris of damaged buildings as their loved ones and rescue workers search through the rubble.

Search teams and civilians picked through the remains of destroyed buildings in the country’s third-largest city, Cali, passing large pieces of concrete and other rubble down a long line of volunteers.

“Our building has basically been left in ruins, and the building next to ours? Completely collapsed,” said Álvaro López, who cradled his dog as he watched the search.

The desperate scene recalled the searches still ongoing in neighbouring Venezuela weeks after that country was devastated by back-to-back quakes in June, the Associated Press reports.

Besides Cali, the quake-ravaged cities across western Colombia including Pereira, Quibdo and Manizales and was felt in neighboring Ecuador and Panama.

The epicentre was in San Jose Del Palmar, a community of about 4,800 people, and the initial quake was followed by two 2.8 and 4.8 magnitude aftershocks.

Local officials confirmed deaths across several regions, including the coffee region of Risaralda and in Valle del Cauca, while rescue teams race to free people trapped under debris of collapsed buildings. Among the worst-hit areas was the city of Pereira, where at least 40 people have been killed, according to the mayor. In the department of Chocó, at least 12 people were killed, according to the local governor there, and at least 27 deaths have been reported in the neighbouring Valle del Cauca department, including at least three children and including 15 people in Cali, Colombia’s third-largest city.

The United States and countries across Europe and Latin America offered support. The Trump administration is “closely monitoring” the earthquake, US secretary of state Marco Rubio said earlier, adding that Washington “stands ready to support” the people and the pro-Trump government. Other countries including Ecuador, France, Mexico and Brazil also offered support.

It all comes less than two months after two earthquakes devastated parts of Venezuela, killing more than 6,100 people.

The mayor of Pereira has declared a state of public emergency and manifest urgency, along with a curfew that will be in effect from 6pm on Monday until 5am Tuesday in the following areas: Centro, Comuna Universidad, and SubCentro de la Comuna Cuba.

A car-free day measure will also start at 4pm on Monday and all day on Tuesday. Classes in educational institutions are also suspended.

“As mayor of Pereira, I must appeal to the solidarity of all Pereirans to go home because we need traffic to flow for emergency response agencies. We need to address this emergency. That is why, starting at this moment, I declare the Exceptional State of Curfew. Starting at this moment and indefinitely, classes are suspended in all educational institutions,” said Mauricio Salazar.

In the city, located in the heart of the coffee-producing mountains of Colombia and around 35 miles from the earthquake’s epicentre, 40 people have been reported dead. According to the mayor’s update, 65 buildings collapsed in the metropolitan area, and people are assumed trapped in 15 of them.

Several clinics were forced to close due either to demand on services or infrastructure risks, while Matecaña airport “suffered damage to its facilities, with several people deceased”.

Several people are also trapped in gondolas in Megacable, and the mayor said the rescue process for them would begin soon, but for the time being “their lives are not in danger at this moment” and “priority is being given to collapsed buildings”.

Colombia’s vice-president, José Manuel Restrepo Abondano, posted on X:

double quotation markMr. President, I heed your instruction. We already have the support of our international allies who have responded with solidarity and commitment. We will not rest until that aid reaches every family that needs it and contributes to the recovery of the affected territories. Today the world extends a hand to #Colombia, and we will stand by every community struck by this tragedy, working tirelessly to help it move forward.

As we reported earlier, world leaders including the US and EU have sent messages of solidarity and offered support to Colombia.

Ecuador’s president Daniel Noboa Azin also offered 47 rescuers, specialized dogs, and equipment with autonomy to operate for 7 days. “We are ready to mobilize whenever you require,” he wrote on X.

Mexico’s president Claudia Sheinbaum also wrote: “Of course, all the support that the people of Colombia may require; we’ll be there.”

Brazil’s Lula also expressed his solidarity, writing on X: “Brazil remains at Colombia’s disposal to provide the necessary support.”

Nayib Bukele, president of El Salvador, said he was in communication with Colombian officials and was “ready to provide immediate support with our rescue teams, medical personnel, paramedics, supplies, or any other assistance that our Colombian brothers and sisters deem necessary”.

In Europe, French president Emmanuel Macron said: “I extend, on behalf of France, my most sincere thoughts to the Colombian people. I think of the victims, their families, the injured, and all those who have been affected by this disaster. Our solidarity also goes to the rescue teams and all those who are working, with courage, to assist the affected populations. In this ordeal, Colombia can count on our friendship and our support.”

Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez also offered “affection and solidarity with the Colombian people” and said Spain “stands with Colombia” at this difficult time.

Italian PM Giorgia Meloni said she was “anxiously” following updates on the earthquake. “In these difficult hours, Italy stands in solidarity with the Colombian people, the affected families, and all those engaged in rescue and assistance operations,” she said.

And Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine stands in “full support” and offered his condolences to those who have lost loved ones. “We call on everyone around the world who can support the affected people and countries right now to step up and help,” he wrote on X.

Colombian pop star Shakira has said her heart is with “everyone who felt this earthquake today”.

“In times like these, we Colombians know how to come together and support one another,” she wrote on X. “All my strength and love for my homeland. Let’s embrace tightly and stay tuned to the instructions so we can help as soon as possible.”

European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said on Monday that the European Union was “ready to provide more support” to Colombia.

“Tonight, Europe’s heart is with the people of Colombia after the terrible earthquake in the Choco region. We have already mobilised Copernicus, our satellite service, to help with rescue operations,” she wrote on social media.

Santiago Velázquez, an industrial advisor, was driving to his son’s school in the suburbs between Pereira and Cartago, in Colombia’s Risaralda province, when the quake hit.

All the cars had to stop because they were being thrown around as the earth shook, Velázquez said.

He was already outside when it happened. “But people were falling and being struck by things as they tried to get out of their buildings,” he said.

Traffic is totally stuck at the moment, so Velázquez is getting a motorbike into the centre to try and help friends and family.

He knows of one landslide that carried away a few houses, and he had heard reports of some five-storey buildings in the suburbs that are “totally cracked”.

Some areas were without water, light or gas. A “disaster”, Velázquez said.

In an address to the nation around midday (local time), president de la Espriella said his government had deployed all of its capabilities “to protect lives, assist affected ‌communities and deliver aid wherever it is needed”.

“The first priority is rescuing the people trapped under the rubble,” he said.

The 7.4 magnitude quake struck at a depth ⁠of 107 km (66 miles) in Choco, a sparsely populated province on Colombia’s Pacific coast, but was felt in major cities nationwide.

Colombia’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said the death toll from the earthquake has now reached 111, Reuters is reporting.

At least 87 were injured and 61 buildings collapsed, he said, noting the rescue of survivors was his priority.

The death toll continues to climb after a powerful earthquake hit western Colombia on Monday.

At least 82 people have been confirmed dead, Reuters is reporting.

The province of Risaralda, in Colombia’s coffee-growing region, has suffered the highest toll so far, with governor Juan Diego Patino reporting 42 fatalities.

Dozens of injuries and heavy damage to buildings were also reported in Choco, the province closest to the epicentre of the 7.4 magnitude quake.

Abelardo De La Espriella, who was only sworn in as president a few days ago, has declared a national state of emergency to coordinate rescue efforts.

In the last hour, President Abelardo De La Espriella officially declared a situation of national disaster as the preliminary death toll rose to at least 72.

This will allow the executive branch to bypass bureaucratic hurdles to more quickly mobilise emergency funds and reallocate state resources to the most affected regions.

The decision was taken as the president convened an emergency meeting at the crisis room of Colombia’s National Unit for Disaster Risk Management in Bogotá.

articles.title: Michigan Dem Senate nominee comes under fire over resurfaced blog post linking football to 'toxic masculinity'
articles.excerpt:
DiJonai Carrington went to Threads to claim "white privilege" following her takedown flagrant foul of Sophie Cunningham despite her intentionally clotheslining her in the face.

Michigan's Democratic ...
articles.body_text:
DiJonai Carrington went to Threads to claim "white privilege" following her takedown flagrant foul of Sophie Cunningham despite her intentionally clotheslining her in the face.

Michigan's Democratic Senate nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, is taking heat after resurfaced writings exposed his sweeping attacks on traditional masculinity and U.S. sports culture.

According to a report by The Midwesterner, El-Sayed authored a 2021 Substack post taking aim at the gridiron in the wake of former Las Vegas Raiders coach Jon Gruden's resignation over leaked emails.

In the post, the progressive favorite laid out an aggressive critique of male sports culture, writing that "the toxic masculinity at the heart of America’s most popular sport, and men’s sports culture more generally, is way deeper than a few emails or a Jay-Z turnaround."

Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks after a radio appearance at Dr. Horace Sheffield's GOTV Community Rally on Aug. 1, 2026, in Detroit, Mich. El-Sayed holds a 15-point lead against Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) according to a recent poll. (Getty Images)

El-Sayed, who played high school football as a starting center at Andover High School, used his past experience to argue that traditional athletics breed bigotry. While noting he felt free on the field, El-Sayed claimed that "on the sidelines and in the locker room, I was fed a hefty dose of the worst kinds of racist taunting," adding that within men's sports, "racism, misogyny, and homophobia were lingua franca." He also unloaded on the NFL directly, accusing the league of "deep-rooted racism."

‘SPECIAL SAUCE OF CRAZY’ — MIDWEST DEM CANDIDATE’S POLICIES TOO EXTREME FOR VOTERS: OPPONENT

Rather than leaning into classic athletic grit, the Democratic nominee pushed a soft-spoken, progressive rebrand of manhood centered on Hollywood fiction.

El-Sayed urged coaches to abandon traditional toughness and instead copy the lead character from the soccer comedy "Ted Lasso," praising the fictional soccer coach because "Ted cries. He talks through his problems. He encourages his players. He bakes biscuits for his boss. He smiles ... like, all the time."

Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks to supporters at an election-night rally at the Majestic Theatre in Detroit, Mich., on Aug. 4, 2026. His race against U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens in the state Democratic primary ended too close to call. (Getty Images)

His political theories on sports extend beyond American boundaries. In a separate 2021 Substack entry cited by The Midwesterner, El-Sayed explicitly tied his sports preferences to his far-left ideology, writing, "European soccer also speaks to my politics. Compared to American sports leagues, the sport is also deeply egalitarian."

The resurfaced posts expose a massive gap between El-Sayed's academic gender theories and his recent campaign trail efforts to build street cred with young male voters by bragging about his own high school wrestling and football history.

Now facing Republican Mike Rogers in the general election after narrowing out Rep. Haley Stevens in the Democratic primary, El-Sayed has some explaining to do to working-class Midwesterners who prefer football over progressive lecturing.

Abdul El-Sayed, a candidate for U.S. Senate in Michigan, speaks before Sen. Bernie Sanders takes the stage at Mumford High School on May 3, 2026, in Detroit, Mich. Sanders is visiting the Midwest on his Fighting Oligarchy: Where We Go From Here tour. (Getty Images)

Send us your thoughts: alejandro.avila@outkick.com / Follow along on X: @alejandroaveela

Alejandro Avila is a longtime writer at OutKick, living in Southern California.

articles.title: Iran installs new war chiefs as Tehran signals ‘prolonged confrontation,’ expert warns
articles.excerpt: IRGC Commander Ahmad Vahidi is reportedly central to Iran's negotiation strategy, with analysts describing him as a radical hardliner. Fox News correspondent Jeff Paul details Vahidi's rise during the...
articles.body_text:
IRGC Commander Ahmad Vahidi is reportedly central to Iran's negotiation strategy, with analysts describing him as a radical hardliner. Fox News correspondent Jeff Paul details Vahidi's rise during the Iran-Iraq War and his alleged connection to terror attacks, including the 1983 Beirut bombing and the 1994 Argentina bombing, highlighting growing concern over who is truly controlling Iran's military decisions.

Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei formally appointed six senior military commanders Monday, cementing a wartime reshuffle as Tehran rebuilds a command structure impacted by months of U.S. and Israeli strikes.

The appointments, announced by Khamenei’s office and promoted on social media, fill posts across Iran’s armed forces, the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and the Basij paramilitary force, with a counterterrorism expert warning the timing and language of the decrees signal Tehran is preparing for "prolonged confrontation" and not a settlement with Washington.

"Strategically, the announcements made were issued in English, on X, while Iranian and Omani negotiators finalize the coordinates of a proposed shipping route through Hormuz, which is deliberate sequencing," Dr. Omar Mohammed, director of the Antisemitism Research Initiative at George Washington University’s Program on Extremism, told Fox News Digital.

"Tehran is establishing its command structure as a fact on the ground before it signs anything."

TRUMP SAYS IRAN WILL PAY — WHAT IT TAKES TO END THE WAR REMAINS UNCLEAR

Iran’s Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. (Fox News)

Mohammed also pointed to language in the appointment announcements blaming the deaths of predecessors on what Iran called the "Zionist-American enemy."

"That phrase, in formal state documents, codifies the United States as a co-belligerent," Mohammed said.

Khamenei appointed Ali Abdollahi as chief of staff of the armed forces and Kioumars Heydari as his deputy. He also formally named Ahmad Vahidi commander-in-chief of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, promoting him to the rank of major general.

Mostafa Izadi was named deputy IRGC commander, Ali Azmaei as commander of the IRGC Navy and Hossein Taeb as commander of the Basij.

Mohammed said Vahidi was also instructed to maintain readiness for "powerful offensive operations against the enemy," by the Supreme Leader, while Abdollahi was tasked with completing the integration of the General Staff into the Khatam al-Anbiya wartime joint command.

"States exiting a conflict dismantle their wartime command arrangements, but Iran is now institutionalizing its own," Mohammed said. "The decrees here describe a leadership planning for a prolonged confrontation, not a settlement."

Former Iranian Interior Minister Ahmad Vahidi attends an event. (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Several of the newly appointed commanders have previously faced U.S. or European sanctions or allegations tied to terrorism and violent crackdowns.

Vahidi is the subject of an Interpol Red Notice requested by Argentina over his alleged involvement in the 1994 bombing of the AMIA Jewish community center in Buenos Aires, which killed 85 people.

Taeb, a former chief of the IRGC Intelligence Organization and former Basij commander, is on the U.S. Treasury Department’s sanctions list.

The United States first designated him in 2010 over serious human rights abuses following Iran’s disputed 2009 presidential election.

Heydari was also sanctioned by the United States in 2022 after the Treasury Department said he had publicly acknowledged his forces’ involvement in the violent response to Iran’s November 2019 protests, in which hundreds of protesters were killed.

The European Union has also sanctioned him.

IRAN’S UNSEEN SUPREME LEADER BECOMES WEAPON IN ESCALATING POWER STRUGGLE, EXPERTS SAY

Iran’s former Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei speaks in Tehran, Iran, on Jan 3. (Iranian Leader Press Office/Anadolu via Getty Images)

The reshuffle comes as Iran continues rebuilding its political and military leadership after a series of U.S. and Israeli strikes killed senior figures across the regime.

Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who had served as supreme leader since 1989, was killed in a Feb. 28 strike at the start of the war. Mojtaba Khamenei, was selected as Iran’s new supreme leader in March.

Ali Larijani, then secretary of Iran’s Supreme National Security Council and a major figure in the country’s security and foreign policy establishment, and Gholamreza Soleimani, commander of the Basij, were killed in strikes on March 17.

The latest appointments come amid continuing questions about Mojtaba Khamenei’s health and public absence.

President Masoud Pezeshkian claimed Monday that he had held a nearly seven-hour meeting with Khamenei, only the second meeting the president has publicly disclosed since the new supreme leader took office, Iran International reported.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian, Gholam-Hossein Mohseni-Eje'i, the head of the judiciary and Alireza Arafi, (right) deputy chairman of the Assembly of Experts, attend the meeting of the interim leadership council of Iran in an unknown location, amid the U.S.-Israel conflict with Iran, in Iran, March 1, 2026. (Handout via Reuters)

Khamenei has not appeared publicly since being selected in March and is believed to have been wounded in the Feb. 28 strike that killed his father.

Pezeshkian said the two discussed economic conditions, sanctions and other domestic challenges and that Khamenei emphasized the need for "unity and cohesion."

The military rebuild, however, has not extended fully into Iran’s sensitive intelligence apparatus, according to Mohammed.

"The IRGC Intelligence Organization and its counterintelligence arm have no announced chiefs, and Iran has no permanent defense or intelligence ministers," the expert said.

"The appointments require assigning responsibility for the counterintelligence failures that enabled the February decapitation.

"Whoever wins that argument — the supreme leader’s circle or the Guard’s institutional leadership — is the actor actually in control."

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title: Jackie, a beloved bald eagle and livestream star, dies of mysterious illness
articles.excerpt:
Thousands mourn the death of the eagle at California’s Big Bear Lake, whose life was closely followed via livestream

Jackie – the beloved bald eagle at California’s Big Bear Lake whose livestream was...
articles.body_text:
Thousands mourn the death of the eagle at California’s Big Bear Lake, whose life was closely followed via livestream

Jackie – the beloved bald eagle at California’s Big Bear Lake whose livestream was followed by millions of viewers as she birthed and raised chicks – died on Monday due to a mysterious illness. She was 14.

Jackie had been receiving treatment at the Ojai Raptor Center since mid-July when she was found weak and unable to fly after a scuffle with two younger eagles. Experts at the center had discovered that she was suffering from severe anemia, and suspected she had been sick for weeks before the fight grounded her.

“We know this news will be deeply felt by the many thousands of people around the world who have followed her journey, hoped alongside us, prayed for her, and supported the people caring for her,” the raptor center staff wrote in an Instagram post announcing Jackie’s death. “Our team is heartbroken. It has been an extraordinary privilege to care for her. “

Despite administering a number of tests including a CT scan and bone marrow biopsy, experts at the center said they could not determine what had sickened Jackie.

The center is in consultation with the US and California fish and wildlife services about Jackie’s condition, and “will provide a more comprehensive statement including additional information on her treatments and test results” at a later date, it said.

The public had been watching Jackie’s nest since a livestream was first set up in October 2015 – it was then inhabited by her parents Ricky and Lucy. In 2018, the public watched as Jackie defended her nest against an intruder, dubbed Mr B. Then, Shadow – the male eagle who became her mate – moved in. Greater and greater numbers of viewers tuned in during the pandemic to watch the couple build their lives together and welcome several clutches of fluffy hatchlings.

In January, the couple’s clutch of two eggs was eaten by ravens. Jackie laid two more eggs in February, and thousands watched as the couple hatched their two youngest – Luna and Sandy. The latter was named after Sandy Steers, the executive director of Friends of Big Bear Valley, who had recently died from cancer.

The couple inspired the public to fight for the environment they inhabited. The Friends of Big Bear Lake launched a $10m effort to buy land near the eagles’ nest which had been slated for development – drawing support from the local elementary school, as well as from OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman and his wife, Anna. The non-profit will now steward 63 acres of the land.

Fans of Jackie shared messages of grief following the news of her death – and celebrated her legacy of inspiring a massive public campaign for preserving natural habitat.

articles.title: Trump signs order to limit childhood vaccines and split MMR shots
articles.excerpt:
Watch: Trump signs executive order on childhood vaccines, claiming discredited link between vaccines and autism

President Donald Trump has signed an order that calls for fewer childhood vaccines and ...
articles.body_text:
Watch: Trump signs executive order on childhood vaccines, claiming discredited link between vaccines and autism

President Donald Trump has signed an order that calls for fewer childhood vaccines and also recommends splitting the mumps, measles and rubella (MMR) shots.

"Decades ago, children received only a small fraction of the vaccines required today," Trump said on Monday. "In those times, people were much healthier and of course the high rates of autism now observed did not exist."

The president has long cast doubt on the safety of MMR vaccines, but multiple studies have found no connection between the shots and autism.

The order also recommends that the number of childhood vaccines drop to 11 from the existing 18 recommended by the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP).

Speaking in the Oval Office, Trump said that his administration "is recognising gold standard childhood vaccine recommendations for only 11 core vaccinations against the most serious and dangerous diseases".

The immunisations recommended for all children under the order are for measles, mumps, rubella, diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis, polio, Haemophilus influenzae type B, pneumococcal disease, human papillomavirus, and varicella or chicken pox.

"We're reducing them," Trump said. "It's not only that you're doing fewer vaccines, or jabs, as they say, but you're doing them in a series of visits to the doctor."

The president suggested that the MMR vaccine could be "quite lethal" if given at once. He compared it to pouring a bottle of soda into a child's body.

Experts say that allowing time between jabs means children are more likely to contract diseases in the interim or that they are more likely to miss appointments if there are multiple shots.

According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, external (CDC), there is "no published scientific evidence that shows any benefit in separating the combination MMR vaccine into three individual shots".

The agency says "most people who get MMR vaccine do not have any serious problems with it", and that getting the vaccine "is much safer than getting measles, mumps, or rubella".

Trump's Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) Robert F Kennedy Jr said the proposed changes were meant to give parents choice, not prohibit access to childhood vaccines.

The federal government does not have the authority to implement the new recommendations. Shots that are required for school attendance are set at the state level.

Dr Andrew Racine, president of the American Academy of Pediatrics, called Trump's executive order "disheartening" and "dangerous", pointing out it comes as measles cases reach a 35-year high in the US. Measles cases have also been rising globally.

"Instead of ensuring every family can access life-saving vaccines for measles, influenza, RSV and more, federal leaders are once again spreading misleading claims," Racine said in a statement on Monday.

He said there was no new evidence to justify the significant changes, adding that the order was not based on "gold-standard science".

"Delaying or skipping shots is risky, especially as measles continues to spread and children go back to school," Racine said.

Republican Senator Bill Cassidy also admonished Trump's executive order on Monday, labelling it "wrong".

"The President does not have the expertise to make these changes," Cassidy, who is a physician, wrote on social media. "Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism."

The lawmaker, who chairs the Senate health committee, urged parents to "listen to their child's pediatrician about vaccines rather than listening to an inaccurate executive order".

Experts fear that if parents refrain from getting their children vaccinated as a result of the discredited idea that childhood vaccines are linked to autism, it risks the re-emergence of diseases like measles.

Multiple studies have found no link between the MMR vaccine and autism. A recent high-quality study from Denmark in 2019 looked at 657,461 children and concluded that the data did not support the MMR vaccine causing or triggering autism.

On its website, the US CDC recommends that two doses of the combined MMR vaccine be given to children, starting with the first dose at 12-15 months and the second between the ages of four and six.

How often and how many vaccines children in the US receive is based on the times when vaccines will work best with their immune systems and when they are most vulnerable to certain diseases, according to the AAP.

There is no medical reason to delay or skip recommended immunisations, the AAP says.

Why Trump's comments on vaccines and paracetamol risk child health

articles.title: Unlicensed NYC boat operator allegedly ignored safety warnings before mother, baby died in capsizing: feds
articles.excerpt:
A woman and child were killed after a boat capsized in New York Harbor Saturday night. (FNTV)

A New Jersey man accused of running illegal boat tours allegedly ignored multiple safety warnings before ...
articles.body_text:
A woman and child were killed after a boat capsized in New York Harbor Saturday night. (FNTV)

A New Jersey man accused of running illegal boat tours allegedly ignored multiple safety warnings before an overcrowded New York Harbor excursion turned deadly, killing a 5-month-old baby and her 27-year-old mother.

Manuel Hernandez, 46, of Manville, was charged Monday with two counts of misconduct and neglect of a ship officer resulting in death after the Yamaha AR210 he was piloting capsized Saturday night.

Hernandez appeared Monday before U.S. Magistrate Judge Valerie Figueredo on the two charges, each of which carries a maximum sentence of 10 years in prison.

DRUNK REPEAT OFFENDER CALLED A 'TICKING TIME-BOMB' BEFORE 80-MPH BOATING COLLISION KILLED WOMAN: PROSECUTORS

Courtroom sketch of Manuel Hernandez, 46, during his federal court appearance following the deadly New York Harbor boat capsizing. (Jane Rosenberg)

Federal prosecutors say Hernandez was not licensed to carry paying passengers, had 14 people aboard a boat with a maximum capacity of 10 and knowingly took the infant out without an appropriate life vest.

According to the federal complaint, it was not Hernandez’s first time allegedly taking paying customers onto New York Harbor without the required credentials.

After his arrest, Hernandez allegedly told investigators he had previously piloted at least two other boat tours for the same tour company using his own vessel.

He allegedly acknowledged he lacked the required Merchant Mariner Credential and Coast Guard Certificate of Inspection for those trips and said he was paid about $1,000 for each.

COAST GUARD OPENS FIRE ON BOAT SMUGGLING 25 CHINESE NATIONALS NEAR FLORIDA AFTER IT REFUSED TO STOP

A social media advertisement from the tour operator promoted boat charters for up to 12 people for $1,200 over four hours, according to the federal complaint. (U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York)

Coast Guard Investigative Service Assistant Director Josh Packer said illegal charter operations "gamble with human life."

"In this case, the alleged conduct led to an unthinkable tragedy," Packer said.

Before Saturday’s fatal trip even began, Hernandez allegedly asked the baby’s parents whether they had an infant-sized flotation device. When they said they did not, Hernandez told them the boat did not have one either, according to the complaint.

Despite that, Hernandez allegedly instructed one parent to wear a life vest and hold the baby throughout the tour. The child’s mother did so.

OVERCROWDED MIGRANT VESSEL WITH 240 PEOPLE ON BOARD INTERCEPTED NEAR TURKS AND CAICOS

A crane lifts the capsized Yamaha AR210 from New York Harbor after the vessel overturned during an Aug. 8, 2026, paid boat tour. (U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York)

About three hours and 20 minutes into the excursion, Hernandez allegedly made a U-turn while heading toward the Statue of Liberty, bringing the vessel into a swell that may have been caused by the wake of a larger passing boat.

Hernandez tried to accelerate through the swell, but it swamped the bow and the vessel "immediately capsized," prosecutors allege.

All 14 people were thrown into the harbor. Eleven passengers and Hernandez survived, while the mother and baby were recovered unresponsive and later pronounced dead at a Brooklyn hospital.

"The defendant allegedly flouted those regulations when he transported paying customers on a commercial vessel without appropriate licenses, overcrowded the vessel, and took on a five-month-old infant passenger, with no infant life vests onboard," U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said.

The boat used in the fatal trip belonged to a friend and was smaller than Hernandez’s own vessel, which needed mechanical repairs, according to the complaint.

CARNIVAL CRUISE PASSENGER, 67, FOUND DEAD WHILE SNORKELING OFF THE COAST OF AUSTRALIA DURING EXCURSION

The overturned Yamaha AR210 is tied to a pier after capsizing in New York Harbor on Aug. 8, 2026. All 14 people aboard were thrown into the water, and a 27-year-old mother and her 5-month-old daughter died, according to federal prosecutors. (U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York)

Hernandez allegedly told investigators he did not know the borrowed boat’s maximum capacity and had expected 12 passengers before ultimately agreeing to take 13.

The victims were identified in a GoFundMe organized by friends and colleagues as Sara Sanchez, 27, and her 5-month-old daughter, Antonella Garcia. Sanchez’s partner and Antonella’s father, Andres Garcia, was also aboard the boat and survived.

Sara Sanchez is pictured with her partner, Andres Garcia, and their older son in a family photo shared with a GoFundMe organized after the New York Harbor tragedy. Sanchez and her 5-month-old daughter, Antonella Garcia, died in the capsizing, while Garcia, who was also aboard the boat, survived. (GoFundMe)

Garcia is now grieving their deaths while caring for the couple’s 6-year-old son, Salvador, according to the fundraiser, which is raising money for funeral expenses and other costs. "No amount of money can replace Sara or Antonella," organizers wrote.

NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said Hernandez showed "a complete disregard for the safety of his passengers."

"This tragedy could have been prevented, and now a family is left to grieve the unimaginable loss of a mother and her five-month-old daughter because of his negligence," Tisch said.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

articles.title: Top Senate Dem’s new tax idea gets torched as critics warn nearly every American could pay
articles.excerpt: O’Leary told Fox News Digital that speeding up data center development is essential for U.S. economic and national security interests, warning that regulatory delays could allow China to gain a critic...
articles.body_text:
O’Leary told Fox News Digital that speeding up data center development is essential for U.S. economic and national security interests, warning that regulatory delays could allow China to gain a critical advantage.

The top Democratic lawmaker on the Senate Finance Committee has floated increasing taxes on data centers, a move critics say could raise costs on services used by practically all Americans.

Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore., released a white paper proposal last week calling to end tax incentives for data centers and to impose an ongoing tax on data centers operating in the United States. Critics of Wyden’s proposal argue that the costs of the new tax could ultimately be borne by all Americans by increasing the costs of common services.

"This tax will be paid by anyone who uses the internet. A tax on data centers is a tax on your email, family photos, small business operations, cloud storage, and your Instagram, X, TikTok and Facebook posts," Americans for Tax Reform director of innovation technology James Erwin said. "Senator Wyden is betraying his legacy as a champion of a free and open internet accessible to all."

TEXAS GOV. GREG ABBOTT EFFECTIVELY PAUSES NEW DATA CENTER PROJECTS PENDING STATEWIDE GRID AUDIT

U.S. Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR) leaves a Senate Democratic meeting at the U.S. Capitol Building on Oct. 3, 2025 in Washington, DC. The federal government shut down early Wednesday after Congress and the White House failed to reach a funding deal. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

Americans for Tax Reform dubbed Wyden’s proposal a "national internet tax."

Wyden’s office did not respond to a request for comment when reached by Fox News Digital on Monday.

Wyden’s white paper acknowledges that there is some difficulty in applying a tax to data centers, given how common such facilities are and how wide their utilization is.

"Generally, a data center is a facility that primarily contains electronic equipment used to process, store, and transmit digital information, and may be free-standing or within a larger structure that uses environmental control equipment to maintain the proper conditions for the operation of electronic equipment," the white paper reads. "This definition alone would be broad, so carveouts would be developed to focus the tax on data centers as commonly understood, rather than trip-wiring ancillary operations into the tax."

To solve this problem, Wyden suggests excluding "internet infrastructure" from his proposed tax, but does not define what that term means or what kinds of facilities it would cover. The paper does, however, suggest that cloud computing, a highly important piece of internet infrastructure used by many industries, would not be exempted under his tax.

A SOUTHERN STATE JUST TOOK THE TOP SPOT IN ONE OF THE WORLD’S FASTEST-GROWING INDUSTRIES

On Friday, President Donald Trump shared his support for the Protect College Sports Act with a post on Truth Social. (Getty Images)

In addition to excluding data centers from many tax incentives, Wyden’s proposal would hit their owners with a "low single-digit" annual tax on gross receipts, not their profits.

Though Wyden cites land use, local power prices and local water use as the concerns that prompted him to propose the new taxes, he also advocates for taxing any data centers that are built in the Earth’s orbit.

"President Trump is cementing American AI dominance over China while ensuring data centers pay for their own power, water and other utilities," White House assistant press secretary Liz Huston told Fox News Digital when asked about the Wyden plan. "The President’s commonsense approach will beat China, harness this technological boom and deliver lower costs and new opportunities for working families and small businesses."

FOX NEWS POLL: MOVE OVER BIG BROTHER, VOTERS SEE BIG TECH AS GREATER THREAT TO US

Data center development is surging across Texas, with North Texas taking the top spot in a new global ranking of the industry’s leading markets. (Mikala Compton/The Austin American-Statesman/Getty Images)

Wyden’s proposal clashes with President Donald Trump’s push to accelerate artificial intelligence development and expand the infrastructure supporting it. While Wyden seeks to prioritize assistance for workers and communities disrupted by data center construction, the Trump administration emphasizes maintaining economic growth and ensuring the United States retains a technological edge over China.

The two do have common ground in seeking to limit the impact of data center construction on energy and water prices, though the president has a different way of going about that. A White House official told Fox News Digital that the administration has brought together over 200 utilities, data center developers, cooperatives and state leaders into its "Ratepayer Protection Pledge," an initiative uniting different stakeholders to facilitate to creation of more energy sources to keep prices low.

The Oregon senator’s approach, however, is less aggressive than the calls for a total moratorium on data center construction, which Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y. have advocated for.

articles.title: Ceuta mayor calls for migrant detention amid mass influx crisis
articles.excerpt: Ceuta’s leader has demanded the detention and expulsion of thousands of asylum seekers and undocumented migrants roaming the streets in the Spanish North African territory after last month’s mass cros...
articles.body_text:
Ceuta’s leader has demanded the detention and expulsion of thousands of asylum seekers and undocumented migrants roaming the streets in the Spanish North African territory after last month’s mass crossing from Morocco.

“A space that acts as an internment centre for foreigners must be set up, where these people can be held and remain confined,” Ceuta’s Mayor-President Juan Jesus Vivas of the conservative Popular Party told reporters.

He said the measure “must be achieved urgently” so that the migrants “are not in our streets and that expulsion proceedings can be handled with greater speed and ease”.

A surge of asylum seekers and migrants swam or used inflatable rafts to cross from Morocco to Ceuta at the end of July, sparking a debate about the external borders of the European Union and controversy between Spain and other EU members.

Spanish authorities on Monday updated the estimated number of irregular migrants who made the journey to 80,000.

The Spanish government says 70,000 migrants and asylum seekers returned to Morocco within two days.

But the thousands who remained, including hundreds of unaccompanied children who cannot be summarily deported under Spanish law, are struggling to access food, water, shelter and sanitation, putting a strain on Ceuta’s resources.

Their future has sparked a political battle between Spain’s leftist central government and regions governed by the main conservative Popular Party and far-right Vox, which oppose taking in unaccompanied children under existing legal provisions.

Ceuta Mayor Vivas estimates that between 8,000 and 11,000 migrants are still in the Spanish territory and says the situation is “unsustainable”. He disputes the government’s statistics that only 2,500 asylum seekers and undocumented migrants remain.

Police said that 5,000 Ceuta residents gathered to protest on Sunday over the handling of the migration crisis that they say has left the enclave unsafe.

The Spanish government minister responsible for relations with the regions, Angel Victor Torres, assured Ceuta’s population that police and troop numbers had been ramped up, including 40 percent more civil guards.
