articles.title: Amber heat-health alerts issued for most of England as temperatures could reach 36C or higher this week – latest updates
articles.excerpt:
The upgraded alerts will be in place from 9am on Tuesday until 6pm on Wednesday

There is no single definition for a drought, but one way of describing it is a prolonged period of abnormally low rainf...
articles.body_text:
The upgraded alerts will be in place from 9am on Tuesday until 6pm on Wednesday

There is no single definition for a drought, but one way of describing it is a prolonged period of abnormally low rainfall, leading to a shortage of water.

The Environment Agency defines three main types of drought, which can occur separately or together. They are:

Agricultural drought: when there isn’t enough rainfall and moisture in soils to support crop production or farming practices.

Environmental drought: when lack of rainfall has a negative impact on the environment and ecology.

Water supply drought: when a lack of rainfall leads to concerns from water companies about supplies for their customers.

As we mentioned in the opening post, the whole of Wales and half of England has already been declared in drought. Here is a full list of the affected areas in England:

Wessex (covering Dorset, Somerset, Wiltshire and south Gloucestershire)

More than 25 million people face restrictions on water use, according to the Environment Agency, with millions under hosepipe bans, including all South East Water and Thames Water customers.

Another record is likely to tumble this week after Sunday was the 34th day this year on which temperatures exceeded 30C somewhere in the UK, equalling the record set in 1995.

The extreme weather of summer 2026 has so far included two record-breaking heatwaves in May and June that were linked to more than 2,800 excess deaths.

Two further heatwaves in July, along with the driest July in England and Wales since records began in 1836, have fuelled drought and wildfires.

The EU’s Earth observation programme, Copernicus, said average temperatures across western Europe reached 21.61C for June-July, breaking the record set in 2022. Globally, this year is just behind 2024 and 2025 as the hottest on record.

Amber heat-health alerts have been issued for five regions of England from 9am on Tuesday until 6pm on Wednesday: the West Midlands, East Midlands, south-east, London, and the east of England.

Amber alerts mean an increased likelihood of health impacts for those aged 65 and older and people with pre-exisiting conditions, although there may also be impacts to younger people too. The weather impacts are likely to be felt across the whole health service under this category, which is below red, the most severe.

The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) has also issued a yellow heat-health alert for the north-east and north-west, which are under a yellow alert for the same period. The south-west of England and Yorkshire and the Humber regions are already under a yellow alert, which remains in place.

According to the UKHSA, yellow alerts are issued when most people are unlikely to be affected by the weather, but could impact those who are particularly vulnerable.

Dr Paul Coleman, consultant in public health at the UKHSA, said:

double quotation markTemperatures are forecast to rise above 30°C across central and southern parts of the country over the next few days, and generally hot weather is expected across most regions of England.

These kind of temperatures can result in serious health outcomes across the population – particularly in those who are vulnerable, such as the elderly or those with serious health conditions – so it is important that everyone takes sensible precautions while enjoying the sun.

The National Drought Group (NDG) is expected to meet this afternoon and declare that more parts of England are officially in drought, as parts of the UK head into a potential fifth heatwave of the year this week.

All of Wales and more than half of England are already in drought after an unprecedented period of dry, hot weather over the summer.

The NDG includes the Met Office, the government, regulators, water companies, the National Farmers’ Union, the Canal & River Trust, anglers and conservation experts.

It reviews the impacts of droughts and helps draw up mitigation plans to respond to them as wildfire risks increase, rivers run dangerously low and food production/security is affected by long periods of little or no rainfall.

The lack of rainfall has seen millions of people be put under temporary hosepipe bans, with water supplies having been severely depleted, particularly in the south and south-east.

The heat and continuing drought conditions are being intensified by the worsening climate crisis, putting huge pressure on vulnerable people, critical infrastructure and wildlife across affected areas.

Temperatures could reach 36C (97F) or higher this week, forecasters have said. Monday will be slightly cooler before temperatures rise again on Tuesday.

articles.title: Mother of Briton fatally shot by father in Texas urges Miliband to press US for new inquiry
articles.excerpt:
Jane Coates says foreign secretary should draw attention to coroner’s finding that Lucy Harrison was unlawfully killed

The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is being urged to push US authorities to ...
articles.body_text:
Jane Coates says foreign secretary should draw attention to coroner’s finding that Lucy Harrison was unlawfully killed

The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, is being urged to push US authorities to reopen an investigation into a man who shot dead his 23-year-old British daughter while she was visiting him in Texas.

Lucy Harrison, from Warrington in Cheshire, was fatally shot on 10 January 2025, the day before she was due to fly home to the UK.

Her father, Kris Harrison, who admitted holding the pistol at the time, has never been arrested.

A Texas grand jury decided not to prosecute the telecoms executive, originally from Liverpool, last year after what Lucy’s family described as an “inadequate” police investigation.

Earlier this year, the senior coroner for Cheshire ruled that Lucy had been unlawfully killed and that Harrison’s actions amounted to gross negligence manslaughter.

Lucy’s mother, Jane Coates, on Monday wrote to Miliband urging him to press the US authorities to reopen the investigation into her former husband, in light of the coroner’s findings.

She wrote: “I understand that the British government cannot interfere in the American justice system or direct US prosecutors to take a particular course of action.

“However, the Foreign Office can use appropriate diplomatic channels to draw attention to the coroner’s conclusion, raise the serious concerns surrounding the original investigation and ask the relevant US authorities to review the case.”

A number of UK politicians, including the former justice secretary Robert Buckland, are also urging Miliband to intervene.

Buckland said on Monday: “This is such a terrible situation for Lucy’s family and there are serious questions here that must be answered. This case must be reopened in the US.

“The new foreign secretary, lord chancellor and, indeed, prime minister should pursue this for those grieving for someone who left us at such a young age and in the most appalling of circumstances.”

Harrison, a telecoms executive, had bought a pistol for $500 (£370) from a colleague two years before Lucy’s death. Gun owners over the age of 21 are not required to obtain training or a licence in Texas, one of the most firearms-friendly US states.

An inquest in Cheshire was told that Lucy had expressed concern to friends about her two younger siblings being in the house with her father’s Glock 9mm semi-automatic pistol.

It also heard that the pair had an argument about Donald Trump in the hours before the fatal shooting, although Lucy’s family say this is not why she was shot.

Despite an officer smelling alcohol on Harrison’s breath, he was not breathalysed. During his police interview, a Texas ranger explained to Harrison that the “gun would only discharge if the trigger was pressed”, according to a report released to the UK inquest. “Kris said ‘OK’,” it noted. Yet authorities said they were unable to arrest Harrison because they could not prove intent.

Sarah Hall, the Labour MP for Warrington South who has raised the case in parliament, said the Foreign Office should also address why the family was not given “adequate support” from the UK government after Lucy’s death.

In her letter to Miliband, Coates said: “I must also express my disappointment at the response we received from the previous administration. There was no meaningful action to help us seek justice.

“The formation of the new government under Andy Burnham has given us renewed hope. We have been struck by the prime minister’s determined tone, and by his emphasis on taking action and getting things done. We sincerely hope that this approach will extend to Lucy’s case.”

The Foreign Office has been approached for comment.

articles.title: Drugs and alcohol nearly cost World Series hero Scott Spiezio everything, including his life
articles.excerpt:
Scott Spiezio tells Fox News Digital in a recent interview how his relationship with God evolved during his harrowing journey with alcohol and drugs.

Scott Spiezio underwent an MRI for back pain in 2...
articles.body_text:
Scott Spiezio tells Fox News Digital in a recent interview how his relationship with God evolved during his harrowing journey with alcohol and drugs.

Scott Spiezio underwent an MRI for back pain in 2018. The results of which would seem inconsequential.

When Spiezio exited the MRI, he was yellow. He had jaundice; his liver was failing after years of battling alcoholism.

The World Series champion, who was 47 at the time, was given a 20% chance to surviving.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE SPORTS COVERAGE ON FOXNEWS.COM

Scott Spiezio #26 of the St. Louis Cardinals poses during Photo Day on Feb. 26, 2007, at Roger Dean Stadium in Jupiter, Fla. (Doug Benc/Getty Images)

Spiezio was told by doctors he had to stop drinking for six months before he could receive a liver transplant to save his life. He wasn’t sure he would be able to.

"I didn't think that I'd be able to do it. I went from a guy that never drank alcohol to thinking I don't know if I can go six months without drinking to save my own life," Spiezio said.

Scott Spiezio’s father, Ed, was a two-time World Series champion and played Major League Baseball for nine seasons.

Scott remembered his dad telling him at a young age, "You’re going to be better than me."

"As soon as he was born I knew he was going to be a ballplayer," Scott’s mother, Verna Spiezio, said in the upcoming documentary, "Spiezio."

Ed said Scott was born to be a baseball player, and he made sure that would happen.

The two spent days working together, trying to achieve the goal of making it to the big leagues

Their basement was set up for Scott to do drills. Throughout his youth, every practice ended with the same situation: a 3-2 count, two outs, bases loaded, down one run, bottom of the ninth inning, Game 7 of the World Series.

Scott and Ed Spiezio stand together. (Spiezio Family)

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

In high school, they would arrive at the gym at 6 a.m. to hit in the batting cage, work out, and then Scott would go to school.

Everything was done with the intention of making it to the big leagues.

"I think for a long time that's what my dad thought, and, I did too. That (baseball) was my purpose in life. (It) was to be a better baseball player than him and to win championships," Scott said.

And Scott did just that. Not only did he win a World Series, but he hit one of the biggest home runs in Angels’ franchise history.

In Game 6 of the 2002 World Series, the Angels were down 3-2 in the series to the San Francisco Giants. Spiezio was up in the bottom of the seventh inning with two runners on base and the Angels down 5-0, with their season hanging in the balance.

Spiezio had been practicing for a situation like this life his entire life.

Giants manager Dusty Baker brought in reliever Felix Rodriguez to retire Spiezio and neutralize the Angels’ threat. It looked like Rodriguez was going to do it, too.

He got ahead 1-2 in the count and had Spiezio on the ropes. But Scott didn’t quit. Foul ball, ball, foul ball, ball, and he worked the count full at 3-2, a count he was quite familiar with. Spiezio then turned on a fastball and deposited it into the right-field seats.

"Everything was in slow motion. I was running to first, I was watching the ball, I was literally praying, like, God, please push this out, like let this go," Spiezio said. "And then I heard the loudest noise in my life."

Scott Spezio of the Anaheim Angels hits a home run against the San Francisco Giants during Game 4 of the World Series in Anaheim, Calif., on Oct. 27, 2002. (Chuck Solomon/Sports Illustrated via Getty Images)

WHITE SOX MANAGER WILL VENABLE FORGETS KEY RULE IN INEXPLICABLE BLUNDER, COSTS TEAM IN LOSS

Spiezio’s blast cut the lead to 5-3 and sparked an Angels comeback, as they went on to win Game 6, 6-5, and eventually won Game 7 of the World Series, bringing the Angels their first World Series title in franchise history.

The home run also made Spiezio in demand. It’s when he said his ego started to kick in.

However, "ego," to Spiezio, meant something different. For him, ego is an acronym: "edging God out."

After the World Series win in 2002, Spiezio said he began edging God out, and things took a turn for the worse.

"People tell you how great you are and you start believing. And for me, ego stood for edging God out, and I started edging him out and started believing the hype and started drifting a little bit as a person," Spiezio said.

After the World Series win, David Letterman wanted him on the Top 10 List. Jay Leno and Carson Daly wanted Spiezio on their shows. Spiezio had a band, and they were playing concerts in front of 1,500 people.

Jay Leno stands with Anaheim Angels players David Eckstein, John Lackey, Scott Spiezio, Tim Salmon and Troy Percival on Oct. 28, 2002, during an episode of "The Tonight Show with Jay Leno." (Paul Drinkwater/NBCU Photo Bank/NBCUniversal via Getty Images via Getty Images)

Back in his hometown of Morris, Illinois, billboards went up calling Spiezio a hometown hero. The mayor gave him a key to the city, he was honored at his high school, the town named a street after him: Scott Spiezio Drive.

Scott Spiezio was at the top of the world.

Spiezio left the Angels after the 2003 season and signed with the Seattle Mariners on a three-year, $9 million contract.

In spring training, Spiezio was playing third base for the Mariners. As he tried to catch a popup over the pitcher’s mound, he tripped on the mound at full speed and hurt his back. Spiezio blew out his thoracic T6 and T7 discs.

Another collision for him would risk paralyzing him. It was the first serious injury Spiezio had suffered in his life, and it sent him down a troubling path.

"When I got hurt, kind of started feeling sorry for myself and drifted from God. More like, ‘Why I've done everything you wanted me to do? Why am I being punished?’ And instead of turning to him, I turned to alcohol," Spiezio said.

"They told me I might be paralyzed. I might not play again, and I got depressed, anxious and all these things that I thought people made up."

In Seattle, an unfamiliar city, and without an established friend group, and now with a serious injury, Spiezio was out of his element.

"I'm with a new team. I went out to try to fit in and I ended up drinking too much, and before you know it, that first night out turned into an everyday thing and I was on a roller coaster ride of becoming physically addicted to alcohol."

Scott Spiezio of the Seattle Mariners looks on against the San Diego Padres during a Spring Training game on March 3, 2005, at Peoria Stadium in Peoria, Ariz. The Mariners won 5-4. (Nick Laham/Getty Images)

Spiezio went from someone who was hesitant to take Advil or Tylenol, to drinking every day.

Spiezio went from winning the Oakland Athletics’ Dave Stewart Community Award in 1997, to being the Angels’ Roberto Clemente nominee in 2003, to being someone who worked with DARE, to becoming an alcoholic without knowing it.

He still believed in God, but Spiezio said he began to stray from His ways throughout his struggles. Spiezio said he was spending $2,000 to $3,000 a night on bottle service.

His relationship with his father became frayed as he started drinking more. He ended up having an affair with his future second wife and got divorced from his first wife. He began using cocaine recreationally.

As things were starting to spiral, Spiezio had a meeting at his parents' house, when his father told him that things had gotten "crazy" and that "they had to stop." As Scott tried to get into his car and leave, he pushed his father away, and the neighbors called the police. His kids witnessed it all and ran into the backyard.

After that night, he stopped speaking to his father.

Spiezio ended up getting released from the Mariners during the second season of his three-year contract, and he called it a reprieve. The following offseason, he ended up getting married to his second wife.

Yet none of his friends wanted to go to his wedding. Spiezio said at that point he was drinking nearly a handle of vodka a day. He was a different person than the one his friends knew.

In 2006, the St. Louis Cardinals invited him to spring training as a minor league invitee, and it rejuvenated him, coming back to the team his dad played for, and returning home. Despite not speaking to his dad, he donned his dad’s No. 26.

With the Cardinals, he had a resurgent season, hitting .272 with 13 home runs and 52 RBI while playing all over the field. Spiezio played a massive role on their World Series-winning team.

However, this World Series victory was different for Spiezio. He didn’t get to celebrate with his dad, as he did in 2002.

Spiezio won a World Series for the Cardinals, just like his dad, but he wasn’t able to share the moment with him.

The fanfare was also much different. There was not another party at the high school. He wasn't being covered the same way by the newspapers. His reputation didn’t warrant the same celebration it did 2002.

His relationship with his dad had deteriorated so much that he wasn’t sure he would be invited to his funeral.

On Opening Day 2007, and the St. Louis Cardinals were awarding players their World Series rings from 2006.

The Cardinals had a special surprise for Scott Spiezio. They were bringing out his father, Ed, to give him his World Series ring.

Ed, who still had not spoken to Scott since that fateful night at his house, wasn’t sure he should go.

"I didn’t feel I should go down there, but for this event I did," Ed said.

As the Cardinals announced that Ed was presenting Scott with his ring, the son burst into tears.

Scott Spiezio at a ring ceremony with his dad, Ed. (Spiezio Family)

"The Cardinals brought my dad back without me knowing to give me my ring in 2007. The first time in history and only time in history that a father and son have won with the same organization. They called him up and presented my ring to him and then called me up and he presented my ring to me and we hugged and that was the prodigal son moment that turned everything around," Scott said.

Ed said there wasn’t a dry eye in the whole stadium.

Scott called that moment a pivotal moment in their relationship. While he wished he had gotten sober right then and there, at least he knew he had his dad back in his corner.

St. Louis Cardinals utility player Scott Spiezio receives his World Series ring from his father Ed during a ceremony before the game against the New York Mets at Busch Stadium on April 3, 2007, in St. Louis, Mo. (Scott Rovak/Getty Images)

Later that year, Scott spoke at Christian Day in Busch Stadium after a game, and his father attended.

"I think he started realizing that there was a greater purpose and uh we started opening up to each other after I spoke at Christian Day at Busch Stadium with the Cardinals. And he told me at that moment, we hugged and he said, ‘I'm proud of you. Like, I couldn't be prouder of you,’" Scott said.

However, while his dad was back in his life, his relationship with alcohol worsened. During games, Spiezio was drinking alcohol out of water bottles in the dugout and was playing baseball drunk.

The legal limit is .08. Spiezio theorized he was playing at 0.20. He would drink during the game because he had the shakes, and he had cocaine on him so he wouldn’t sleep.

Spiezio eventually collapsed in front of the Cardinals' trainers, and they sent him to an outpatient rehab facility in St. Charles, Missouri, near St. Louis.

The proximity of the facility to St. Louis was a detriment because people knew who he was in St. Charles, and Spiezio didn’t share at all and waited until it was over.

He checked a box and was in the Cardinals lineup 28 days later, but he was still an addict and an alcoholic.

After the 2007 season, Spiezio was involved in a hit-and-run, and went to rehab in Tucson, Arizona. He rejoined the team in 2008 but then got released after a warrant went out for his arrest.

The Atlanta Braves then signed him to a minor league deal, but he retired from baseball in 2008 because he didn’t want to be too far from home. Upon his retirement, Spiezio dove straight back into alcohol and cocaine.

He divorced his second wife in 2010. Spiezio was drinking one to two handles of vodka a day and spending thousands of dollars on cocaine per week.

From 2007 to 2016, Spiezio was in 11 different rehabs. He spent hundreds of hours in AA meetings and with counselors. At that point, Spiezio ceded control of his property and the money he had left to his parents.

"(My parents) strung me along to bring me food and would help me. They saved my property so I had somewhere to live. Otherwise, I would have spent everything and thrown everything away. And yet I was smart enough to give – I trusted them so much that I gave them power of attorney and I got rid of all my cars, got rid of all my credit cards, got rid of my checks, and let them do everything so I wouldn't have access to money," Spiezio said.

At one point, things got so low for Spiezio that he had a death wish.

If you or someone you know is having thoughts of suicide, please contact the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 1-800-273-TALK (8255).

"I remember the cops were called," Kevin Donoho, Pastor of Crossbridge Community Church said in the documentary.

"And basically (Scott) had taken off on foot and he was out in the field. The cops are out looking for him and basically they see him. And he said, ‘I’m going to run at them so they shoot me and they can just put an end to all of this. I just thought, ‘That’s as low as it gets.’"

Spiezio was weighed down with guilt and shame over letting his kids down, letting his town down, letting his parents down and wasting his platform. His life revolved around drugs and alcohol for a decade.

For so long, Spiezio asked God for help, then took over the wheel and went back to his old ways. He got a wake-up call when an MRI for his back in 2018 changed his life.

"I would ask God for help, and he would help me and then I'd take the wheel back. And then finally I think he was like, ‘Hey man, you're not getting this. I'm going to have to wake you up.’ And I ended up getting jaundice," Spiezio said.

Scott Spiezio with jaundice in the hospital. (Spiezio Family)

His liver was failing. Doctors gave him a 20% chance to live. If he could make it six months without drinking, they could do a liver transplant.

Spiezio didn’t think he could stop drinking to save his own life.

"I went from a guy that never drank alcohol to thinking I don't know if I can go six months without drinking to save my own life. I just cried out to God. I said, ‘God, take away my cravings.’ And that was April 6, 2018," Spiezio said.

"From that day on, I've had zero cravings. When I see alcohol, I get physically ill when I see it. I feel like I'm going to throw up."

Spiezio said he was going to do what God wanted him to do. He knew it was his last chance.

Every couple of weeks, he returned to the hospital to have two liters of fluid drained from his abdomen. Slowly but surely, Spiezio felt better.

When he returned to Northwestern Hospital for the fourth time, the doctors were dumbfounded by what they saw.

"By the fourth time I went in, they read my scans, they looked at my blood work and said, ‘We don't know how to explain it, but your liver is normal and your blood work is great. We've never seen anything like this before. All we can say is somebody upstairs is looking out for you,’" Spiezio said.

"And I knew that that God had performed a second miracle on me."

Moving sticks in the yard so he could mow the lawn. Then he got a wheelbarrow and created a burn pile with the sticks. Just that simple action gave Spiezio the motivation to go out and talk to people.

He started building his relationship with the Lord. He was going to church more. He asked Donoho if he could work at the church and started cleaning the office complex.

He started reading the Bible. Spiezio started reconnecting with friends. His relationship with Jesus grew stronger. He felt a calling to share his story.

Spiezio used to have millions. According to Baseball-Reference, he made more than $16.5 million playing baseball. Yet now he lives month to month and is happier now than he has ever been.

Spiezio has a documentary coming out Sept. 10, titled "Spiezio," which details his tumultuous journey. He released a memoir in July, called "The Hardest Comeback."

For his memoir, there was a reason why he settled on "The Hardest Comeback."

"I thought of a bunch of different titles for the book and one of them was ‘It's never too late,’ and ‘Never Give Up. Like there was all sorts of of titles. We went with ‘The Hardest Comeback' because we wanted to people to realize how hard it really was. I had the comeback with the Game 6 home run in the World Series, but the hardest comeback was this by far," Spiezio said.

For people who are struggling with addiction or mental health, Spiezio wants them to know that there is hope.

"I want people to know that there's hope, if you're vulnerable and you let people in your life that that can steer you in the right direction and can hold your hand while you're going through stuff, you have to be willing to want to stop. And I can tell you from a guy that thought I couldn't stop drinking in order to save my own life to a guy that wonders why in the world I ever put any of that stuff in my system," Spiezio said.

Scott Spiezio with his family. (Spiezio Family)

Spiezio now runs a baseball facility and gives one-on-one lessons to kids. He shares his faith anytime he gets a chance, and is very involved with his church. He goes to schools to talk about the dangers of drugs and alcohol.

He is repairing his relationships with his kids. He has a 26-year-old, 24-year-old, 22-year-old, and an 11-year-old. Spiezio said the 11-year-old is teaching him how to fish.

He lives back in his hometown, because the community helped him get back to his roots and remember who he really is.

Scott Spiezio with his sons, Cody (L) and Tyler (R). (Spiezio Family)

"I had millions and millions of dollars. Now, I live month to month. But I'm happier now than when I had seven cars and three houses and was hanging out with all these, you know, famous people. I have true joy now because I know how the story ends. And the biggest thrill for me is when people tell me that, you know, after talking to you I've saved my marriage," Spiezio said.

"Or I've restored my faith in God or have 12 months sober or five years sober or 30 days sober. There's nothing like getting those texts where people are like, thank you for taking the time."

"It's never too late. I always say as long as you got a breath, you got a pen to write a great ending. As long as you got a pulse, you got a purpose. It's never too late to get sober. It's never too late to mend broken relationships."

At least 13 people have been killed in a Ukrainian drone strike on the Russian republic of Tatarstan, officials have said.

One child w...
articles.body_text:
A refining and petrochemical plant in Nizhnekamsk (stock photo)

At least 13 people have been killed in a Ukrainian drone strike on the Russian republic of Tatarstan, officials have said.

One child was among the victims with 75 more people injured, Russian authorities said, in one of the deadliest single attacks on Russia since the start of Moscow's full-scale war in Ukraine.

Kyiv has not yet commented on the strike on the city of Nizhnekamsk, which is more than 1,100 kilometres (680m) from the Ukrainian border.

Ukraine's Armed Forces confirmed Nizhnekamsk's Tanevo oil refinery had been hit, while Ukrainian defence technology manufacturer FirePoint said its FP-1 drones had been used in the attack.

The strike lasted several hours overnight and into the morning, local sources say.

Unverified images on social media show large plumes of smoke and flames rising into the sky in daytime, with air raid sirens howling in the background.

Although there is no official information yet on the target of the attack, Kyiv has recently stepped up its strikes on facilities it says contribute revenue and logistics to Russia's war on Ukraine.

Moscow confirmed industrial facilities were targeted as well as residential areas. "Civilian individuals who were not involved in any military operations were present,"   Russia's Investigative Committee said. The BBC has not independently verified this information.

The head of Tatarstan, Rustam Minnikhanov, confirmed the strike and shared his condolences with the families of the deceased.

"This is a tremendous pain for all of us," said Nizhnekamsk mayor Radmir Belayev.

A period of mourning has been declared in Tatarstan.

Ukraine's defence forces previously struck oil refineries in Nizhnekamsk on 12 June.

More than 450 Ukrainian drones were also shot down by the Russian air defences overnight, Moscow said.

Kyiv has become increasingly successful at carrying out long-range strikes on Russia, often targeting warehouses or energy infrastructure, with civilian casualties mounting.

Russia, meanwhile, continues to target Ukraine with regular large-scale aerial attacks on cities and residential centres mounting. Last week, a combined drone and missile strike on Kyiv killed 21 people.

And in Kharkiv, near the front line, five people were killed overnight in a Russian artillery attack.

articles.title: Prince William was 'fuming' over request for Kate Middleton to spell her name differently: book
articles.excerpt:

Prin...
articles.body_text:
Christopher Andersen, author of "Kate!," tells Fox News Digital that the Princess of Wales’ modern approach, family values and "soft power" make her a vital asset to the royal family and the UK.

Prince William was reportedly "fuming" after King Charles III and Queen Camilla suggested that Kate Middleton change the spelling of her first name when she joined the royal family, according to a new book.

"Charles and Camilla each had a royal monogram that consisted of interlocking C’s beneath a crown, and they expressed concern that a third royal cypher with a C was overkill," Christopher Andersen wrote in his biography "Kate! The Courage, Grace, and Power of the Woman Who Will Be Queen." "Would Kate mind if she changed the spelling of her full name from ‘Catherine’ to ‘Katherine.’"

Andersen added, "Offended by yet another command from on high essentially aimed at placating Camilla, a fuming William replied on his wife’s behalf. The request was nothing less than ‘insulting,’ he told his father, not only to Kate but to her entire family."

KATE MIDDLETON IS 'INDISPENSABLE' TO ROYAL FAMILY AS SLIMMED-DOWN MONARCHY FACES MOUNTING PRESSURE: EXPERT

Prince William was "fuming" after then Prince Charles asked if Kate Middleton would change her name from Catherine to Katherine, according to a new book. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)

A Kensington Palace spokesperson told Fox News Digital they don't comment on books.

"The entire nature of Charles and Camilla's request — that Catherine was adding too many C's to the royal crests — shows just how much image and branding means to members of the royal family. The monarchy really is a giant game of one-upmanship," Andersen told Fox News Digital, adding that from the very beginning of their relationship "William has gone to war for Kate."

William’s top concern has always been for the Princess of Wales’ "safety," but he also came out "guns blazing" in her defense after topless photos of her sunbathing were published in France in 2012.

"He angrily ordered Palace lawyers to sue and even wanted to see those involved prosecuted criminally under French privacy laws," Andersen said. "When they started a family, it was William who made sure that Kate was not forced to take on too heavy a royal workload if it meant that she would have to spend too much time away from their children."

PRINCE WILLIAM, KATE MIDDLETON FINALLY FEEL FREE TO SHOW AFFECTION IN PUBLIC: EXPERTS

But, he said the king and Camilla "expected her to go along because she has always been a nice, cooperative team player … but didn't take into account the fact that she personally prefers to be known as Catherine and feels very strongly about the name her parents gave her."

While most of the world knows her by her nickname, Kate, her real name is Catherine.

The princess is "genuinely fond" of Charles and assumed that he got the "absurd" idea from someone else, Andersen explained, adding that she didn’t hold any ill will toward him.

Prince William has "gone to war for Kate" since the beginning of their relationship, royal author Christopher said. (Samir Hussein/WireImage)

"Besides, it wasn't long before they were having to deal with their simultaneous cancer diagnoses, which put everything else in stark perspective," he added.

KING CHARLES CONSIDERED QUEEN CAMILLA 'NON-NEGOTIABLE' AFTER PRINCESS DIANA, AUTHOR CLAIMS

"Kate!: The Courage, Grace, and Power of the Woman Who Will Be Queen" by Christopher Andersen is available now. (Gallery Books)

And although Middleton comes off as "kind and compassionate," she still has a "will of steel," he said.

"Kate is very secure about who she is and how she wants to be perceived by the outside world," Andersen said. "Changing her formal given name for such a bizarre, almost comical reason was a bridge too far."

British broadcaster and photographer Helena Chard called the issue a "nonstarter" and a "lost cause," telling Fox News Digital that Charles and Camilla were thinking with a "business head" since she was known to the world as Kate anyway.

"Although a hopeless endeavour, I can see both sides of the coin," she admitted, explaining that William was not only offended for his wife but for his in-laws as well.

PRINCE WILLIAM REFUSES TO QUIT HOBBY THAT TERRIFIES KATE MIDDLETON: EXPERTS

King Charles III, Queen Camilla, Prince William, Prince of Wales, and Kate Middleton pose for a photograph at Buckingham Palace in 2023. (Getty Images)

But "the concerns were brushed aside. It wasn’t important enough to cause a fight. They had bigger fish to fry."

Royal broadcaster Ian Pelham Turner called it a possible "volatile moment" between Camilla and the princess as she joined the family, "but nowadays William was there to protect her. Since then, Kate has managed to stay one step behind when Charles and Camilla are around so as not to out stage them."

KING CHARLES SENDS 'DEFIANCE' MESSAGE TO PRINCE WILLIAM WITH BUCKINGHAM PALACE ROOM OFFER TO HARRY: EXPERT

He noted, however, that more recently the 44-year-old is "building a stronger brand in her own right as William tries to take on the reins of Kingmanship."

"If true it’s idiotic," royal expert Richard Fitzwilliams told Fox News Digital of the story. "The idea is simply stupid. And why? Because her name began with C and theirs did!!"

Andersen also felt the incident "speaks volumes about how conscious the royals are of all the bells and whistles — not just the gold coaches, the castles, and the crown jewels, but things as small as the letters in their crests and coats of arms. It may seem trivial to the rest of us, but to them things like this mean everything."

Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: 2,200-year-old alcohol found sealed inside ancient tomb — and there's nearly a gallon of it
articles.excerpt:
Talea Beer founders Leann Darland and Tara Hankinson join 'Fox & Friends' to discuss how they rediscovered former President George Washington's beer recipe from over 200 years ago.

Researchers in Chi...
articles.body_text:
Talea Beer founders Leann Darland and Tara Hankinson join 'Fox & Friends' to discuss how they rediscovered former President George Washington's beer recipe from over 200 years ago.

Researchers in China recently uncovered a very unusual find: a large bottle containing an alcoholic drink buried for more than 2,200 years.

The ancient alcohol was found sealed in a bronze vessel in a Qin tomb at the Shanjiabao cemetery in China's Ningxia Hui Autonomous Region. The findings were published in the June issue of the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports.

The tomb dates to the Warring States period (475-221 B.C.), a turbulent era of rival kingdoms before China's first unification.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNCOVER FREEZE-DRIED POTATOES OLDER THAN THE US IN 'EXCELLENT' CONDITION

The preserved liquid was determined to be an ancient cereal-based alcoholic beverage, a fermented grain drink sometimes loosely described as "beer."

Unlike other recent discoveries in which archaeologists found only residue from ancient drinks, the bottle contained an impressive 3,740 milliliters, or 3.74 liters, of preserved liquid.

Archaeologists in China uncovered more than 3.7 liters of an ancient cereal-based alcoholic beverage sealed inside a bronze vessel for over 2,200 years. (Ruru Chen)

The researchers were surprised when they encountered the liquid, said Ruru Chen, a researcher at Northwest University's School of Cultural Heritage in Xi'an, China.

"What surprised us even more was the very large volume and the exceptional state of preservation," Chen told Fox News Digital.

SECRET CACHE OF 130-YEAR-OLD WINE UNCOVERED BENEATH MEDIEVAL CASTLE CHAPEL FLOOR

"Considering that this sample dates to the Warring States period, such a good level of preservation is extremely rare."

There was "no noticeable odor and a small amount of sediment at the bottom," she added, and the liquid "appeared clear and light blue-green."

Researchers say the exceptionally well-preserved liquid dates to the Warring States period, making it an exceptionally rare discovery. (Ruru Chen)

It was found in a bronze bottle with a "garlic-shaped mouth," which Chen said was commonly used by the Qin people to hold alcoholic beverages.

"By combining evidence from organic chemistry, metabolomics, starch grain analysis, yeast remains and other microscopic analyses, we can directly identify the type of beverage once stored inside the vessel and even reconstruct how it was brewed," she said.

"To our knowledge, this represents one of the largest volumes of alcoholic beverage residue ever recovered from a Warring States-period archaeological sample, making it an exceptionally rare discovery."

Based on starch grain analysis, researchers found the beverage was brewed primarily from broomcorn millet, with a smaller contribution from wheat and/or barley, Chen said.

"It would have been most similar to a non-distilled alcoholic beverage made from millet, or from a mixture of millet and wheat/barley."

Researchers identified high concentrations of lactic and oxalic acids, along with dozens of other organic compounds consistent with an ancient cereal-based alcoholic beverage.

"Therefore, it would have been most similar to a non-distilled alcoholic beverage made from millet, or from a mixture of millet and wheat/barley," she said.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

"It would not have resembled a distilled spirit."

Looking ahead, researchers are still hoping to solve some unanswered questions, including why the liquid survived so well for two millennia.

The bronze bottle's distinctive "garlic-shaped mouth" is consistent with vessels used by the Qin people to store alcoholic beverages. (Ruru Chen)

"The relatively dry local environment may have played an important role, but we also suspect that factors such as the bronze vessel itself, its sealing method and the burial conditions contributed to its preservation," Chen said.

"These are questions we hope to investigate further in future research."

Researchers also hope that the discovery "will encourage greater interest in the study of ancient Chinese alcoholic beverages and traditional brewing techniques," Chen said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The research follows a similar recent discovery, when researchers in China uncovered evidence of ancient fermented beverages at a Bronze Age cemetery in northwestern China.

"To our knowledge, this represents one of the largest volumes of alcoholic beverage residue ever recovered from a Warring States-period archaeological sample," said Chen. (Ruru Chen)

Researchers found microscopic residue inside pottery vessels, shedding light on how people brewed beer-like drinks from millet, rice, wheat and barley more than 3,000 years ago.

Andrea Margolis is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital and Fox Business. Readers can follow her on X at @andreamargs or send story tips to andrea.margolis@fox.com.

In June 2025, a sluggish and thin Gabar Choli, with sunken te...
articles.body_text:
Gabar Choli tells of how, for months, he was shackled, pinned and forcibly fed – and the physical and emotional scars the ordeal has left

In June 2025, a sluggish and thin Gabar Choli, with sunken temples and bones visible under his skin, braced himself for the immigration detention center guards to charge into his cell once again.

Choli was in a solitary confinement medical cell inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention facility in south Texas where immigrants arrested in Donald Trump’s anti-immigration crackdown are detained.

Choli, a 40-year-old Kurdish asylum seeker with a thick beard and long dark hair, had been on hunger strike for over two months, demanding improved conditions for detained immigrants and to be released or deported. That day in June 2025, Choli’s nose was swollen, his throat hurt and he could still taste blood from previous days of treatment for which he never gave his consent, he said.

The film-maker and activist for an independent Kurdistan has spoken out for the first time, talking exclusively to the Guardian last week from Canada about the ordeal in the United States that he said “broke him”.

He recounted the vile routine as the detention center guards would rush towards him and wrestle him to the concrete cell floor, shackle his wrists and ankles, and drag him to the detention center infirmary. There, the guards pinned Choli on a bed while medical staff forcibly inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his throat, and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach. Choli was being force-fed by ICE.

“Two guards would hold my feet; two hold my hands; one hold my head – and they would shove tubes in my nose,” Choli said. “It’s not easy to be wrestled to the ground twice a day by men that are stronger than you. And you just take it. You have 60cm of tube going through you and you just feel every centimeter of it.”

An investigation by the Guardian, based on dozens of pages of court records and interviews with medical and legal experts, found that Choli was quietly and intermittently force-fed by ICE for nearly eight months – from late May 2025 until he was deported in January.

He was not alone – he even met a fellow hunger striker, an Afghan man the Guardian also learned about, as they were both forcibly fed in the same ICE facility.

Force-feeding is an excruciating and traumatizing process that has been widely condemned by human rights organizations as torture. For Choli and others, refusing food is a last resort to protest against harsh conditions and lack of progress in their immigration cases, but sometimes brings only harsher conditions.

“I understood the necessity of making a stand for what was right,” Choli said, speaking by phone with the Guardian, talking in a very matter-of-fact way about his recent experience. At various times, Choli would sarcastically chuckle, almost incredulous now when remembering the officials’ actions. “I was respectful. I just told them I am protesting for humane treatment, nothing else. But they were determined to break me,” he said.

Choli suffered swollen sinuses, a damaged esophagus, stomach problems and psychological torment, according to court records and his own account.

“It just broke me, mentally broke me,” Choli said gravely. After sometimes twice-daily sessions “they would take me to [a] solitary cell and I would just choke on my blood and drink the blood from inside [my throat],” he said, describing how the feeding tube would scrape him inside. Many of his court records remain sealed and he did not have a lawyer – and medical staff there did not respond to the Guardian’s reporting – so some details in Choli’s account remain uncorroborated.

The Trump administration has not officially acknowledged force-feeding anyone in immigration jails. But an investigation by the Guardian found that since January 2025, the administration used court orders in plans to subject at least 10 hunger strikers in ICE detention to involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding.

However, it has since emerged that the number is even higher. Sources with the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), ICE’s parent agency, later told the Guardian that between January 2025 and 4 August 2026, ICE received “a court order for involuntary treatment for 18 hunger strikers”.

DHS did not respond to questions concerning Choli’s specific case, but a spokesperson said in a statement: “ICE respects an individual’s right to refuse medical treatment where appropriate. However, when an individual’s medical condition presents a serious risk of death or permanent harm, or when other compelling legal or operational interests are implicated, ICE may seek judicial authorization for appropriate medical interventions consistent with applicable law.”

“Any involuntary medical treatment is undertaken only pursuant to legal authority and under the direction of qualified medical professionals,” the spokesperson added.

The US attorney’s office in the southern district of Texas did not respond to a detailed request for comment.

“This likely amounts to torture,” said Dr Chanelle Diaz, an assistant professor of medicine at Columbia University’s medical center, in New York. Diaz has medically evaluated other ICE force-feeding cases and advocated for hunger strikers’ release. She reviewed the limited court records available for Choli’s case, at the Guardian’s request. “I would say that it’s even difficult to capture the degree of risk that he was being put at, long-term,” she said.

Choli, a deeply religious Muslim, had been living in Vancouver, where he was a film-maker and activist campaigning for an independent nation of Kurdistan, having come to Canada in 2007 from what he considers occupied territory in Iran. His life was and is complicated. He said he had previously served nine months in prison in Canada following a 2012 drug-smuggling charge and court records show the case was related to receiving just over one kilogram of opium in the mail from Turkey.

Then his activism for Kurdish independence drew death threats and in 2022 he crossed the border into the US in Blaine, Washington and requested asylum. He was quickly released by the authorities and made his way to Los Angeles to try to pursue his ambitions in film while his asylum case played out, attending regular mandatory check-ins with ICE and qualifying for a work permit. Court records say a judge denied his asylum claim in 2024 but granted him protection from deportation to Iran.

Then Donald Trump returned to the White House after campaigning on a promise of mass deportation and, at a 25 February 2025 check-in with ICE, Choli was arrested. He was first sent to the Desert View Annex in California, an immigration detention center that has been repeatedly criticized for substandard conditions. While in detention, Choli says he was pressured by ICE officials to sign a deportation order to be sent to Iran. He refused and after demanding better conditions and a fairer resolution to his immigration case, he began his hunger strike on 24 March, court records show.

“I am not suicidal,” Choli would later write in a declaration to a federal judge. “I am using hunger strike as the only available option to protest the abuse and mistreatment.”

Choli was then transferred to the privately-run Port Isabel facility in Texas for a “higher level of medical care”, an ICE court declaration says. There, Choli refused to end his strike and was placed in a solitary medical cell, which ICE describes as administrative segregation, meaning he was under frequent observation by medical staff. It features a perpetually illuminated cell, alongside other cells in that unit with suicidal or other medically vulnerable detainees.

Almost 10 days later, ICE sought their first court order to force-feed Choli. He broke his strike, believing the federal court’s involvement could help his immigration case move along. “God opened a door for me,” he said he was thinking, and wrote a letter to the federal judge requesting assistance.

But three weeks later, Choli said he learned the case was closed and no one had responded to his letter. Furious, he stopped accepting meals again. On 23 May 2025, ICE and the US attorney’s office for the southern district of Texas filed a second request for a court order to conduct involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding. According to ICE’s request, a social worker at the detention facility evaluated Choli and found he was “operating under his own free will”.

The World Health Organization and other medical organizations “have said that it is an individual’s right to decide to go on hunger strike, as long as they are of sound mind – which he was”, Dr Parveen Parmar said about Choli after reviewing some of his records shared by the Guardian. Parmar is a doctor and expert with Physicians for Human Rights, a New York-based advocacy group. Like Diaz, she has provided expert medical testimony in other ICE force-feeding cases and also reviewed the limited court records available for Choli’s case.

“Patient autonomy is one of the core tenets of medicine,” Parmar added.

But as Choli’s hunger strike went on, it threatened his health and also, in the government’s opinion, posed “a serious threat to the security and good order” of the facility, ICE argued in court filings. “The public interest is served by not allowing [Choli’s] attempts to manipulate the immigration system and by maintaining prison and inmate safety and security,” the case documents say.

Such filings not only contradict federal silenceor denials about hunger strikes going on intermittently in various ICE detention facilities, but they appear to speak to a desire by authorities to limit such protests from spreading.

In Choli’s case, doctors working for ICE, Dr Benjamin Salinas and Dr Shauna Kincheloe, also submitted declarations to the court last May requesting the procedures take place – and continue. One day later, the federal judge, Rolando Olvera, ordered Choli to be force-fed, without hearing from Choli himself.

When contacted, Salinas told the Guardian: “Thanks for reaching out, but I’m not interested.” Kincheloe did not respond to requests from the Guardian for comment. Olvera’s assistant declined to make the judge available for comment.

“Immigration detention is civil, it is not necessary,” Diaz said, referring to the fact that many alleged immigration violations, such as remaining in the US without legal status, involve civil, not criminal law. She said that ICE’s court arguments “feel like a false dichotomy”, adding that detained immigrants “could be released, that is always a choice. And that should be the default, not force-feeding.”

In most cases seen by the Guardian, federal judges will often approve ICE’s requests without hearing from the hunger strikers first, or their lawyers – those that have one.

Choli did not have an attorney during his detention and the entire force-feeding proceedings, records show, and was not provided with one by the government.

“In my view, those proceedings shouldn’t continue without the person having legal representation if they don’t have it already,” said Rebecca Sharpless, the founding director of University of Miami’s immigration clinic. Sharpless is not familiar with Choli’s case but represented an ICE hunger striker in 2021 who was ordered force-fed. “It makes a big difference when people understand that there are people who are fighting for them – both in terms of their legal case but also their right to make choices about their body.”

The very first time Choli was force-fed, he had voluntarily gone with the guards to the detention center’s infirmary. But after experiencing the painful and traumatic process for the first time, he began to resist.

“First I did not resist. But after I saw they were torturing me, I started protesting: ‘I’m not coming with you people,’” he said.

Then the guards, employees of the private prison company Akima Global Services, “started wrestling”, he said. Many ICE detention centers are run by private US contractors. Akima and its parent company did not respond to detailed requests for comment.

During the first days of Choli’s force-feeding, his nose and throat were swollen from the repeated tube insertions and removals, according to Choli and court records. He recalled an occasion in which, while being restrained, an ICE nurse “shoved the tube so hard” that “he tore my nose from the inside”. His nose bled for days, Choli wrote in a declaration to the court recounting the incident.

Parma of Physicians for Human Rights said repeated force-feeding can produce such symptoms and is “just inhumane from beginning to end”.

The rapid administration of nutrients after Choli had been starving himself also triggered stomach problems. During one early session last June, Choli said he immediately had diarrhea. He was then taken to a cell with no toilet, he said, where he further defecated on himself.

“I kept looking at my soiled body and clothing and went on crying,” Choli wrote in the declaration to the judge. “I cried for being objectified and inhumanely treated, for seeking a humane treatment.”

Weeks passed and Olvera, the judge, continued to extend the force-feeding order. Choli, with swollen sinuses, presented his declaration to the court at one hearing in mid June, telling Olvera he could not afford a lawyer and requested a court-appointed attorney.

Olvera denied Choli’s request, writing in his court order that attorneys are not guaranteed in civil proceedings and that, even if Choli had one, it would be of no use – he would continue to grant force-feeding orders.

The twice daily process became a grim routine.

Weeks turned to months. At one point, Choli recalled a guard’s rough treatment injuring his ribs, making breathing painful for weeks. At another, guards who were restraining him “pressed so hard on my shoulder, I thought my chest was going to break in half”.

“I lost my breath” and he heard the doctor say, “‘Take him to the hospital, he’s dead.’ [Then] I completely went ‘out’,” Choli said in an interview.

Another time he recalls that despite his warnings a medical staffer incorrectly inserted the tube and it entered his lung, causing him to choke and then cough that end of the tube up into his mouth.

Choli remembers that as he was passing out, he “lost [his] senses” and vaguely remembers “reaching for [the guard’s] hand with my mouth”. DHS, ICE and Akima did not respond to this specific allegation.

Choli said that at one point he made a deal with the facility staff: on Fridays, he agreed to drink the nutritional liquids if they allowed him to pray with other detainees. “That was my opportunity to socialize,” Choli said, calling those Fridays his “peace days”.

Late October rolled around. It was Choli’s birthday and, incredibly, he recalls that Kincheloe, one of the facility doctors, and other nurses sang “Happy Birthday” to him in Spanish. The Guardian has not been able to verify thisdetail. Choli does not remember whether he drank the nutritional liquids that day or was force-fed.

“In Choli’s case, where he was force-fed for eight months, you’re looking at easily over 100 NG tube placements, possibly over 200… that is just not medical care, that is torture,” Diaz said, referring to nasogastric tubing.

ICE finally deported Choli to Canada on 6 January this year, where he reunited with his siblings who also live in Canada.

He told the Guardian how, the next day, he nervously ate his first solid meal in months, a small, simple salad. He was fine, but his jaw hurt for days.

“It may sound strange, but I had to learn how to eat [again],” Choli said. He is still struggling today, physically and mentally, but hopes that speaking out may help others in ICE detention.

“The price of [the hunger strike] was my life,” Choli said in an angry but level and determined tone. “The price of it was my kidneys, my gallbladder. My intestines. My being. My bladder, you know, is damaged. Every time I twist and turn, I feel pain. But this is the price you pay for making a stand for what is right.”

“Trump is just one person,” he said, indicating his problem is with the broader treatment of immigrants and refugees by the US. “Trump is not here torturing me.”

ICE and the US attorney’s office requested Choli’s force-feeding court case be dismissed in January, saying he was no longer in their custody. An envelope addressed to Choli, containing the dismissal notice, was sent to the Port Isabel detention center. The envelope was returned to the court.

“Return to sender”, “Not here,” the envelope read.

Read more from our Force-fed by ICE series

articles.title: Apple Pay text scam threatens $8,250 loss in 35 minutes
articles.excerpt:
JPMorgan Chase Head of Consumer Fraud and Scam Prevention Darius Kingsley discusses bank scams in an interview with Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson for the "Beyond Connected" podcast.

Paul C. in Washington,...
articles.body_text:
JPMorgan Chase Head of Consumer Fraud and Scam Prevention Darius Kingsley discusses bank scams in an interview with Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson for the "Beyond Connected" podcast.

Paul C. in Washington, D.C., received an alarming text claiming Apple Pay had already charged him $8,250 and another $8,250 would go through in 35 minutes. That is the kind of message designed to make your stomach drop before you have time to think.

Paul did the smart thing. He stopped, avoided the callback number and sent the text to us. Let's break down every red flag and show you how to verify a charge without handing control to a scammer.

New! Free live CyberGuy class: Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats

Join us Saturday, Aug. 29, at 10 a.m. ET for a free CyberGuy LIVE class covering five simple steps to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson will explain how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. You’ll also receive our financial protection checklist, and every registrant will get a link to the class recording afterward.

Reserve your free spot today at CyberGuyLive.com.

FAKE BOOKING.COM TRAVEL CREDIT SCAM TARGETS TRAVELERS

A scam text falsely warns of an $8,250 Apple Pay charge and threatens another $8,250 transaction within 35 minutes to pressure recipients into calling scammers. (Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson)

The message claimed $8,250 had already been charged through Apple Pay and warned that a duplicate $8,250 transaction would "auto-approve" in 35 minutes. It told Paul to call an 855 number, quote "Case CA-3321" and "verbally kill the pending charge." We partially masked the callback number so no one calls it accidentally.

The message looks chaotic, but nearly every phrase has a purpose. The sender uses dramatic wording, fake authority and a tight deadline to push Paul toward one action: calling the number in the text.

The message came from a number beginning with +44, the international calling code for the United Kingdom. Yet it claims to come from "Apple Pay Account Services" and tells Paul in Washington, D.C., to call a separate 855 toll-free number. A different callback number does not automatically prove fraud. However, an overseas sender directing a U.S. recipient to an unrelated support line should make you stop before calling.

The text uses the Apple Pay name several times and signs off as "Apple Pay Account Services." It also arrived as a blue iMessage with the word "Encrypted" shown beneath it. Those details can make the message feel official. However, encryption only means the message was protected while traveling between devices. It does not confirm that Apple sent it. The signature also sounds generic. It does not name Paul's bank, identify the card involved or provide an official Apple support channel.

The first line reads: "$8,250.00 APPLE PAY - 35-MINUTE DEADLINE". The message then claims $8,250 has already disappeared and warns that a duplicate $8,250 charge will be approved in 35 minutes. That raises the threatened loss to $16,500. The exact 35-mcxxcxxcxinute deadline feels calculated. It gives Paul enough time to call while discouraging him from checking Wallet, opening his bank's app or asking someone else for advice.

The message says Paul's Apple Pay account has "hemorrhaged" money. It calls the situation a "catastrophic fraud event" and claims his contactless limit has been "crushed" to $0. It later tells him to "verbally kill the pending charge." Those words sound dramatic because they are meant to produce fear. A legitimate financial alert would normally use clear terms such as charged, declined, frozen or pending. It would not describe an account as hemorrhaging money or ask you to kill a charge.

The first transaction allegedly happened at: "an agricultural processing surplus in Stockton, CA". The second supposedly involved: "a payday lending chain in Modesto". Neither phrase identifies an actual merchant. They sound specific at first because they include industries and real California cities. However, they fall apart when you look closer. A legitimate transaction alert would usually show the merchant's name. It would not rely on vague descriptions such as "agricultural processing surplus."

The sender claims Paul's contactless spending limit has been "crushed to $0." In the same message, it says the second $8,250 transaction is pending and "will auto-approve in 35 minutes." Those claims do not fit together. If the sender had already blocked contactless activity, why would another contactless charge automatically go through? The contradiction matters because it shows the message was written to create panic rather than explain a real account problem.

The message says: "Do not ignore this." It then orders Paul: "You must call." The sender provides a case number, tells him to "verbally kill" the charge and warns that the money will be "gone forever" if he fails to respond. It also threatens to blacklist his account and calls this his "only warning." That language gives Paul one supposed solution: call the number in the text. The message never tells him to open Wallet, check his bank's official app or call the number printed on his card. That is the biggest red flag of all. Every part of the message funnels him toward a stranger waiting on the other end of the phone.

AMAZON RECALL TEXT SCAM COMES WITH RED FLAGS

Apple Pay users should verify suspicious charges through Wallet, their bank’s official app or the number printed on their card — not contact information in an unexpected text. (Qilai Shen/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The text serves as bait. The phone call allows the scammer to take control of the conversation. Once you call, the person may claim to see your account. They could ask for your name, card number or Apple Account email. Next, they may request a verification code and describe it as a way to cancel the charge.

A scammer could also ask you to install a remote-access app. That would let the person view your screen or guide you through financial transactions. Some callback scams eventually instruct people to transfer money into a "safe" account. Others claim they sent an oversized refund and demand that the extra money be returned.

The FTC warns that fake support agents may seek remote access, steal card information or convince people to move money. CyberGuy previously heard from another person whose Apple Pay scam text nearly led to a $15,000 loss. In that case, the caller used personal information and pressure to keep her on the phone while she drove to her bank.

Do not call the number in the text. Instead, check through channels you already trust:

Apple notes that Wallet may not display the complete transaction history for every card. Your bank or card issuer remains the best source for questions about an Apple Pay charge. Do not rely on a phone number from a text, caller ID or sponsored search result.

Before deleting the message, save a screenshot that includes the sender information.

Apple recommends emailing screenshots of suspicious Apple text messages to its phishing address. It also lets iPhone owners report junk directly inside Messages. For more ways to handle messages like this, see our guide on how to protect yourself from tech support scams.

Hang up as soon as you suspect fraud. Then take action based on what you shared:

FAKE SHINYHUNTERS SEXTORTION EMAIL USES CARNIVAL BREACH DATA

Apple says malicious websites could exploit a Safari flaw to steal passwords or payment information from unpatched iPhones and iPads. (Photographer: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

These steps can help you check the warning safely without following the scammer's script.

A deadline can make a fake warning feel real. Give yourself time to check the account independently. A legitimate fraud department will still be there after you close the text and open the official app.

Do not call the number in the text or reply to the sender. Instead, open Wallet or your bank's official app and review recent transactions. You can also call the number printed on the back of your card. Never rely on contact information supplied in an unexpected message.

A security code can approve a login, password reset or payment. Never read one to a caller, even when the person claims it will cancel a fraudulent charge. Also, do not install an app or share your screen because someone says they need access to fix the problem. Apple representatives will not ask for your password, device passcode or two-factor authentication code.

The message Paul received contains no link. Therefore, antivirus software would not stop the pressure created by the text or phone call. However, scam campaigns can quickly change tactics. A later message may include a fake Apple login page or another dangerous site. Strong security software can detect malicious links and warn you about known scam pages. Get my picks for the best 2026 antivirus protection winners for your Windows, Mac, Android and iOS devices at CyberGuy.com.

The text sent to Paul did not include his name or other private details. However, callers may use information from data brokers or past breaches to make their stories sound credible. A data removal service can reduce the amount of personal information available through people-search sites. It cannot erase every record or stop every scam. Still, less exposed data gives criminals fewer details to use against you. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting CyberGuy.com.

Consider stronger monitoring if you shared sensitive information or continue receiving targeted financial scams. Identity theft protection can alert you when someone opens a new credit account. It may also notify you when monitored information appears in known breaches. The service cannot prevent every form of identity theft. Therefore, you still need to review alerts and secure affected accounts. See my tips and best picks on Best Identity Theft Protection at CyberGuy.com.

Reporting the message may help Apple and your carrier identify similar scams. On an iPhone, tap Report Spam or Report Junk beneath the message, depending on the option shown. Then block the sender and delete the conversation. You can also forward the text to 7726, which spells SPAM. Because this message impersonates Apple, take a screenshot and email it to reportphishing@apple.com.

This Apple Pay scam piles on fear from the opening line. The $8,250 charge grabs your attention, while the 35-minute deadline tries to stop you from checking whether any of it is real. Even the strange phrases serve a purpose because they keep the message sounding urgent and severe. Paul made the right move by pausing instead of calling. When an unexpected fraud alert arrives, leave the message and check through Wallet, your bank's official app or the number printed on your card. Never give a caller a verification code or access to your screen.

Have you received a convincing Apple Pay alert or another scam text that nearly fooled you? Write to us at CyberGuy.com and tell us what the message said and how you spotted the warning signs.
